#5662. A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut

A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible. New preclinical research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center reveals how fasting and beneficial microbes work together to activate the body's natural tissue repair mechanisms.

The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment. By improving the intestine's ability to recover from radiation exposure, researchers hope to reduce serious side effects and potentially make radiation therapy safer and more effective.

Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine.

"Fasting helps prepare intestinal cells to respond more quickly and effectively after injury, almost like training the cells with an emergency preparedness plan," Piwnica-Worms said. "This study helps explain how that plan is organized and identifies a key bacterium involved in coordinating the response."

Why Radiation Therapy Can Damage the Intestines

Radiation therapy is widely used to treat cancers in the abdomen, including pancreatic, colorectal, and gynecologic cancers. Although radiation can destroy cancer cells, it can also harm nearby healthy tissue. The small intestine is particularly vulnerable because its delicate lining is highly sensitive to radiation exposure.

When this protective lining becomes damaged, patients may experience nausea, diarrhea, and infections. Severe injuries can cause life-threatening complications. These risks can also restrict the amount of radiation doctors can safely administer, potentially limiting treatment options.

Previous preclinical research from the Piwnica-Worms Laboratory showed that fasting before radiation exposure helped the intestines recover afterward. However, researchers had not fully determined why going without food produced this protective effect.

The latest study provides an important piece of that puzzle by identifying a specific gut bacterium and explaining how it helps intestinal cells prepare for injury.

Researchers found that 24 hours of fasting increased the abundance of a beneficial bacterium called Akkermansia muciniphila, also known as AKK, in the small intestine. This microbe produces a substance called propionate, which helps trigger changes inside intestinal cells that make them better prepared to regenerate following radiation damage.

Propionate works alongside other metabolic changes caused by fasting to modify proteins known as histones. These proteins serve as structures around which DNA is packaged inside cells. Small chemical markers added to histones can influence which genes become active without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

These modifications make portions of DNA more accessible, allowing cells to activate genes involved in tissue regeneration. During fasting, a population of intestinal cells carrying these repair programs becomes more abundant.

In effect, fasting helps prepare these cells with the biological instructions they will need if an injury occurs. When the intestines are subsequently exposed to radiation, the prepared cells can expand and help rebuild the damaged intestinal lining.

One Gut Bacterium Proves Essential for Recovery

To determine how important AKK was to this process, the researchers selectively removed the bacterium. Without it, fasting no longer produced the same regenerative benefits.

Even more revealing, the protective response returned only when the bacterium was restored in combination with fasting. This demonstrated that neither component alone was sufficient to reproduce the full effect observed in the study.

The results suggest that fasting does more than temporarily change the gut's metabolism. Together with AKK, it alters the activity of intestinal cells before radiation exposure, placing them in a state that supports more efficient recovery after damage occurs.

By uncovering this connection between nutrition, gut bacteria, and cellular regeneration, the researchers have identified a potential new way to strengthen the body's response to tissue injury. The discovery could be especially valuable for protecting healthy organs during cancer treatment.

Could Gut Bacteria Make Cancer Treatment Safer?

Although the results are promising, the research remains preclinical. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether the same protective mechanism operates in humans and whether it can safely improve outcomes for patients receiving radiation therapy.

One possibility is that the newly discovered pathway could be used to help other healthy tissues recover from cancer treatment. Researchers are particularly interested in tissues with rapidly dividing cells, including bone marrow, which can also suffer treatment-related damage.

If further investigations support the findings, clinical trials could eventually explore whether activating this repair mechanism benefits patients undergoing abdominal radiation therapy.

Importantly, the discovery may also provide ways to achieve these effects without requiring patients to fast. Treatments involving beneficial bacteria or the molecules they produce could potentially stimulate similar repair processes while avoiding the practical difficulties of food restriction during cancer care.

"Fasting is not always practical for cancer patients, and this work supports several other potential ways to enhance recovery after treatment," Rai said. "Whether through dietary interventions, targeted microbes or their metabolites, the goal is to help repair healthy tissue more effectively while patients receive the cancer therapies they need."

The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT).

#5661. FDA Rejects Promising Cancer Drug Developed in China

— Ivonescimab failed to meet overall survival endpoint in pretreated EGFR-mutant lung cancer trial

The FDA declined to approve a closely watched drug developed in China for an indication in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), drugmaker Summit Therapeutics announced, though the investigational bispecific antibody could soon have other chances at approval.

The company said the FDA issued a complete response letter explaining that it could not approve ivonescimab, which targets PD-1 and VEGF, because a late-stage trial in previously treated EGFR-mutant locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC failed to demonstrate a significant overall survival (OS) benefit.

In the phase III HARMONi trial, the combination of ivonescimab and platinum-containing chemotherapy did prolong progression-free survival (PFS), the other co-primary endpoint. Among patients treated with standard chemotherapy after progressing on third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, median PFS was 6.8 months with ivonescimab versus 4.4 months with placebo (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.41-0.66, P<0.0001), though a greater PFS benefit was demonstrated in Asian patients compared with a North American/European subset.

A numerical difference in median OS favoring ivonescimab (16.8 vs 14 months with placebo) failed to meet statistical significance (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.62-1.01, P=0.057).

"The FDA indicated that the PFS benefit in the absence of a statistically significant OS benefit does not support a positive benefit-risk profile in support of approval," Summit said in its press release.

The drug is approved for several NSCLC indications in China.

Results from the HARMONi-6 trial, presented at this year's American Society of Clinical Oncology annual meeting, showed that ivonescimab combined with chemotherapy significantly improved OS in an all-Asian population with advanced squamous NSCLC compared with tislelizumab (Tevimbra) plus chemotherapy.

Meanwhile, in updated results from the HARMONi-2 trial presented this year at the World Conference on Lung Cancer, ivonescimab significantly improved OS compared with pembrolizumab (Keytruda) in Chinese patients with PD-L1-positive advanced NSCLC.

The HARMONi-3 trial is evaluating ivonescimab versus pembrolizumab as a frontline NSCLC treatment in a global population, including U.S. patients.

The HARMONi-7 trial is also assessing ivonescimab as a first-line treatment for metastatic NSCLC in a PD-L1-high population.

Summit purchased the U.S. rights to the drug from Akeso Biopharma, which developed the drug and markets it in China.

Ivonescimab is also being evaluated in other solid tumors, including colorectal cancer, urothelial carcinoma, and renal cell carcinoma.

When it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

In recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing new opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

With digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

If you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.

#5656. For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise

For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight. But growing scientific evidence suggests that full-fat dairy may not carry the health risks many have come to expect.

A new Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence. Researchers found that adults who consumed three servings of full-fat dairy each day for 12 weeks did not experience harmful changes in body weight, body composition, energy metabolism, or blood cholesterol levels compared with participants following a diet containing little dairy.

Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy showed improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several important nutrients.

The findings, published in The Journal of Nutrition, raise new questions about longstanding dietary recommendations and suggest that the health effects of dairy may be more complicated than its saturated fat content alone would indicate.

For decades, nutrition guidelines in Canada and many other countries have recommended choosing low-fat or fat-free milk, yogurt, and other dairy products. The main concern has been saturated fat, which can raise levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood.

Often called "bad" cholesterol, LDL can contribute to fatty deposits in the arteries. Over time, this buildup can increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and other cardiovascular problems.

Because full-fat dairy contains more saturated fat than reduced-fat alternatives, health authorities have traditionally encouraged people to limit their intake.

However, research examining what happens when people actually consume full-fat dairy has produced a more complicated picture.

Anderson, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto's Temerty Faculty of Medicine, points out that numerous studies involving humans have failed to find a clear association between full-fat dairy consumption and poor health outcomes.

Other research has even identified potential protective effects. That includes a recent study led by Temerty Medicine professor Kozeta Milliku, which found an association between whole-fat milk consumption and a lower risk of childhood obesity.

These findings have prompted scientists to investigate whether dairy foods behave differently in the body than their individual nutrients might suggest.

What Happened When Adults Ate Full-Fat Dairy Every Day?

To explore the question, Anderson and his colleagues conducted a 12-week study involving 74 adults with overweight or obesity.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three dietary approaches. The first group followed a calorie-restricted diet containing little dairy. The second consumed three daily servings of dairy while maintaining an energy-neutral diet, meaning their calorie intake was intended to match the energy their bodies used. The third also consumed three servings of dairy each day but otherwise ate without specific calorie restrictions.

All participants received guidance based on Canada's food guide, and the researchers supplied full-fat dairy products during the study.

At the end of 12 weeks, the team compared several measures of metabolic health, including body weight, body composition, and cholesterol levels.

The results challenged expectations. Participants who consumed three servings of dairy daily did not show meaningful differences in weight gain, body composition, or blood cholesterol compared with those who ate little dairy.

The higher-dairy groups also experienced improvements in blood pressure and consumed more calcium, protein, and vitamin D. These nutrients play essential roles in maintaining healthy bones, supporting muscle function, and regulating numerous processes throughout the body.

"Those that had three servings of dairy didn't have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance," says Anderson.

Blood lipids are fats and fat-like substances circulating in the bloodstream, including cholesterol and triglycerides. Insulin resistance occurs when the body's cells become less responsive to insulin, making it harder to regulate blood sugar and increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Although the results are encouraging, the study was relatively small and lasted only three months. Longer and larger studies are needed to determine whether the findings translate into lasting health benefits or changes in cardiovascular disease risk.

Why might full-fat dairy have different health effects than researchers would predict from its saturated fat content?

One possible explanation is the dairy matrix hypothesis, an idea that emphasizes how the physical structure of food influences the way the body processes its nutrients.

Rather than treating milk, cheese, or yogurt as simple collections of fat, protein, vitamins, and minerals, this theory considers how those components interact within the food itself.

"With dairy products, it's got two proteins -- casein and whey -- that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in," says Anderson.

Casein and whey are the two major types of protein found in milk. Both provide amino acids that the body uses to build and maintain tissues, but they are digested and absorbed at different rates.

According to Anderson, the complex arrangement of proteins, fats, and other nutrients in dairy products can help regulate how quickly those nutrients are released during digestion.

This means the body's response to eating a whole dairy food may differ from its response to consuming an equivalent amount of saturated fat on its own.

The broader implication is that a food's health effects cannot always be predicted by examining a single ingredient. Its structure, nutritional composition, and interactions among nutrients may all matter.

Why the Findings Could Be Important for Older Adults

The researchers believe these results could be particularly relevant for older people, who often need to obtain sufficient protein and essential nutrients while consuming fewer calories.

As people age, their overall energy requirements frequently decrease. However, maintaining muscle mass, bone strength, and other important bodily functions still requires adequate nutrition.

That can make it difficult to meet nutritional needs, particularly for people with smaller appetites.

Anderson explains that dairy products offer a familiar, convenient source of concentrated nutrition. They provide protein, calcium, and other nutrients in foods that many older adults already enjoy and regularly consume.

The new findings suggest that including full-fat dairy in a balanced diet may help people meet these nutritional requirements without necessarily worsening cholesterol levels or markers associated with diabetes risk.

However, the study did not directly establish whether long-term consumption prevents or increases diabetes, heart disease, or other chronic conditions.

Rethinking Nutrition Advice Beyond Individual Nutrients

Beyond the debate over dairy fat, the research highlights a broader challenge in nutrition science: judging the health effects of entire foods rather than focusing exclusively on individual nutrients.

Traditional dietary advice has often emphasized reducing specific components, such as saturated fat. Although these recommendations are grounded in evidence about cardiovascular risk, researchers increasingly recognize that different foods containing the same nutrients may not have identical effects on health.

The University of Toronto findings contribute to this discussion by showing that full-fat dairy can be incorporated into certain diets without the unfavorable short-term metabolic changes that might be expected from its saturated fat content.

That does not mean saturated fat is harmless or that everyone should switch to full-fat dairy. Instead, it suggests that the overall food, its nutritional structure, and the broader dietary pattern deserve consideration.

For people trying to navigate changing nutrition recommendations and conflicting health messages, Anderson favors a practical approach rather than complicated dietary rules.

"Keep it simple, eat a variety of foods and not too much of anything."

This research was supported by Dairy Research Cluster 3 under the Canadian Agricultural Partnership AgriScience Program, and the Mitacs Accelerate program.

Materials provided by University of Toronto. Original written by Betty Zou. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5655. Fellow Physicians, Let AI Fill in the Blanks

— This new technology can make it easier to get it all done

A few weeks ago, I saw a patient for a regularly scheduled follow-up for a problem they'd been having, and they told me they were scheduled to see a specialist to address this problem the following week.

When I looked through my schedule at the patient's chart that day, I noticed there was already a note for that date in the future that had been created a few days earlier. Curious, I opened the note up to see what it contained.

Had the patient been mistaken or had I misunderstood? Had they already seen this specialist?

The note was apparently authored by a member of that specialist's office staff, and seemed to be a nearly completely fleshed-out office visit record addressing the problem, except for a few placeholder stars (***) that apparently were what was going to be added on the day of the actual visit.

"This patient with a past medical history of X, Y, and Z presents with a complaint of *** that has been going on for *** days, at its worst *** out of 10 in intensity, radiating to their ***, made worse by ***, alleviated by ***."

Then there was a lot of other templated material pulled from the patient's chart, including their chart-noted past medical history, past surgical history, social history, medications, allergies, and the results of recent labs and several relevant imaging studies.

At the end there was an assessment and plan: "The patient presents with *** and the following options were offered to the patient, ***, ***, ***. The risks, benefits, and alternatives of *** were discussed with the patient, including the following potential outcomes and the patient wishes to proceed."

You get the picture -- fill in the blanks.

With the incredible amount of documentation we're required to do, shortcuts and ways to make things easier are definitely a good thing. In most cases, no one really reads the charts that carefully, but it is useful to have it all there so that critical information can be ascertained and so we all know what is going on.

In our electronic medical record, there are some amazing tools (and seemingly more every week), including ambient listening that crunches our conversations with patients and turns them into medical text, artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted responses to patient portal messages, and form fillers that can churn out a printed copy of standard medical forms.

As we keep building on these systems, and finding more sophisticated ways to make the lives of our patients and our own lives better -- especially freeing us up from administrative tasks that don't need clinical brainpower -- I'm hopeful the rest of this rote stuff will fall away, and that the documentation and everything else that needs to be done can happen smoothly and quickly.

I envision a day when really smart predictive and generative AI systems will be listening along, working by our sides, making sure we don't miss anything, and helping us accomplish all the administrative and bureaucratic tasks heaped upon us. It may even help us with clinical decision-making, ordering tests as necessary, interpreting follow-up results, generating patient instructions, refilling prescriptions.

While I'm sitting there and discussing the patient's medical condition and our plan, it's nice that right now, ambient listening turns that into the patient's History of Present Illness for my office note. But it would also be great if it generated something that could be popped into the After Visit Summary, instructions for the patients to take home.

When I mention the lab testing I want to get, rechecking their cholesterol to see response to a statin, getting electrolytes after newly starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor, rechecking their hemoglobin A1c for ongoing monitoring of their diabetes, the orders should be entered in the system at the same time as I say these words, associated with the correct medical condition and thus the correct diagnosis code, and queued up for me to review and sign.

I never want any of this to be autonomous, running on its own, practicing medicine. But there are so many opportunities for this to safely take a leap, to truly make our healthcare system more equitable and more efficient and, believe it or not, more caring.

Patients shouldn't have to struggle to get a form completed, to get a refill of their chronic medications, to get a follow-up referral to a specialist they have been seeing for an ongoing medical condition, to order their mammogram or colonoscopy or flu shot or shingles vaccine.

Never take us out of the loop but use this new technology to make it easier for us to take care of them, to get it all done.

#5654. HLTH 2026: Suki unveils agentic OS to automate complex healthcare workflows

HLTH 2026: Suki unveils agentic OS to automate complex healthcare workflows" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Ambient clinical intelligence platform Suki announced Monday the launch of an agentic operating system designed to connect fragmented healthcare technology.

The operating system—dubbed Suki OS—is built on three core pillars, the company says: a partner ecosystem, unified artificial intelligence agents and a performance guarantee. It plans to expand the capabilities beyond its Suki for Clinicians platform over time.

Suki is introducing two initial AI agent initiatives as part of its goal to reduce administrative work.

Suki Prior Authorization will streamline the process by identifying requirements and gathering supporting clinical documentation. Its Clinical Documentation Improvement (CDI) Agent will focus on identifying documentation gaps, improving accuracy and supporting downstream coding and revenue cycle workflows.

Additional agents are planned across clinical, operational and financial workflows as part of the company’s broader strategy to develop agents that can execute complex workflows with human oversight.

Suki’s Partner Ecosystem is comprised of its Insight Partners, which integrate intelligence with Suki patient context, and Platform Partners, which let health tech companies embed Suki’s AI directly into their products.

The Suki Guarantee offers eligible customers up to a 100% refund if agreed-upon performance targets aren't met, the company says.

Suki CEO and Founder Punit Soni told Fierce Healthcare that healthcare has an "execution problem" rather than an AI shortage.

"We've spent years building technology that can understand clinical conversations, but understanding is only the beginning," Soni said. "The real opportunity is to turn that intelligence into action, connecting the systems, people and workflows that make healthcare run."

That’s the motivation behind Suki OS, according to Soni.

"Nearly a decade ago, we pioneered ambient AI, and today, our technology is trusted by more than 450 healthcare organizations, with independently validated clinical and financial outcomes," Soni said. "We've built deep clinical intelligence, integrations across EHRs, and an expansive partner ecosystem. That foundation uniquely positions Suki to move beyond documentation and help automate the complex work that surrounds patient care."

Soni said that the next generation of AI tools have to "do more than save time" as health systems face mounting financial pressures and workforce constraints. "It has to deliver meaningful clinical and financial outcomes," he said.

Soni continued, "Ultimately, the measure of AI's success won't be how many agents we build. It will be how much complexity we remove from healthcare, how much time we give back to clinicians and their patients, and how much measurable financial value we create for the organizations delivering care."

In October, the company secured $90 million in series E funding to accelerate its growth and continue expanding its AI capabilities.

The company has raised more than $250 million to date, executives say. Patient encounters supported by its tools grew more than 190% year over year in 2026, with revenue doubling in 2025 and on track for similar growth this year.

#5653. Democrats settle on a message: ‘Medicare for More’

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Amanda Erickson is a news editor at STAT.

Good morning and happy Monday! Today’s newsletter features some pretty saucy tidbits. We’ve got a doctor on why hot baths and “wellness modules” can’t cure the profession’s burn out, two medical school professors on why med school just isn’t working, and a (well-placed? wildly cliche?) Charles Dickens reference. Thanks for reading!

“It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.”

That line was written to describe the sprawling complexity of 18th century Europe. But it could just as easily apply to the Department of Health and Human Services. Sure, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is facing an oppositional Democratic Congress, a growing measles epidemic (with two more deaths recorded, bringing the total to 10), and a weakened MAHA movement.

And yet, sources told STAT’s Chelsea Cirruzzo that Kennedy has new pep in his step, thanks to recently-appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. Miller is purportedly a MAHA superfan, with a particular interest in vaccine schedule shakeups and redefining ultra-processed foods. And one week into the job, he’s already handed message control back to cabinet secretaries.

Kennedy and his team are preparing to charge hard at major MAHA targets. One close aid is even telling staff that it’s go time for MAHA. Read more here.

Meanwhile, Democrats have been preparing plans on their own …

It doesn’t have quite the same ring to it as “Medicare for All.” But coming out of a retreat, House Dems have coalesced around a top health policy priority — bringing government-run health care to more Americans by allowing people to access Medicare earlier in their lives. A related proposal, ‘Medikids,’ would provide coverage from birth to 26 years old.

“I think we’ve got to lower the age of eligibility as it relates to Medicare,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told reporters after the Denver gathering. “I think we gotta make sure we cover hearing, vision, and dental. And we’ve got to make sure that every child in America can be able to see a doctor with high-quality, affordable health care.”

STAT’s John Wilkerson writes that this unified message is new territory for a party once split between “those who support Medicare for All and those who prefer incremental changes.” But the comity could obscure deeper differences down the road. Find out more here, and read to the end for a crystallizing boat metaphor from New York Times columnist Ezra Klein.

China’s ascendant drug industry is no monolith, despite the way it’s often described by Western competitors, pundits and policymakers. The country is home to scores of companies with diverging ambitions, founded last year or last century, each vying for attention and capital amid a domestic scientific renaissance and a geopolitical standoff.

It’s complicated. To help make sense of it, STAT and the risk intelligence platform WireScreen on Monday published China’s Biotech Powerhouse 25, a ranking of the country’s most valuable publicly traded firms that tracks the varying strategies — and fortunes — of the world’s rapidly growing new medicine chest. — Damian Garde

As a physician on the edge of burnout, Frances Mei Hardin heard all the tips. Light some candles. Pop over to the doctor appreciation pizza party. Complete these mindfulness worksheets.

“The advice to take a warm bath for respite particularly appealed to me, although before long one bath per day became two,” she writes. “That yielded a yeast infection, which does not exactly help one unwind.”

The problem with all of these suggestions, Hardin writes, is that they put the onus on the physician rather than on the increasingly broken system many doctors operate in: “We already know what works for physicians, and it isn’t any of that level one relaxation stuff. A meta-analysis from 2017 found a 2.5 times greater effect from measures such as workload reduction and schedule changes than stress management and mindfulness education for physicians on an individual basis.” Read her column here.

Increasingly, the tranquilizer medetomidine is making its way into the U.S. drug supply, almost always laced into opioids.

Medetomidine is a powerful sedative, and standard overdose treatments like naloxone won’t always reverse all of its effects. Now, the American Society for Addiction Medicine has released new guidance on how to treat patients who’ve taken the drug. A key piece of advice — providers need to know whether medetomidine is in their local drug supply, since its symptoms can mimic other conditions, including sepsis. Read the full writeup here.

Nearly as soon as doctors-to-be reach medical school, they begin to prepare for the U.S. Medical Licensing Exam Step 1. Step 1 is a bear of a test, and the first two years of medical school are theoretically meant to prepare students to pass.

But a lot of students have concluded their courses just aren’t that useful for this purpose. Many (50 percent, by some estimates!) skip lectures, instead spending thousands of dollars on top of tuition for commercial prep material.

This has created an untenable situation, two medical ethics professors write. Their solution: Break medical school apart. Let students prepare for Step 1 by any approach that makes sense for them — on their own, through an online course or one-year program, as part of pre-med. Once they pass, they can apply for a shortened medical school focused on clinical experience, professional identity formation, and deeper dives into ethics and population health.

This could help lower the cost of medical school attendance, the authors write, while also diversifying the pool of candidates who apply to school. It would also let medical schools refocus their resources on the training that matters. “We strongly believe that medical school should be about learning how to be a doctor, not how to pass a test,” they write. #5652. HLTH 2026: Calibrate, Withings study finds wraparound care boosts GLP-1 weight loss by more than 60%

HLTH 2026: Calibrate, Withings study finds wraparound care boosts GLP-1 weight loss by more than 60%" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

As health plans and employers continue to evaluate the costs and outcomes associated with GLP-1 weight loss drugs, a new study found that wraparound clinical care and behavior change support can make expensive GLP-1 treatments more effective and durable.

A two-year real-world study from Withings Health Solutions and Calibrate Health suggests that pairing GLP-1 medications with Calibrate’s integrated obesity care program produced substantially greater weight loss than GLP-1 treatment alone, and Calibrate members sustained more of their weight loss.

The study followed 4,961 U.S. adults who began GLP-1s between 2022 and 2024, comparing 3,422 Calibrate members with 1,539 Withings users taking GLP-1s without the program. After adjustment for differences between the groups, Calibrate members lost 17.3% of their starting weight at two years versus 10.7% for the GLP-1-only group, a more than 60% relative difference.

The study was a real-world observational analysis, not a randomized controlled trial. Because Calibrate members chose to join the program, the two groups differed at the start. Before comparing, a statistical adjustment made them comparable on age, sex, race, BMI, health conditions and GLP-1 treatment. Weight was followed for over 24 months.

The study findings, shared first with Fierce Healthcare, underscore that GLP-1 treatment may work better when medication is paired with personalized clinical management, behavioral coaching and continuous monitoring, rather than being treated primarily as a prescription benefit, according to Calibrate, a digitally integrated obesity management solution.

The study results also reinforce that obesity should be treated as a disease, another chronic metabolic condition requiring intensive, ongoing support, rather than a medication-only problem, Linda Anegawa, M.D., Calibrate Health’s chief medical advisor, told Fierce Healthcare.

“With any chronic disease, like hypertension for example, you won’t get as good outcomes if you just hand someone a medication and don’t support them across other pillars of health, like self-monitoring blood pressure, physical activity and stress reduction. Type 2 diabetes is another good example; you can give high doses of insulin, but medication can’t do the job alone without nutrition education and support,” she said.

“[The study results] make it very clear that treatment [for obesity] shouldn’t stop at just drug coverage,” she added. “As we envision the future, I’d like to see obesity care looking very similar to diabetes care, with insurance covering the full range of necessary services from medication treatment to nutrition education and overall lifestyle support. Obesity is a complex, chronic disease deserving of the same coverage parity as any other."

Treating obesity as such not only prevents health complications and improves quality of life, but it will also lower overall long-term health systems’ costs of care, Anegawa asserted.

The advantage of the integrated care program persisted despite weight regain, the study found. While both study groups regained some weight after reaching their lowest point, the Calibrate members remained about 16.6% below their starting weight, according to the study results. The GLP-1-only group reached a best point of 12.6% weight loss and was about 9.2% below baseline at the peak of its rebound.

There was a body-composition benefit as well. In a subgroup of 974 participants followed for body composition, the muscle-to-fat ratio improved 49.3% for Calibrate members versus 39.9% for GLP-1-only users at 18 months, roughly a 9-point difference.

The study data is based on two years of daily weigh-ins from Withings-connected scales, analyzed with causal-inference methods. Body composition was followed over 18 months in 520 Calibrate members and 454 Withings users.

The study reinforces the importance of evaluating body composition, rather than weight alone, in obesity treatment, Anegawa said.

“We know that abnormal visceral fat accumulation and dysfunction is what drives most of the metabolic conditions we treat, so if we aren’t equipping members to maximize visceral fat loss and preserve muscle, we can actually end up making people sicker. Losing muscle has severe consequences—it isn’t just scaffolding. Muscle is a critical metabolic organ that regulates energy balance, hormonal signaling and insulin sensitivity,” she said.

Adding the insights of body composition to Calibrate's clinical and metabolic data allows the company to better monitor trends and adapt care based on quality evidence, she noted.

There are several key factors that make an integrated obesity care program more effective than a medication-only program, Anegawa said.

"Physician-led personalized care that includes medication optimization for each member’s needs, tailored wraparound support, and features that drive continuous engagement—all of which are designed to maximize clinical outcomes," she said.

"Breaking this down, we start with a comprehensive clinical evaluation for each member, vs. other programs, which only require a questionnaire for a prescription. This helps us get to know each member’s medical and weight histories in detail. We analyze comprehensive lab data to understand their baseline metabolic profile. This information is then used by our expert clinicians to personalize clinical care from day one," Anegawa said.

Live one-to-one coaching support focuses on four pillars of healthy weight maintenance: nutrition, activity, sleep and mindset shift. Tailored education and anticipatory guidance help members manage side effects and stay on treatment, while connecting members to their personal motivations helps sustain engagement through challenges and supports lasting improvements in metabolic health, according to Calibrate.

Calibrate Health has been working with connected health device maker Withings for over five years. The company's members use Withings devices regularly as a required part of the program, according to Anegawa.

"We were already getting body composition data that gave us additional insights into individual members’ health. That data led to additional questions, such as are there significant differences that we can see in aggregate? If so, how large are the differences, and are they changing clinical outcomes? Can we use these data to inform and improve the evolution of our protocols and clinical care? So in asking these types of questions, it became clear to both the Calibrate and Withings teams that we should formalize this into a collaborative study," she noted.

The use of smart devices, specifically Wi-Fi or Bluetooth-connected scales, provides continuous data to help identify weight loss patterns that might not have been apparent through traditional clinical measures, noted Antoine Pivron, vice president of Withings Health Solutions.

"Today, most people on a GLP-1 are monitored through a keyhole. A patient whose primary care doctor prescribes the drug might be weighed a few times a year, and each reading reflects one day: what they ate, the time, the clothes they wore. Between visits, nobody knows whether they plateaued in month three, started regaining in month five, or stopped the drug altogether," he said.

"Specialty programs do better, but many rely on self-reported weights from whatever scale the patient owns. And people tend to stop reporting exactly when things go wrong, which is the moment the care team most needs to know," he added.

Body composition is the biggest blind spot, Pivron asserted. Withings' smart scales track weight and detailed body composition metrics to help identify whether the weight coming off during treatment is fat or muscle.

"In the study we did with Calibrate, two years of data let us see the full shape of the journey: the drop, the low point, and the partial regain that follows. We could also see the quality of the weight loss, not just the quantity. Program members improved their muscle-to-fat balance more, but part of their extra weight loss was muscle. That tells a program exactly where to focus next: protein and strength training," Pivron said.

Withings, a French consumer electronics company, launched its B2B health solutions division in 2019 to meet the growing market around virtual care and remote management in the U.S.

Pivron expects connected health devices like smart scales to play a growing role in GLP-1 treatment programs and broader chronic disease management.

"A GLP-1 prescription isn’t a care plan. The programs that work combine three things: the drug, the clinical and coaching support around it, and the data that shows whether it’s working. Miss one, and real-world results rarely match what we see in trials," he said.

Body composition will become standard in GLP-1 care, Pivron asserted: "That’s where the clinical definition of obesity is already heading."

Connected devices provide the data layer—continuously tracking weight and body composition, predicting when patients may be veering off course and identifying additional risks such as hypertension.

"But a risk score is not a diagnosis. A notification with no next step just creates anxiety. These signals belong inside a care program with a protocol: confirm with a cuff, see a clinician, treat if needed," he said. "Employers and payers are moving toward paying for outcomes. Connected devices are how a program proves it delivered them."

Employers face rising healthcare costs—projected to climb 9.5% next year—and GLP-1 treatments are a major contributor to that cost growth.

The study provides evidence of better outcomes with wraparound care, but it did not evaluate the impact on healthcare spending.

Anegawa contends that improvements in markers associated with high metabolic risk, like Hemoglobin A1c, the liver enzyme ALT and lipids, would point to meaningful cost savings.

Calibrate data from separate evaluations show substantial improvements in these markers among Calibrate members.

“Among Calibrate members who started the program with diabetes or prediabetes, 80% reached normoglycemic status at one year. Among those with abnormal ALT, 79% shifted to the normal range, and 68% of those with abnormal triglycerides were normal at year one," she said.

Withings' body composition data builds on Calibrate's prior data and gives the company another lens on the whole picture, "suggesting that lower healthcare spend is likely,” Anegawa said.

Greater treatment persistence could also ultimately reduce costs. An integrated approach helps keep members engaged so they stick with treatment and get the full benefit of therapy, she noted.

Along with weight loss and metabolic improvements, Calibrate members also report compelling health and productivity outcomes, Anegawa said. Among members with a high work-related burden at intake, 82% no longer reported it at one year.

“My favorite evidence of all is that 90% report that Calibrate improved their overall quality of life, and 94% say that their health is better than a year ago - the most clinically meaningful to me overall,” she said.

#5651. How Impactful Is Stock Epinephrine for Anaphylaxis at Schools?

— Survey of school nurses suggests failure with relying on students to carry autoinjectors

Most schools that keep a stock epinephrine autoinjector available to treat allergic reactions also require children with known severe allergies to bring their own, a survey of school nurses found.

While 87% of their schools carried stock epinephrine, 71.3% of these still required students to bring a personal supply, reported Mahi K. Singh, MD, of University of Chicago Medicine, at the American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology (ACAAI) annual meeting.

With 10% of nurses reporting an emergency when epinephrine was not available for a student who needed it, schools without stock were 4.42 times more likely to report epinephrine unavailability when needed compared with schools that did have it (P<0.001).

All U.S. states now have laws that authorize students with severe allergies to carry and self-administer epinephrine. By 2023, all but four had laws to allow or require schools to stock emergency supplies of epinephrine autoinjectors.

"In anaphylactic emergency, having stock is extremely helpful, even if the school is also requiring personal supply," Singh told MedPage Today. However, "there's a lot of overlap suggesting potentially a lot of excess supply," she said, pointing to a high rate of unused, expired autoinjectors.

"That's also underscored by the fact that epinephrine use in schools is infrequent," Singh added. Almost three-quarters of schools reported no epinephrine administration in the past year, from either personal supply or stock; 97.0% never used more than two epinephrine devices in a single day.

Despite this excess supply, most nurses surveyed (73.6%) said they still favor a dual-coverage model over stock-only supply.

"Our thought was that potentially we could switch or propose switching to a stock-only model to prevent some of this excess or unused supply," Singh said. "It would be more cost effective, and also it would reduce administrative burden on students and families and school nurses. But there remains this discomfort with moving to a stock-only model ... So that definitely needs some more exploration, because nurses know what's happening in schools more than any of us do."

Stock epinephrine doesn't help if there are no school nurses or they don't feel comfortable administering it, commented Jay Lieberman, MD, of the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis.

Newer forms of epinephrine might help both with hesitancy and other obstacles, he said. "A teacher may be much more willing to do a nose spray on a kid or drop a little film under the kid's tongue rather than jab him with an autoinjector."

The approved nasal epinephrine spray (neffy), a sublingual film he presented data on at the conference, and a nasal dry powder all show better stability data than the autoinjectors, both withstanding freezing and then thawing as well as higher temperatures before degrading, Lieberman said.

And whereas an autoinjector might have an expiration date a year from purchase, the nasal spray lasts typically 2 years, he said. "That helps out a school ... Less changing out of the device if they ever were to stock it. And obviously our patients, because if they don't use it lasts them longer."

The cross-sectional survey presented by Singh was distributed to a national database of 1,847 U.S. school nurses from August through December 2025. The 349 nurses who responded (18.9% response rate) represented 31 states, although almost 40% came from Illinois, where the University of Chicago holds an annual conference for school nurses. Nearly all of the nurses came from public schools (90.8%), with an average of 762 students per school.

Limitations of the study included the low response rate, the outsized influence on the results of Illinois policies, and unknown generalizability to schools that don't have a dedicated school nurse.

#5650. When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining

Eating more plants is widely associated with better health, but scientists are still uncovering exactly why. New research suggests that fiber is only part of the story. Certain plant proteins that resist digestion may also play a surprisingly important role in shaping gut bacteria and determining whether they produce beneficial or potentially harmful substances.

Plant-based diets support digestive health, immune function, metabolism, and cardiovascular health. One reason is that they help maintain a diverse community of microorganisms in the intestines, collectively known as the gut microbiome. Many of these bacteria are beneficial, helping break down food components that the human digestive system cannot process on its own.

Fiber is particularly important because it provides food for gut microbes. Plants also contain phytochemicals, natural substances that often give fruits and vegetables their vibrant colors and help protect them from environmental threats. These compounds can also contribute to human health. Yet researchers have only begun to understand the complicated chemical interactions that occur when gut bacteria digest plant foods.

Two studies led by Jenna AbuSalim and Joshua Rabinowitz, director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, provide important new insights. One, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, shows how plant fiber and certain proteins influence gut bacteria to favor the production of beneficial compounds over potentially harmful ones. The other, published in Nature Metabolism in June, challenges the longstanding belief that many important chemical compounds circulating in the body originate exclusively from intestinal microbes.

"There's growing interest across medical disciplines in manipulating the human microbiome or using its metabolic products themselves for therapy," said Rabinowitz. "Diet holds great promise for controlling the microbiome and its outputs. But to devise effective therapeutic interventions, we need to understand what aspects of the diet control which microbial outputs."

How Plant Foods Change the Chemicals Your Gut Produces

In the PNAS study, researchers examined a group of substances called phenol metabolites. Metabolites are chemicals formed when the body or microorganisms break down and process nutrients. Some are essential for normal biological functions, while others can contribute to health problems when they accumulate.

The phenol metabolites investigated by the team are produced when gut bacteria process two amino acids, tyrosine and phenylalanine. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, but the compounds they ultimately produce can have very different effects on health.

Two metabolites derived from phenylalanine, phenylpropionate and hippuric acid, are associated with healthy body weight and better gut health. In contrast, two compounds derived from tyrosine, p-cresol sulfate and phenol sulfate, have been linked to worse outcomes in cancer patients and harmful effects throughout the body in people with kidney disease.

The researchers wanted to understand whether different components of plant foods could influence which of these substances gut microbes produce.

"Our studies showed that both the fiber and indigestible proteins from plants -- which we call 'proteins imitating fiber,' or Prif -- shift the balance of phenol metabolites from the harmful kind made from tyrosine to the healthful variety derived from phenylalanine," said AbuSalim.

An Overlooked Plant Protein Works Alongside Fiber

Although the health benefits of dietary fiber have been studied extensively, scientists have paid much less attention to plant proteins that pass through the digestive system without being fully broken down.

The researchers found that these indigestible proteins, which they call Prif, can reach the gut microbiome and serve as material for bacterial metabolism. In doing so, they influence which microbes thrive and which chemical compounds are produced.

Importantly, these proteins do not work in isolation. They cooperate with plant fiber to change how gut bacteria process nutrients, shifting their activity toward the production of beneficial phenol metabolites.

This discovery suggests that the nutritional value of plant foods may depend on more than their familiar concentrations of fiber, vitamins, and minerals. The amount and type of protein that escapes digestion could also help determine how food influences the gut microbiome.

When Gut Bacteria Run Low on Fiber, They May Feed on Your Gut's Protective Mucus

One of the most intriguing findings concerns where gut bacteria obtain the raw materials used to produce harmful metabolites.

To investigate, the researchers labeled proteins with stable (non-radioactive) isotopes, allowing them to track exactly where the proteins traveled and how they were processed in the digestive systems of mice. This technique works by giving molecules a detectable chemical signature without making them radioactive.

The experiments revealed an important difference between the sources of beneficial and harmful phenols.

The potentially harmful phenols came from gut bacteria breaking down proteins belonging to the host, including proteins found in the mucus layer that coats the intestines. This protective mucus helps separate intestinal microbes from the cells lining the gut and forms part of the body's natural defenses.

Meanwhile, the beneficial phenols were produced almost entirely from indigestible proteins supplied by food.

Fiber helped suppress the bacterial breakdown of the gut's protective mucus, reducing the production of harmful phenols. The indigestible plant proteins (Prif), in turn, supplied more dietary protein to gut bacteria, encouraging them to produce beneficial compounds instead.

Together, the findings reveal two complementary ways plant foods can influence intestinal chemistry. Fiber helps discourage bacteria from consuming proteins in the gut's protective mucus, while Prif provides an alternative source of nutrients that supports the production of healthier metabolites.

"We think Prifs represent an emerging class of dietary nutrients that shape the composition of the gut microbiome and could have a far-reaching influence on metabolic health," said AbuSalim.

The implications could eventually extend to nutrition labels and dietary recommendations.

"Food packaging may eventually list Prif right below fiber," said Rabinowitz.

A Second Discovery Challenges What Scientists Thought About Gut Bacteria

The companion study in Nature Metabolism addressed another important question: Are gut bacteria really responsible for producing all the metabolites traditionally attributed to them?

Along with phenol metabolites, the researchers examined indole metabolites, which are formed from tryptophan, another amino acid found in dietary proteins.

These substances have attracted considerable scientific interest because they participate in biological processes linked to inflammation, immune activity, and disease. Researchers have investigated their involvement in inflammatory bowel disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and cancer. Some indole metabolites have also been found to influence the spread of cancer and the immune system's ability to attack tumors.

Scientists have generally assumed that gut bacteria are the source of these compounds. That belief has encouraged efforts to develop probiotics and dietary interventions that increase the production of potentially beneficial indole metabolites.

However, this approach depends on an important assumption: that intestinal microbes are responsible for producing most or all of the compounds researchers want to influence.

If the body's own cells make substantial amounts of these metabolites, changing the microbiome may not be the most effective way to control their levels.

Your Body Can Make Compounds Once Attributed to Gut Microbes

To investigate, the research team used isotope tracing in mice, rats, and human cells to follow how different metabolites were produced.

The results challenged conventional thinking. Mammalian cells were capable of generating numerous phenol and indole metabolites independently of intestinal bacteria.

Among these were indole-3-lactate and indole-3-acetate, two biologically important compounds previously considered products of microbial metabolism.

The researchers also examined what happened when antibiotics disrupted the intestinal microbiome. If certain metabolites depended entirely on gut bacteria, their concentrations would be expected to decline sharply when those bacteria were depleted.

But many metabolites remained at substantial levels in the blood of antibiotic-treated mice. A similar pattern appeared in samples from patients receiving antibiotics, including people undergoing cancer treatment.

Other compounds behaved differently. Levels of indole-3-propionate and p-cresol sulfate, which are produced exclusively by microbes, declined following antibiotic treatment.

These results provided further evidence that some metabolites depend on intestinal bacteria, while others can also be manufactured by the body's own metabolic processes.

The distinction matters because it could change how researchers develop treatments intended to increase beneficial metabolites or reduce harmful ones.

What These Discoveries Mean for Nutrition and Future Treatments

Together, the two studies offer a more detailed understanding of how diet, gut microbes, and the body's own metabolism interact.

The first identifies an overlooked category of plant proteins that works with fiber to influence bacterial activity, potentially helping shift the balance away from harmful metabolic products. The second demonstrates that the body itself can produce many compounds once believed to originate exclusively from gut bacteria.

Both findings have implications for research into metabolic disease, digestive health, cancer, and other conditions involving the microbiome.

They also suggest that attempts to manipulate gut chemistry through diet, probiotics, or other therapies will need to account for both microbial activity and the body's own metabolic capabilities.

Much of the experimental evidence comes from animals and laboratory studies, so additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms influence long-term health outcomes in people.

Nevertheless, a better understanding of the relationship between different food components and microbial metabolism could eventually make dietary advice more precise and help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies.

"Beyond that," said Rabinowitz, "a clearer picture of how different foods interact with the microbiome to modulate the production of bacterial metabolites will help sharpen the guidance nutritionists and doctors can give to people for disease prevention and therapy."

These studies were funded by the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, the National Institutes of Health, the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the Princeton Alliance for Collaborative Research and Innovation, Princeton University.

Aside from his post as Director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, Joshua Rabinowitz is Professor in the Department of Chemistry & Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics and a member of the Rutgers Cancer Institute.

#5647. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5645. Wegovy Reduces BMI in Kids With Obesity as Young as 6

— Nearly 40% of young children taking the GLP-1 drug dropped below obesity threshold

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. -- Young children ages 6 to 11 years with obesity lost significant weight with the GLP-1 medication semaglutide (Wegovy), according to results from the phase III STEP Young trial.

At week 68, mean body mass index (BMI) decreased by 13.5% with semaglutide compared with an increase of 2.7% with placebo, meeting the trial's primary endpoint (estimated between-group difference -16.2 percentage points, 95% CI -19.4 to -12.9, P<0.001).

By the end of the 104-week treatment period, mean BMI change was -9.4% with semaglutide versus +8.4% with placebo (between-group difference -17.8 percentage points, 95% CI -22.2 to -13.3), reported Ania Jastreboff, MD, PhD, of the Yale School of Medicine in New Haven, Connecticut, and colleagues.

In addition, 38% of participants in the semaglutide group reduced their BMI below the obesity threshold (the 95th percentile for age and sex) by week 68, compared with 2% in the placebo group. At week 104, those rates were 33% and 2%, respectively.

"What we cannot capture with the numbers is the transformation that occurred in these visits. You would walk into the room and the child and their family just felt so different. These children were thriving," Jastreboff said at the ObesityWeek annual meeting.

The findings were simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

Semaglutide is approved for adolescents with obesity ages 12 and older, but obesity treatments for younger children are largely restricted to lifestyle modifications, with rare off-label medication use or bariatric surgery. An older daily GLP-1 drug, liraglutide (Saxenda), is approved in the European Union for children ages 6 and older.

"Although lifestyle modifications are a central part of obesity management and support overall health, associated reductions in the BMI are modest (-0.7), with limited evidence for durability," the authors noted, adding that an estimated one in five U.S. children ages 6 to 11 years have obesity. "Thus, the need for more effective treatments is leading to investigation of pharmacotherapeutic options for children."

During a presentation at the meeting, co-author Martin Wabitsch, MD, PhD, of University Medical Center Ulm in Germany, said children with severe obesity have a quality of life "similar to that of children diagnosed with cancer," adding that a 4-year-old with severe obesity has a life expectancy of just 39 years without weight loss.

However, using potent weight-loss medications in prepubertal children carries potential risks, particularly regarding linear growth and lean muscle development. In a subgroup of 50 children assessed via dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), semaglutide led to a greater reduction in fat mass percentage and a greater increase in lean soft-tissue percentage than placebo.

Median height gain was lower with semaglutide than placebo at both week 68 (5.7 cm vs 7.8 cm) and week 104 (8.8 cm vs 12.1 cm), accompanied by slower annual height velocity. Bone age, bone mineral density, and pubertal progression (Tanner staging) were similar between groups. Because children with obesity often experience accelerated growth prior to puberty, the researchers suggested the slower height velocity may simply reflect BMI normalization.

Conducted from July 2023 to July 2026 across 48 sites in nine countries, the double-blind STEP Young trial randomized 167 children (2:1) to once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide (n=112) or placebo (n=55) for 104 weeks, followed by a 7-week off-treatment washout period. All participants received lifestyle counseling.

At least 30% of enrollees were required to have severe obesity (BMI ≥120% of the 95th percentile) or an obesity-related complication such as hypertension, dyslipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, or type 2 diabetes. Children with syndromic or hypothalamic obesity, or prior or planned bariatric surgery, were excluded. Maximum weekly doses were capped at 2.4 mg for children weighing more than 132 lb at baseline and 1.7 mg for those weighing 99 to 132 lb.

Participants had a mean age of 10 years; 59% were female, 73% were white, and most were at Tanner stage 1. Mean baseline BMI was 32.4 in the semaglutide group (32.5 in placebo), mean baseline weight was 158.1 lb (159.2 lb in placebo), and just over half had at least one obesity-related complication.

At week 68, secondary cardiometabolic measures, which were not adjusted for multiple comparisons, also favored semaglutide:

In an exploratory analysis, reversion from prediabetes (HbA1c ≥5.7%) to normoglycemia occurred in 93% of semaglutide participants versus 56% of placebo participants at week 68, and in 94% versus 44% at week 104.

"When I am seeing children developing type 2 diabetes at a very young age, this is the type of data that we are really looking for to better understand how these medications can prevent progression," said Daniel Hsia, MD, of Emory University and Children's Healthcare of Atlanta, who was not involved with the study.

As expected with GLP-1 therapies, gastrointestinal issues were the most frequent adverse events. They were mostly mild to moderate, transient, and peaked during the 16-week dose-escalation phase.

Through week 111, rates in the semaglutide versus placebo groups were:

When compared with clinical trial data of semaglutide in adults and adolescents, the proportion of participants who experienced vomiting was lower in STEP Young, Hsia pointed out. "We have to remember that children can have lots of gastroenteritis and other reasons for vomiting, so the high rate of vomiting can be partially explained by that."

Only one child in the semaglutide group discontinued treatment due to gastrointestinal side effects. Serious adverse events -- primarily respiratory or gastrointestinal infections -- occurred in 9% of participants in both groups (10 in the semaglutide group, five in the placebo group). Psychiatric events occurred in 21% of the semaglutide group and 24% of the placebo group. No deaths or new safety signals were reported.

Nearly 40% of children in the placebo arm discontinued injections by week 104, which the authors noted was unsurprising given the lack of weight-loss progress. Other limitations included a predominantly white study population and the absence of baseline screening for eating disorders.

Drugmaker Novo Nordisk has not yet announced plans to submit data from STEP Young to the FDA.
