#5589. How Training Veterans in Skilled Trades Could Speed Up Homebuilding and Ease Housing Costs

A severe shortage of skilled workers entering the residential construction sector has had a major impact on affordability, but the Home Builders Institute (HBI) believes the country’s large veteran population may be part of the solution.

The skilled labor shortage has led to an increase in construction time, with each home taking nearly two months longer to build, according to an HBI study. Due to the delays, there was a reduction of 19,000 homes built in 2024, representing an economic loss of over $8 billion, the study found.

Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) estimated that the construction industry needs to attract roughly 349,000 net new workers in 2026 and 456,000 new workers in 2027 to meet demand for construction services.

There are a number of factors in the past 30 years that have led to the labor shortage, according to HBI CEO Ed Brady. First, a strong push for four-year degrees led many young people toward academic careers rather than trades. With more people retiring from the workforce than entering, the shortage began.

The issue was compounded during the financial crisis of 2008, when the residential construction field lost tons of skilled workers because there wasn’t enough work. Without enough housing construction, workers left for jobs in manufacturing and hospitality or retired early, according to Brady.

More recently, rocky immigration policies have challenged the skilled labor workforce, Brady explains.

When finding a solution to the shortage became dire, HBI believed that the veteran and transitioning military population was “an untapped market.” The result was the HBI Military Services Program, which trains veterans, transitioning military service members, and their dependents in skilled trades.

On Monday, HBI and Invitation Homes announced a new partnership that will continue HBI’s mission to create opportunities for transitioning military service members, veterans, and their families.

The partnership includes an unspecified investment from Invitation Homes in HBI’s Military Services Program. It will also open doors for former military service members who complete HBI training to access job opportunities with the premier leasing and management company.

For nearly a decade, HBI has been raising awareness of the benefits of a career in a skilled trade among former members. It has proceeded to train, certify, and assist veterans and their families in finding successful careers.

HBI’s Military Services Program was supported early on by major companies like The Home Depot Foundation and Dewalt. It was recently given a $1 million gift from Google.org, and now Invitation Homes has joined the worthy cause.

These vital investments help HBI reach even more service members on their mission, according to Brady.

“It provides scale. We’re not changing our model—we feel like our model works. We introduce them to the industry, we train them in the industry, we certify them, we connect them to the industry to get a job,” Brady tells Realtor.com®.

“But the dollars from Invitation Homes, the dollars that Google have given us to apply into the veteran space just gives us more scale. We can provide better service, and we can grow our programs to serve more veterans, more transitioning military, even the spouses of veterans.”

Expanding training programs for former military could make a huge difference in the skilled labor shortage being experienced by residential construction.

“In many cases, the demographic of soldiers that want to be outside, want to work with their hands, and have that physicality, it’s natural for them to look at our industry,” says Brady. “They’ve got more discipline, they know how to create a task and how to do a job. They have a desire to be productive and build a career.”

Brady has also observed that many veterans want to “control their own destiny” once they leave the military. The desire to not be dependent on anyone else or an organization makes them great candidates for entrepreneurship, business ownership, and contracting roles.

For Philip Shealy, HBI offered a path when he was unsure of next steps.

After spending five years as an Army infantryman at Fort Drum in New York and Fort Stewart in Georgia, he had no clue what he wanted to do next, Shealy recalls. He decided to take advantage of the DoD SkillBridge to learn some skills before departing the service.

“I saw the HBI program and thought, even if I don’t go into the skilled trades like that, that will be information I hold for the rest of my life. It’ll be great for owning a home or just knowing a thing here or there,” Shealy tells Realtor.com.

“But the program does a pretty cool thing where they bring in recruiters from local companies. And they brought one in that sounded like something I wanted to do. So I applied with him and ended up getting the job.”

Shealy now works for Ace Electric, an electrical contractor in southern Georgia, alongside several fellow veterans who went through the same HBI program.

The three-month program was conducted right at Fort Stewart. Participants learned everything they needed to enter a career in carpentry or electrical work, and they even built little homes on base as part of the training.

Shealy recalls one of the instructors being former military himself, so he was able to communicate effectively by building upon military skills and terminology and translating them to trade terms.

Many skills emphasized by the military, such as leadership and the ability to take instruction and corrections well, have transferred well to his career in a skilled trade.

Shealy shares HBI’s belief that trade jobs and the military attract the same type of person, making it a logical next step for many leaving the service.

“People that like to work with their hands, many of which are going to be hard workers and aren’t going to stop until the job gets done and done well—I think a lot of it transfers well over,” says Shealy.

For those still considering next steps, he says to give the SkillBridge and HBI programs a shot, because you may just end up finding a great path.

“When we’re getting out, it can be a very scary thing, not knowing where you’re going to end up,” says Shealy. “From my personal experience going through HBI programming, I had no clue what I wanted to do, and then I ended up finding something I’ll enjoy doing for a long time.”

Brady also emphasizes the longevity of a trade career.

“This is a career path, not just a job. Getting into the trades is something that you can hang your hat on for your career,” says Brady. “And it’s not a career that’s going to be diminished by technology or AI. Certainly innovation will make it more efficient, but you’re not going to take away roofers. You’re not going to take away plumbers.”

In this Breaking Analysis, we’re joined by its author, Amit Eyal Govrin, lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and CEO of Agentcy Labs, to talk about why he wrote it, what sovereignty is and what it isn’t, and what surprised him most in the findings.

The full scores are in the report. Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide https://siliconangle.com/sovereign-or-not

Dave: As someone who’s been leading the thought leadership in this domain, how did you come up with the inspiration to research this topic and write the report?

Amit: To understand the how, it helps to understand the why. I’ve been thinking about this subject for a while now. It hasn’t always been called “sovereignty,” but the tenets have always been the same.

It all started around four years ago, as I’ve been a builder in this space for that long. First with Kubiya, one of the industry’s first agentic implementations, deploying agents in enterprise production environments as early as September 2023, before agents were even an industry term.

We were deploying as a software-as-a-service company, and many of those concerns were legitimate. As a software company, we got to keep our intellectual property and license it out. If we were successful, we would create dependency, which effectively meant customers lost control of their crown jewels.

When we started Agentcy Labs earlier this year, customers familiar with our work approached us, and many of these points crystallized for us. What they told us: We’re relieved you are no longer at Kubiya. It’s not that we ever doubted your technology or the value it brings. Quite the opposite. That was what they were afraid of. Kubiya creates a dependency, adoption balloons, and they lose control of their costs. Or a vendor changes the meter on them because of shareholder pressure or regulatory controls.

What clicked for us is that their resistance was never about Kubiya or our technology. It was about the loss of control of their alpha. Namely, the Agentic Operating System, the key driver of their artificial intelligence transformation, which falls under our technological pillar.

It doesn’t matter if the vendor is a startup, an AI lab or a hyperscaler. No enterprise can afford to mortgage its entire business on an external dependency on such a key issue. It’s far too strategic not to own outright.

That finding forced us to rethink the model behind software, dig deeper into sovereignty as an issue of control, and help the industry define it in a more standardized way.

Dave: So control is the heart of it. But when most people hear sovereignty, they think about where the data sits. Is that the wrong way to look at it?

Amit: Sovereignty goes well beyond territory, which is often the most misunderstood aspect. People hear sovereignty and immediately revert to the sovereign state: government initiatives, national security, on-premises air-gapped environments. That can be true in some cases. But by and large, our sovereignty discussions involve enterprises and regulated industries that have sovereignty as a core tenet of their AI initiatives.

It goes beyond buzzwords and sovereign-washing claims. Think back to the explosive Alex Karp interview on CNBC claiming enterprises are losing their alpha to frontier labs. I largely agree with that claim, by the way. Only he finished his pitch by offering customers to move it over to Palantir. In other words: Stop mortgaging your alpha to Anthropic and OpenAI, come rent it from us.

That interview was my trigger point to take up arms and educate the industry on sovereignty: what it is, what it isn’t, and most importantly, what you, as a buyer of AI, can do about it.

Dave: And you’ve been out in the field with buyers ever since. What did those conversations teach you, and how did that shape the framework?

Amit: Since then, we’ve been included in dozens of engagements with enterprises, governments and policymakers around the world, from Washington to Brussels, New Delhi, Sydney and even Riyadh. We are in the room when sovereignty discussions happen. That helped us shape our view, tease out the concerns, and focus on what really matters and why. From those discussions came the 5 Pillars of Sovereignty framework. We use it today to assess all vendor relationships, policy and regulation, and geopolitical events.

Dave: Which brings us to the report. You started with the hyperscalers. Walk us through how you approached it.

Amit: In our first edition, Sovereign or Not? The Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide, we take the buyer’s lens and assess each hyperscaler by its sovereignty posture.

Hint: By definition, working with any hyperscaler means ceding a good portion of control over your Operational, Technological, Legal and Financial pillars. Oftentimes that’s the reality in the real world.

My view: Sovereignty is not a purity test. It’s perfectly acceptable to go with a hyperscaler, as long as it’s a known dependency you priced in as an acceptable risk. If that’s the case, let us guide you through these considerations to the best path forward for your organization.

Dave: OK, let’s get to the part everyone wants to know. Who scored what, and why?

Amit: We looked at seven hyperscalers and 40 of their offerings, from the point of view of buyers in five regions: the U.S., Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the rest, including the Middle East and Africa. Everything is scored out of 5.

The short version: The most sovereign product a hyperscaler sells is the one the hyperscaler itself can’t reach.

On these tests, sovereignty often runs inverse to how a hyperscaler is built. A shared global control plane and services the vendor runs for the customer make a cloud easy to adopt, but every layer the vendor runs is a layer the buyer does not control. Amazon Web Services and Google built their platforms around that abstraction, which becomes a hindrance once a buyer needs to run the stack without them. The grades measure how much control a buyer can take back, not the quality of the cloud.

Who came out on top, who came in last, and by how much, is in the report. And every score is backed by a source. Don’t like your grade? Publish the document and we’ll re-score it.

Fair is fair, though. Every one of the seven owns some ground:

Dave: What surprised you most when you went through the findings?

Amit: None of the hyperscalers has a practical solution for the U.S. CLOUD Act, and that alone has created a real legal clawback on non-U.S. companies.

In plain English: The U.S. government can ask an American cloud company for data it controls, no matter which country the data sits in. A sovereign cloud in Brandenburg, run by a German subsidiary, doesn’t change the answer. It’s still owned by an American company.

The vendors aren’t hiding it. AWS told us as much on the record. Microsoft’s own lawyer in France told the French Senate he couldn’t guarantee French data would never reach U.S. authorities. That’s honesty, and we don’t penalize honesty. It’s the law, and it applies to every American cloud the same way.

The fixes buyers are being sold, like keeping data local, holding your own encryption keys, or a contract promise to fight requests, don’t change who the government can go to.

Dave: So what’s a non-U.S. buyer supposed to do about that?

Amit: There’s no perfect answer today, only partial ones.

Going with a hyperscaler is fine, as long as you know the risk and priced it in. What’s not fine is believing a data center in Brandenburg, on its own merits, solved your sovereignty problem.

Dave: And this is just the first of several. Where do you go from here?

Amit: This is the first of a series: neoclouds, OEMs, telcos and specialized sovereign initiatives, wherever you happen to be, whether you’re a U.S., EU, Latin American, APAC or Middle Eastern buyer. Every edition covers the 5 Pillars, plus security, regulation and exit costs. Readers will be surprised by how deep we got, including quotes from the hyperscalers themselves and surveys of actual buyers. I truly think this will be valuable to everyone listening and reading.

Dave: That’s phenomenal, Amit. This is a cutting-edge report on a truly important and timely subject. If previously you were building on the frontier, you’re now squarely on the frontier of research. The scores, the vendor answers and the buyer data are all in the full report.

Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

#5587. Court Report: Compass Attempts to Divide and Conquer in MLS War

Editor’s note: The COURT REPORT is RISMedia’s weekly look at current and upcoming lawsuits, investigations and other legal developments around real estate.

A day after Compass sued 15 MLSs in separate lawsuits, the brokerage again made a move to divide and conquer in its campaign against several MLSs.

Facing a separate lawsuit brought by seven MLSs against Compass—including Arizona Regional MLS (ARMLS), bridgeMLS, Canopy MLS, REcolorado, MLSListings, Hive MLS and Doorify MLS—the brokerage submitted a letter on Nov. 13 to Southern District of New York Judge, Mary Kay Vyskocil, asking for a dismissal, or a motion to sever and transfer.

Within the filing, Compass alleges that the MLSs in question had sought an extension after the brokerage’s initial Oct. 6 letter, demanding that the organizations cease fining and punishing real estate professionals for “publicly marketing office exclusive listings or face an antitrust suit.”

The letter states that Mitch Skinner—an attorney acting on behalf of ARMLS, Doorify MLS and Hive MLS—spoke to Compass’s chief legal officer and asked for an extension to the demand letter’s deadline, on the grounds that “several decision makers were ill and others were busy and needed more time to work on Compass’ demand.” Later the filing mentions that the other MLSs separately sought extensions for time as well.

Compass allegedly extended the deadline, but accuses the MLSs of using that time to organize their Oct. 21 lawsuit against the brokerage instead of complying with Compass’s demands.

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Compass’s attorneys argue that because the MLSs “(signaled) that a negotiated resolution was under consideration” by asking for extensions, the case should be dismissed.

Alternatively—should the motion to dismiss be denied—Compass requested that the court “sever each MLS’s claims and transfer them to the district where that particular MLS’s Home-District Action is pending.”

By separating each MLS plaintiff into distinct lawsuits, Compass seems to be holding true to its promise, where the brokerage would “spend millions of dollars to sue CRMLS and other MLSs to accomplish those goals,” as stated in the Sept. 8 letter sent to all the MLSs it sued.

Last week, the mega-brokerage Compass took a major step in the battle over listing restrictions by filing lawsuits against over a dozen MLSs, across eight states. Six of the MLSs are based in California, with three in North Carolina and the rest spread throughout a handful of other states around the country.

In one of Compass’s filed complaints—against North Carolina’s Hive MLS—the brokerage accuses the MLS of “using control of a home listing database that real estate agents in eastern North Carolina and the other areas Hive MLS services cannot work without,” to block Compass and protect the brokerage’s competitors.

Several of the MLSs targeted—including Hive MLS, ARMLS, REcolorado, Canopy MLS, Doorify MLS and bridgeMLS—already sued Compass, asking a judge to preemptively declare their rules do not violate antitrust laws. They have characterized their various policies, which restrict how members can market listing off-MLS, as pro-competitive and pro-consumer, and claimed Compass is merely seeking to use its exclusive listings as a “competitive weapon.”

Compass, on the other hand, has repeatedly accused these MLSs of fighting purely to protect their own interests and claimed the MLS industry has long endured antitrust scrutiny from government regulators. It sent letters to many of these MLSs back in September, explicitly threatening to sue and force them to bear the legal costs if they continued enforcing the policies in question.

“It’s almost as if these MLSs are asking people to ignore the evidence that proves their claims aren’t true,” a Compass spokesperson said. “For years, seven of the top 25 MLSs, covering 340,000 agents across 12 states, have allowed agents to publicly market ‘office exclusives’ without fines, and none of the problems they warn about have happened. If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30% of the country?”

While the lawsuits are filed against each MLS, the arguments broadly mirror Compass’s accusations against California-based CRMLS, which it separately sued back in October.

Compass moves to dismiss rent-monopoly allegations

Nearly four months since the case was originally filed, Compass now awaits a judge’s decision on its motion to dismiss the antitrust class-action lawsuit accusing the brokerage of monopolizing the rental market in New York City.

The case—initially filed by Peter Castaneda and Haley Gelfand—alleges that Compass monopolized the non-rent stabilized, multifamily residential real estate units (rental units) in its “conquest to seize control over various housing markets,” according to the original complaint, including efforts to remove Compass listings from New York’s StreetEasy portal.

“Compass, which now owns every other competitor real estate brokerage firm (referring to Anywhere Real Estate, which Compass acquired in January 2026), controls over 80% of the rental unit listings available for renters in Manhattan based on 2025 data,” the complaint continues. “Rather than compete in the relevant market on the merits to attain high profits, Compass instead neutralized Competitors by acquiring them.”

On Nov. 10, Compass submitted a motion to dismiss the plaintiffs’ complaint on the basis that they’ve failed to plead the “bedrock” requirement, failed to prove monopoly power and lacks antitrust standing.

Generally, the “bedrock” requirement refers to a plaintiff’s ability to prove a concrete injury was done, along with proving causation and redressability. Compass’s motion also argues that the renters are unable to prove that the brokerage holds monopoly power.

“By (the) plaintiff’s own account, it is the owners and managers of rental units who ‘set rent prices’ in response to supply and demand using various third-party ‘algorithms’ and ‘tools,’” Compass’ argument states. “The complaint does not allege that Compass owns, manages, or leases a single rental apartment, or that Compass sets rents or controls any of the pricing tools that landlords and owners use.”

But, the plaintiff’s original complaint alleges that Compass’ “campaign to have no competitors” is tied to the brokerage’s conduct when it comes to the publication of rental unit listings.

“Compass, led by its chief executive Robert Reffkin, has been engaged in both a litigative and public relations-based war with Zillow,” the complaint states. “The rerouting of Compass’ listings through REBNY Residential Listing Service (RLS) intentionally results in depriving consumers of free-to-access portals to find rental units and instead mandates the use of a broker to find a rental unit.”

The original complaint also argues that with control of over 80% of the listings in Manhattan alone, Compass can choose to delist them from free-to-use platforms like StreetEasy and thus drive up prices for other apartments listed due to the lack of supply.

While the case is still ongoing, all parties await the judge’s decision on the motion to dismiss.

After nearly 40 years of employment, the former chief financial officer of the National Association of Realtors® (NAR) filed a lawsuit against the association, accusing it of withholding his retirement benefit.

John Pierpoint—who retired from his role in 2025—filed the lawsuit against NAR in the Circuit Court of Cook County in Chicago last Wednesday.

According to a release from Pierpoint’s attorneys, NAR “improperly withheld one year of salary in retirement compensation despite having recorded the anticipated payment in its own financial records for more than a decade.”

The release also points out that NAR has maintained the executive retirement compensation practice for approximately two decades, and pays retiring senior executives a year’s worth of their base salary.

The amount Pierpoint was to receive for his retirement was about $541,000, or his base salary, according to his complaint. Pierpoint likens NAR’s refusal to pay his retirement benefit to their recent settlement in the Burnett lawsuit, where the association paid $418 million to plaintiffs.

Weighed down by the burden of the settlement and legal fees, Pierpoint’s attorneys argue that NAR “directed its finance staff to write the Compensation Reserve off its books, eliminating a liability of several million dollars from its balance sheet during the period in which it was funding its antitrust settlement obligations.”

“Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” David Fish, an attorney representing Pierpoint, stated. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives. We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees.”

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

#5586. Housing Week Ahead: Construction Insights, Rental Trends, and Pending Sales

The coming week holds a packed slate of insights from Realtor.com Economics, as well as vital indicators about the state of the housing market.

On Monday, senior economist Jiayi Xu  published a report on free and clear mortgages, which breaks down trends in where the most homeowners own their home outright.

On Tuesday, senior economist Joel Berner has our third-quarter New-Construction Insights report looking at how new-home prices and homebuilder incentives have trended in the past quarter.

Then on Wednesday, Jiayi is back with a look at October rent trends in our monthly rental report, which will also dive deep into how apartment supply shifts are likely to affect the market.

Finally, on Thursday, senior economist Anthony Smith will analyze our weekly housing data for clues on the latest trends.

Turning to the macro indicators that will be released, both pending home sales and new construction will be released on Wednesday and on Thursday, we’ll see mortgage rates.

October pending home sales, released by the National Association of Realtors®, are likely to be low. In September, the pending data hit a series record low, tumbling more than 7% in the month and 11% from a year ago.

Realtor.com data showed double-digit declines in both pending sales and new contract signings in October. I think we’re likely to see another tough few months for housing activity as we wrap up 2026.

Similar challenges are likely for builders and the high-rate environment is likely to slow October construction.

In September’s construction report from the U.S. Census Bureau, permits, starts, and completions all fell from both the prior month and prior year. Declines were mildest for permits, and single-family fared better than multifamily in starts and completions.

Meanwhile, mortgage rates notched a fourth consecutive week of decline last week, getting all the way down to 7.11%, but I think that streak ends this week.

Last week’s inflation data came in hot, and the bond market reacted, sending the 10-year Treasury yield above 5% for the first time in November.

Home shoppers planning to take out a mortgage will want to prepare, while home shoppers planning to use cash are likely to find a less-competitive housing market to navigate.

Danielle Hale is the chief economist of Realtor.com.

#5585. NeuralSat raises $3.2M to bring high-speed data connectivity and compute to space

German startup NeuralSat GmbH announced Thursday that it has raised €2.9 million, about $3.2 million, in pre-seed funding to develop a 72-satellite data-relay processing network aimed at speeding up the flow of data from space.

Capnamic and Bayern Kapital co-led the round. Other investors participating in the round included ZOHO.VC, Robin Capital, BAB – Die Förderbank für Bremen und Bremerhaven, Mission E and KIEMIS Holding.

Founded in early 2026, NeuralSat’s satellite constellation will allow operators to offload computing and communications. According to the company, its network will deliver up to 50 gigabits per second via optical and high-frequency radio links.

The network will support real-time edge processing, hosted workloads for commercial and defense clients and provide for time-critical missions like Earth observation and signals intelligence.

“We believe the next major evolution in space will… come from connecting satellites to shared infrastructure that enables them to communicate, access computing resources, and operate together,” Chief Executive Mohd Bilal said in a statement. “Just as the internet transformed how computers interact on Earth, we intend to transform how intelligence is connected and delivered in space.”

The company said the funding will help it accelerate plans to launch its first in-orbit demonstration node, planned for October 2027. After that, NeuralSat plans to begin rolling out commercial operational satellites.

The race to develop and build better connectivity and compute capabilities in space is on. Canadian startup Kepler Communications Inc. launched its first commercial space data relay service in January, allowing resilient data transfer and onboard computing, with a next-gen optical relay network announced in August. Skyloom, acquired by quantum computing firm IonQ Inc. in early 2026, deployed 84 optical terminals and a relay architecture in low Earth orbit.

Space is not the optimal place to run processors because heat dissipation becomes a major issue with no air to carry it away. But space technology firms have developed solutions to radiate it from giant sails and other surfaces. Space-based compute may not replace terrestrial data centers, but it can enable edge compute given payload weight restrictions for orbital launch.

Starcloud Inc., formerly known as Lumen Orbit, raised $250 million in August at a $2.3 billion valuation. The company has already tested an Nvidia H100 graphics processing unit in orbit in late 2025, proving that it can scale to multi-satellite AI “data centers.” The company is now collaborating with Nvidia Corp. on upcoming space-grade chips.

Currently, data relay and compute processing in space reduce the need for other satellites to send data to Earth to complete workloads. Talking to a nearby satellite for edge compute can shave significant time off data transfers. Sending data down to Earth can take a round trip of four to more than 30 milliseconds; satellite-to-satellite is slightly faster, at three to 30 milliseconds.

The real boost comes from relaying between satellites rather than routing long distances on the ground to a data center and back, often via optical cable ground networks, which add additional lag. Over long distances across the globe, inter-satellite links are around 30% to 50% faster than sending signals down to Earth for processing.

Companies such as NeuralSat hope to use the advantage of being right there, near the data production, to provide processing capabilities, or swift relay to a satellite closer geographically to terrestrial data center processing to reduce delays.

#5584. Housing Starts Pull Back, but Top Markets Hold Their Ground

Zonda’s third quarter 2026 data shows housing starts over the past four quarters declined 10% from the same period a year ago. More specifically, 22 of the top 25 housing production markets posted year-over-year declines, pointing to a broad-based slowdown. However, the national slowdown can translate into very different competitive conditions depending on geography.

Sarasota was the clear outlier, with starts rising 20% year over year to 9,691 during the four quarters through Q3 2026. Chicago also managed growth, increasing 1% year over year to 7,680 starts, while Boise was effectively flat at 7,303.

At the other end of the spectrum, Las Vegas and Provo posted the largest declines among the top 25 markets, with starts falling 22% year over year in each. Riverside/San Bernardino followed closely with a 21% decline. Washington, D.C., Nashville, Raleigh, and Jacksonville were also among the markets recording double-digit contractions.

Despite declining activity, Dallas and Houston continue to operate on a different scale from the rest of the country.

Dallas ranked first with 37,497 starts over the past four quarters, down 10% year over year. Houston followed with 34,996, down 8% year over year. The two metros operate in a league of their own, each producing more than twice as many starts as any individual market elsewhere in the top 25.

Phoenix and San Antonio were the only other markets to top 15,000 starts, at 16,770 and 15,531, respectively. The rankings also point to relative stability at the top. Every market in the top 10 retained its position from the previous quarter, even as housing production softened nationally.

For industry professionals planning for 2027, the numbers reinforce the importance of looking beyond national trends. The size and direction of the housing adjustment vary substantially by market. Production is still highly concentrated in the Sun Belt metros, but growth in markets like Sarasota and Chicago shows that opportunities remain even against a weaker national backdrop.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

Sean Fergus, Vice President of economic research at Zonda, leads the published research team. Fergus has 20 years of expertise in economic research, market studies, and financial analysis.

#5583. Report: Multiskilling Could Cut Construction Schedules by Up to 38%

A study by the Simplar Foundation found that multiskilled construction crews completed work in approximately 22% to 38% fewer workdays than crews following a traditional single-trade labor strategy. The findings are based on nearly 90,000 labor hours across 18 construction projects involving 11 contractors.

The research, analyzed by Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC), highlights how training workers to perform multiple trades and tasks can help contractors better allocate available labor, reduce downtime, and keep projects moving as workforce demands change.

“America faces a fundamental challenge: We have more to build than our workforce can currently support,” said Michael Bellaman, ABC president and CEO. “This research demonstrates that a solution is already within reach. By investing in our craft professionals, expanding their skills and removing unnecessary barriers to using those skills, we can create more opportunity for workers and greater capacity for contractors to build America.

He continued, “As a new Congress prepares to take office, lawmakers now have powerful evidence to guide policies that strengthen our workforce, promote fair and open competition, and deliver better outcomes for owners and taxpayers. This is an opportunity for the entire construction industry to win.”

Researchers found that relying on single-trade staffing would have left at least one trade short of available labor on 73% of project days. A single-trade approach also required more than one-third additional staffing on the busiest project days.

The study documented 80 unique trade and skill combinations across 18 trades, with multiskilled workers performing an average of 3.2 different trades or skills during their projects.

The findings build on two earlier reports in the foundation’s three-part research series, which found that multiskilling increased the share of workers’ time spent directly advancing construction by 39% and reduced waiting and idle time by 68%. Controlled field trials also showed production rate improvements of 37% to 50%.

The research also emphasizes that productivity gains do not require workers to perform tasks faster or work harder. Instead, allowing properly trained and qualified employees to apply multiple skills can reduce delays between activities, minimize trade handoffs, and improve workflow continuity.

Brian Lines, Ph.D., P.E., the study’s principal investigator and an associate professor at the University of Kansas, said the findings provide measurable evidence of how workforce flexibility can translate into stronger project performance.

ABC is encouraging policymakers to support competency-based workforce development, expand training and upskilling opportunities, and preserve the flexibility of qualified workers to safely perform tasks across multiple skills and trades.

The research was conducted by the Simplar Foundation in collaboration with Arizona State University, the University of Kansas, and the University of North Carolina at Charlotte.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5582. America’s Trillion-Dollar Credit Card Debt Threatens To Lock Millions Out of the Housing Market

With prices still alarmingly high, it comes as no surprise that Americans are increasingly turning to credit cards more than ever.

But doing so could be silently sabotaging any hope of owning a home, if you’re not careful.

Last week, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York published its latest household debt report.

Collectively, credit card balances climbed by $22 billion in the third quarter to a record $1.29 trillion. Balances are up 4.2% from a year earlier, and total household debt, including mortgages, auto loans, and student loans, expanded by $334 billion for the period to a record $19.1 trillion.

High levels of debt are problematic for anyone, but most especially for first-time homebuyers. If your ambitions for 2027 include buying a home, it’s important to get your debt in check before it’s too late.

According to TransUnion’s most recent quarterly credit industry insights report, the number of people with credit cards rose 2% to 178 million up from 174.8 million.

The ease of use means most people turn to credit cards for their everyday purchases, like groceries, gas, and utility bills—all of which have seen a steep increase in prices over the past two years.

Now, if you’re someone who pays off their credit card in full each month, you’re in the clear. If not, the average interest rate on a new credit card offer currently stands at about 24%, and debt can accumulate quickly.

And this can cause an array of issues for first-time homebuyers.

"Issues arising from high levels of consumer debt are amplified for first-time homebuyers as they typically have less savings, limited financial history, and tighter financial conditions,” John Donikian, vice president of Best Interest Financial in West Bloomfield, MI, tells Realtor.com®.

Firstly, carrying too much debt can negatively affect your credit score, a vital metric in getting a mortgage.

While there is no firm number to qualify for a mortgage, a good credit score ranges from 700 to 749, and most conventional loans typically require at least 620. Lenders may accept lower scores if you have a larger down payment or other strong financial factors.

The higher your balances are, the more your score is dragged down, which can not only affect the interest rate a lender can offer you, but also keep you from getting a mortgage with some lenders entirely.

“Your credit score doesn’t just determine if you are approved; it influences your interest rate and the monthly payment you are offered,” says Jake Vehige, president of mortgage lending at Neighbors Bank.

“Even a small difference in interest rates can add up to thousands of dollars over the life of a loan.”

Secondly, as part of the process of getting a mortgage, lenders will look at your debt-to-income ratio to see how much house you can afford.

If a lender looks at your total monthly debt payments against your gross monthly income and your DTI exceeds its caps, your application could be delayed or even denied outright.

But both of those instances can be reversed, with time and a fixed budget that allows you to pay off your debt. In other words, your credit score can rebound.

Where first-time buyers are really at a disadvantage by accumulating so much credit card debt is the drain it will put on their savings.

The money that you’ll need to rack up to pay off the 20%-plus interest on your bills could have been money saved for your down payment, closing costs, and repair funds.

Many lenders also require proof of postclosing cash reserves, which is much harder to build while paying down high-interest debt.

“Ideally, you want to keep your credit card balances at no more than 20% to 30% of your maximum credit limit," explains Jeremy Schachter, branch manager at Fairway Independent Mortgage Corp. in Phoenix.

"For example, if you have a $1,000 limit, don’t go over a balance higher than $200 to $300. Anything that exceeds that amount can lower your credit score and make it difficult to get approved for a mortgage with a good rate.”

Dina Sartore-Bodo is the senior editor at Realtor.com covering real estate news, personal finance trends, and interior design. Her work has also appeared on MSN, Yahoo News, and BlogHer. She is a proud graduate of Emerson College in Boston and is originally from New Jersey.

#5581. Navigating the AI Shift

https://www.lamacchiarealty.com/leadership/kim-beaulieu

Regions served: Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Connecticut, Rhode Island, Vermont, Maine and Florida

Years in real estate: 14 Number of offices: 29 Number of agents: 840, plus 81 employees

What AI developments do employees and agents need to be paying attention to?

The big one is knowing which models give you facts and which ones are people pleasers. Take listing remarks, for example. ChatGPT is excellent at them, but you need strict guardrails on it, because a people-pleaser model prioritizes making you happy over the facts and the rules. Left alone, it will write you a Fair Housing violation and never tell you it did. Beyond that, ask the questions most people skip: How are my competitors using it? How are my vendors using it?

Give us your top tips for HR leaders as they prepare people to successfully navigate the AI shift.

First, keep an open mind, because AI is the newest employee at your business. In addition to needing policies and procedures to follow, it also needs training and oversight just like an employee does. Second, give current employees the chance to utilize AI, and when making future employment decisions, build AI capability into job descriptions. Third, have employees use the paid versions, making sure they’re turning off the learning capabilities. Otherwise, competitors could unintentionally learn closely guarded secrets.

At Lamacchia, we’ve been working on some larger projects and shipping quicker wins along the way. We recently released a branding tool agents install into their own AI, so anything they generate comes out compliant with our brand standards automatically. The next one in beta testing translates forms, documents and flyers into any language.

How will AI change the way brokerages approach recruiting, onboarding, training and employee development?

Real estate is a people business, and the relationship part is the part AI doesn’t touch, but everything around it changes. Recruiting is already moving that way. Sourcing, screening, scheduling, the first follow-up are all getting automated. My caution as an HR professional is that you still own the outcome. If a vendor’s tool screens someone out, that’s your decision, and you need to be able to explain how it was made. Onboarding is where you can save administrative time. New people ask the same 20 questions in their first week, and they ask them at night and on weekends when there’s nobody there to answer. AI answers instantly, and it answers the same way every time. Training and development are where the real gains are. With AI, you can give every agent individualized coaching. You can let them practice a listing presentation, review their own scripts, get feedback at 10 p.m. when they actually have time. None of that replaces person-to-person interactions, but it helps bridge gaps.

What role do you see HR playing in helping people adapt, learn and take advantage of new technologies?

HR has to be at the table early. Historically, HR gets brought in at the end of a technology decision to write the policy after somebody else already picked the tool. With AI, that’s backwards, because almost every risk is a people risk. HR needs to be part of the decision, not the cleanup.

The second piece is making it safe to learn. People won’t experiment with something they think is going to replace them. If your employees believe AI is a threat, they’ll quietly avoid it, and you won’t find out until you’re two years behind. HR helps set that tone.

Third is guardrails: policies, approved tools, what can and can’t go into a prompt, what gets reviewed before it leaves the building. This gives people something to work inside of so they’re not figuring it out alone and making different decisions than you would about your data.

#5580. Agent fleets drag the messaging layer from afterthought to AI’s coordination core

Data center telemetry, sandboxed AI workloads and fleets of agents are pushing more machine-to-machine traffic through infrastructure than ever before, exposing the limits of messaging systems built for steadier demand.

That shift is drawing attention to the Neural Autonomic Transport System, an open-source messaging system that lets applications and services exchange messages by topic. Created in 2010, NATS graduated from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation in November 2026. Its simple design suits AI workloads, according to Andrew Connolly (pictured, left), NATS project maintainer at Synadia Communications Inc., a provider of managed NATS services. When AI tools like Lovable can turn a plain-language prompt into a working web app, the messaging layer has to keep updates flowing as sandboxes come and go.

“What’s changed in the current context, or landscape, is everything is really ephemeral. If you take the Lovable example, connections coming and going really fast, tons of churn, tons of sandboxes, all these things spinning up, spinning down,” Connolly said. “Not every technology can handle that.”

Connolly and Waldemar Quevedo (right), project maintainer of NATS at Synadia, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how NATS handles traffic from short-lived sandboxes, carries data center telemetry and helps AI agents hand off work. (* Disclosure below.)

The demands go well beyond app sandboxes. The project itself has grown from single-cluster deployments into a system that spans data centers, regions and clouds, with one AI app builder recently rebuilding its real-time service on NATS to serve millions of subscriptions, Quevedo noted.

“NATS has evolved to be able to communicate multiple data centers with a super cluster topology with the gateways,” Quevedo said. “It is smart [at routing] the interest graph out to multiple regions, multiple availability zones, multi-cloud.”

Some data center operators use NATS to carry power and cooling telemetry, and Nvidia Corp. built its AI factory event bus on the system as part of its DSX reference architecture, Connolly said. NATS can also route messages across fleets of AI agents, with its JetStream persistence engine and key-value store preserving the state agents need to hand off work.

“In some sense, agentic systems are just microservices systems, but at a bigger scale,” Connolly said. “NATS was good for microservices. It’s going to be great for AI agents.”

#5579. Provo Housing Market: Momentum Meets a Changing Market

As housing conditions shift, a market’s local economy offers an important starting point for understanding where the market is headed. In the Provo, Utah, metro, total nonfarm employment reached 324,000 payrolls in August, up 1.1% from a year earlier, while the unemployment rate declined to 3.4%.

That economic momentum is encouraging, but it is being tested by softer conditions in the housing market.

One important competitive dynamic is the relationship between new and existing home prices. As of July, the median new-home closing price was $495,800, compared with $541,000 for existing homes. That pricing relationship gives builders an avenue to compete with the resale market even as affordability remains challenging.

Sales conditions, however, are mixed. Annualized new-home sales totaled 4,594 units in August, down 6.1% year over year (YOY). Annualized detached sales increased 5.3% YOY, while attached sales declined 17.8%, underscoring different demand conditions by product type.

Supply is another increasingly important part of the story. Finished vacant inventory increased 18.9% YOY to 1,011 units as of Q2 2026. Zonda estimates the Provo market will be 3.89% oversupplied at year-end 2026.

The number of active detached new-home projects decreased roughly 1% YOY as of October while the number of active attached projects was flat. Total building permits are expected to decline by nearly 15% YOY in 2026.

Provo presents a market with two competing realities. Household and employment growth continue to support underlying housing demand, but elevated finished inventory, softer new-home sales, and affordability constraints argue for disciplined production. The projected decline in permitting could eventually help rebalance supply, but near-term execution will remain critical as builders compete for price sensitive buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published in Zonda Enterprise.

#5578. Mapped: Where the Most Homeowners Own Their Homes Outright With No Mortgage

Roughly 3 in 5 American homeowners pay a mortgage every month, yet the share of those who own their property outright is steadily growing—with at least half of all homeowners in three states now completely mortgage-free.

According to a new Realtor.com® data analysis of the recently released 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates, 59% of homeowners carried a mortgage last year, while 41% owned their homes free and clear.

That marks a major shift from 2010, when fewer than a third of homes (32.8%) were owned outright while 67% carried home loan debt.

Mortgaged homeownership has shrunk across all four regions, though reliance on financing still varies significantly by geography. The West had the highest mortgage debt rate at 63.8%, while the South recorded the lowest at 56.8%. The Northeast and Midwest tied at 58.7%.

At the state level, West Virginia led the nation with 56.6% of its homeowners living mortgage-free, followed by Mississippi (52.7%) and New Mexico (50%).

On the other side of the spectrum, Washington, DC, in 2025 logged the lowest share of outright homeownership, at just 26.5%, trailed by Maryland (30.6%) and Colorado (31.6%).

Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu explains that the balance between mortgaged and free-and-clear homes meaningfully shapes housing market dynamics, especially at a time when mortgage rates are high.

"Areas where owners rely more heavily on mortgages are more sensitive to rate changes, because monthly payments and the cost of moving both rise with borrowing costs," says Xu. "Areas with a higher share of outright ownership are less exposed and may feel smaller effects from rate shocks because residents who own their homes outright are likely indifferent to changes in borrowing costs."

Ultimately, those market forces sway inventory levels, home prices, and whether first-time buyers can access homeownership.

With mortgage rates stuck above 7% and the Federal Reserve all but certain to raise interest rates in December—and possibly again in January 2027—to combat inflation, the lock-in effect is poised to chill the market again.

Homeowners sitting on low mortgage rates are reluctant to give them up, keeping much-needed inventory off the market. That supply squeeze, in turn, puts upward pressure on prices and makes it harder for renters to access homeownership.

Free-and-clear owners, however, are not bound by borrowing costs and can list whenever they choose.

"A mortgage-free owner isn’t watching interest rates to decide when to move," Christie Goldman, a real estate agent with Better Homes and Gardens Real Estate Central in Charleston, WV, tells Realtor.com. "They can buy their next home with cash, which makes their offer stronger, and they can close on their own timeline without a lender, an appraisal contingency, or rate risk."

Across the 50 states and the District of Columbia, West Virginia stands out with the lowest share of mortgaged homes, at 43.4%, and conversely the highest share of outright ownership, at 56.6%.

Two main forces drive this dynamic: relatively low median home prices and an older population that tends to hold on to properties longer than residents in many other states.

"In West Virginia, a paid-off home isn’t a someday goal. It's how people here live," says Goldman. "When people put down roots here, they stay."

It is common for a local family to purchase a home, raise their children there, and pay it off, often with the next generation buying property in the same community.

According to Goldman, affordability is what makes that cycle possible.

In October 2026, the median asking price in West Virginia was $259,999, well below the national median of $415,000.

"At those prices, owning your home free and clear is a realistic goal here, not a distant dream," says the agent, pointing to the 2025 United Van Lines’ national study that ranked West Virginia as the second-leading inbound destination for movers.

"Many of those buyers sell a higher-priced home elsewhere and can pay cash here," says Goldman. "Once they discover the mountains, the community, and the pace of life, they don’t want to leave."

Xu also attributes West Virginia's high share of mortgage-free owners to the state's slow population growth, particularly among young adults, which has kept new borrowers from entering the market in large numbers.

Between 2015 and 2025, the population aged 18–34 fell 5% in West Virginia, while the same age group in the U.S. grew 3.8%.

Owning one's home outright offers many perks, sharply reducing monthly expenses and creating a buffer against economic headwinds.

"Mortgage-free homeowners have more financial flexibility, especially with today's higher interest rates and rising living costs," Thomas O’Shaughnessy, vice president and real estate broker at Clever Real Estate, tells Realtor.com. "They don't have monthly mortgage payments, which makes it easier to manage expenses, save money, and handle unexpected repairs or emergencies."

In theory, a high percentage of debt-free homeowners can also help unlock inventory for the next wave of buyers.

"They may be more willing to list, downsize, move elsewhere, or buy again," says O'Shaughnessy. "All of these can improve inventory and help move the market in your community."

In West Virginia, however, Goldman notes that high levels of mortgage-free ownership does not necessarily flood the market with fresh listings because people put down deep roots and tend to stay in their homes for decades.

On the flip side, Washington, DC, and Maryland log the highest shares of mortgaged homes in the nation, at 73.5% and 69%, respectively—a trend Xu links to the region's job market.

"Federal, professional, and contracting employment draws midcareer workers, who buy homes and borrow soon after arriving," she notes.

In 2025, nearly 45% of DC homeowners and 36% of Maryland homeowners were aged 35 to 54. Elevated housing costs also force many buyers to finance: The median listing price in DC was $549,000 and $424,894 in Maryland last month.

Given that local homeowners carry so much mortgage debt, rate hikes hit markets like DC and Maryland particularly hard.

"Many buyers there need loans, so fewer can afford to buy, and homeowners with low-rate mortgages are less likely to sell," says Xu.

The latest ACS data from the U.S. Census Bureau shows that in 2025, homeownership among households aged 75 and up rose to 78.3%, up from 75.7% in 2010.

During the same period, the mortgage-free share among this demographic fell from 79.7% to 71.3%. In other words, most baby boomers still own outright, but the share with a loan rose from 20.3% to 28.7%.

Xu says the two trends—more seniors owning their homes, and more of those owners carrying a mortgage—together shape when senior sellers are likely to list.

"A senior with a low-rate loan faces a lock-in effect in today’s high-rate environment," says Xu. "Selling means giving up that cheap financing for a more expensive loan on the next home, which can keep the house off the market longer and slow the handoff to the next generation."

Meanwhile, seniors who own outright can sell on their own schedule, whether for health, care, or downsizing, so their home is more likely to pass to the next generation when the owner’s circumstances change.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5576. Why Is Crypto Down? $14.2B Stablecoin Drain Turns a Bad Morning Into a Market-Wide Rout

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Why is crypto down? Bitcoin crashed below $69,000 just now, dragging the crypto markets into another brutal selloff. Ethereum slipped below $2,000, while several major altcoins recorded losses exceeding 6%.

The decline comes as crypto faces a dangerous combination of shrinking dollar liquidity, institutional withdrawals, and aggressive leveraged selling. The situation is becoming increasingly uncomfortable. Investors are pulling capital from stablecoins and Bitcoin ETFs, leaving fewer buyers to absorb selling pressure. Once Bitcoin broke below $70,000, leveraged traders faced another wave of forced liquidations.

The biggest warning sign comes from the stablecoin market, where the amount of available dollar liquidity is shrinking rapidly. Glassnode reported that major stablecoin supply declined by $14.2 billion over 30 days. This is the sharpest decline since the 2022 bear market, when the Terra collapse triggered widespread capital withdrawals.

Total stablecoin supply has fallen below $280 billion, returning to levels last seen around September 2025. Meanwhile, CryptoQuant recorded a $6.6 billion decline in USDT market cap over 60 days through November 7. This is concerning because the USDT contraction exceeded twice the decline recorded following the FTX collapse in December 2022.

Stablecoins function as crypto’s cash reserves. Traders use USDT and USDC to move between exchanges, purchase crypto, and maintain liquidity without leaving the blockchain ecosystem. So, when investors redeem stablecoins for dollars, that purchasing power leaves the market. Glassnode itself warned that shrinking supply leaves less fuel available for another rally.

The liquidity problem is arriving alongside persistent institutional selling. US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $1.6 billion across 20 trading sessions. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $47.7 million in net outflows on November 12, extending their withdrawal streak to six consecutive trading sessions.

Bitwise’s BITB led withdrawals with $26.4 million, while Morgan Stanley’s MSBT recorded $3.3 million in inflows. Ethereum ETFs also showed at least $8 million in net outflows in November 12 data.

The combination creates an uncomfortable situation. Crypto is losing dollar liquidity while regulated investment products continue recording withdrawals. There are fewer fresh buyers available to support prices when sellers rush toward the exit.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The liquidity squeeze eventually reached the derivatives market, where falling prices triggered another wave of forced selling. Bitcoin plunged 7% over 24 hours to $68,400 in 15 minutes this morning. Ethereum dropped 6% to $1,920, while BNB declined 6.3% and XRP lost 3.5%.

Liquidations also hit $1.64 billion over 24 hours. Long positions accounted for $1.46 billion, with more than 175,000 traders losing their positions. The damage accelerated after Bitcoin lost the $70,000 level. Traders betting on a recovery suddenly faced liquidation thresholds, forcing exchanges to close leveraged positions.

These forced closures created a feedback loop that pushed prices lower and exposed more leveraged positions. Macro conditions are not helping, too. Stronger US inflation figures increased expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike in December, which is almost certain now.

A stronger dollar and rising Treasury yields also weakened demand for speculative assets. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s leadership crisis unsettled technology markets, adding to the risk-off mood.

Crypto now faces several problems simultaneously. Stablecoin supply is contracting, ETF investors are withdrawing capital, and leveraged traders are being forced out. The combination might answer our question today: why crypto is down.

#5575. The Future of Home: 5 Trends for the Next 50 Years

What does the future of housing design look like? Much like with homes today, trends will be tied to how people live. To predict where design is headed, we need to consider how lifestyles are changing, identify which needs have staying power, and anticipate how homes might evolve to meet them.

DAHLIN Group assembled the top trends for the next 50 years to mark the firm’s 50th anniversary, reflecting on decades of design work to determine what the future looks like. According to DAHLIN, these will be key trends:

BUILDER spoke with DAHLIN’s Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, and Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, for their insight on why these trends will endure.

Fifty years is a long time to forecast residential design trends. How did you decide on these five trends, and what’s behind their staying power?

Wagner: A responsible 50-year view should not claim to know the exact layout, style, or construction method people will use. It should identify what future design must be able to do.

The common principle is agency: giving people more useful choices without requiring them to rebuild their lives or surroundings every time circumstances change.

The solutions to these needs will manifest in dramatically different ways over the next 50 years, but the needs themselves are unlikely to disappear.

How will wellness become more integrated?

Julian: Wellness will move deeper into the core decisions that shape everyday performance.

Daylight, window placement and performance, shading, material choices, air filtration, thermal zoning, and access to outdoor space will be considered together, rather than added as isolated features.

We also expect the idea of restorative space to become more distributed. A home does not need one wellness room if daylight, nature, movement, quiet, and thermal comfort are part of the daily path through the house. That makes wellness more relevant across housing types and price points.

The larger shift is from visible elements to a measurable and felt experience: cleaner air, better control, more useful daylight, a stronger relationship to the outdoors, and spaces that support both activity and retreat.

Design is already leaning away from fully open concept. How might this evolve?

Wagner: People want connection without constant exposure. The open plan still serves cooking, gathering, and shared family life extremely well, but a home now has to absorb more simultaneous activities. A call, homework, quiet conversation, and meal preparation may all happen at once.

People do not necessarily want more rooms; they want more control over how rooms relate.

These allow a space to borrow light and belong to the larger home when open, then become visually or acoustically distinct when needed.

Over time, this can make floor plans less defined. A room may shift between office, study, guest space, care space, or retreat because its boundaries and connections were designed to change.

The goal is not maximum openness at every moment. It is to give the homeowner control over when spaces participate in the life of the home and when they recede.

How will the design partnership with AI evolve?

Wagner: AI can already help teams generate and compare more early visual directions, translate abstract language into discussable imagery, and communicate a concept before investing in a complete visualization package. It can also help align a client and design team when they’re using the same word to mean different things.

The important limitation is that human expertise remains vital in framing the challenge, recognizing what is plausible, selecting the direction that serves the client best, and turning an evocative image into architecture that functions.

AI can quickly generate ideas and multiply options, but the designer must still decide which options deserve to move forward and turn them into a workable, real plan.

The near-term model is therefore collaborative. AI broadens the field of possibilities, while human experts frame the question, curate the outputs, and carry the selected idea into a coherent, buildable design.

Homeowners are placing greater importance on opportunities for social connection. How will future site and community planning support this?

Julian: Instead of relying only on a large destination facility such as a clubhouse or pool area, communities can offer a network of smaller lawns, gardens, play and sport areas, outdoor work settings, cafes or neighborhood retail, and places to sit along daily routes.

Smaller scale can also make participation easier and more approachable. It’s easier to join one of a few seats than to become the only person in a room designed for dozens. The same amount of common area can create more opportunities for connection when it’s placed closer to where people live and is shaped for different levels of participation.

When social space is woven into day-to-day patterns, community becomes a series of low-pressure encounters that can grow into familiarity and belonging.

Why will flexibility be the key to longevity in design?

Julian: Flexibility supports longevity when it reduces the cost and disruption of change. A room that has no assigned use may be flexible on paper, but true adaptability comes from practical decisions: useful daylight, appropriate openings, accessible routes, service relationships, and connections to indoor and outdoor space.

Those decisions determine whether a garage bay can credibly become an office or gym, or whether an ADU can serve a renter, a returning child, or an aging parent at different points in time.

The benefit is not that one design and layout lasts forever. It’s designing change into the bones of the home so that the home can adapt for a wide variety of family configurations without becoming obsolete.

Heather Wright is a senior writer for NewHomeSource and Builder with a background in real estate reporting and home design, decor, and architecture. She has written for a number of print and digital publications in the lifestyle space.

#5574. Mirendil raises $1B in funding to speed up AI model development

Mirendil Inc., a provider of software that speeds up artificial intelligence development, has raised $1 billion in early-stage funding.

The startup stated on Thursday that Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital jointly led the Series A investment. They were joined by more than a half-dozen others including Google LLC.

Mirendil was launched last year by two former Google DeepMind and Anthropic PBC researchers. Chief Executive Officer Behnam Neyshabur is a co-inventor of SAM, a popular algorithm that makes AI models better at tasks they were not specifically trained to perform. Chief Technology Officer Harsh Mehta, in turn, spent his time at Google DeepMind and Anthropic working on pretraining projects. Pretraining is a term for the initial phase of the AI development workflow.

Mirendil’s first product, Lor, is a platform that automates many of the tasks involved in model training runs. The company says that the software does so by splitting work among hundreds of AI agents.

Large language model development involves a significant amount of trial and error. Researchers create multiple versions of an algorithm that differ from one another in small ways and compare them to find the most performant variant. According to Mirendil, Lor can automate that workflow. If an error crops up during the evaluation, the platform fixes it automatically.

Earlier this year, Mirendil asked one of its researchers to build a coding model that can compete with leading open-source LLMs. Usually, such projects are carried out by teams of specialists. Mirendil says that its automation technology enabled the researcher to build the model without any help from colleagues. The project cost $10 million and took about 3.5 months to complete.

The company’s agents wrote more than 99% of the code that powers the model, which is called Mirendil-Base. They set up infrastructure, found a suitable training algorithm and collected training data from the web. The agents then refined both the training dataset and Mirendil-Base’s architecture to boost output quality.

The LLM is the foundation of a specialized coding model called Fern that the company unveiled last month. According to Mirendil, it’s designed to automate programming challenges commonly encountered by AI labs. Fern can process 10 million input tokens per prompt, or 10 times more than Claude Opus 5.5. That’s the equivalent of about a half-million lines of code.

Fern is based on a version of Mirendil-Base with 100 billion to 500 billion parameters. Late last month, the company previewed two upgraded versions of the latter model with between 500 billion and 10 trillion parameters. Mirendil plans to use those algorithms to develop more capable LLMs.

#5573. View Homes Debuts New Brand Identity to Match Future Growth

View Homes has unveiled a new brand identity designed to create a more consistent presence across its operations in Colorado, New Mexico, and Texas.

Led by CEO Natasha Gandhi, the rebrand brings the company’s existing Aspen View, Desert View, and Horizon View divisions together under the unified View Homes name. The new identity will roll out across offices, model homes, communities, and the builder’s public-facing materials in the coming weeks.

“View Homes has spent decades earning a reputation for quality homes and a people-first culture,” said Gandhi, who became CEO in the spring of this year. “This evolution doesn’t change what the company stands for. It gives that foundation the discipline, consistency, and expression it needs to grow.”

The new brand is organized around four pillars: Exceptional Experience, People-First, Design-Forward, and Premium. View Homes, which is No. 73 on the 2026 Builder 100 list, says the framework is intended to establish a consistent standard for the customer experience, design, and quality across its markets.

The visual identity pairs updated typography with photography featuring real-life moments in residential spaces. The rebrand does not change the company’s existing teams, partnerships, or commitments to customers, View Homes points out.

The launch comes as the 35-plus-year-old builder grows its footprint. View Homes currently operates in Northern Colorado, Colorado Springs, Las Cruces, San Antonio, and El Paso, and is expanding into the Denver market at Sterling Ranch.

“We build homes with intention and care that are designed for the way people actually live,” Gandhi said. “Premium doesn’t mean out of reach. It means doing it right at every price point, in every market we build in.”

The new identity is anchored by the brand line, “View Homes. Uncompromising quality. Genuine heart. Built to last.”

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5572. Contractor at Site of Brooklyn Building Collapse Was Previously Sued for Negligence

The general contractor overseeing the construction site adjacent to a deadly building collapse in Brooklyn, NY, was previously accused in a lawsuit of compromising the structural integrity of nearby properties during an excavation project, court records show.

Signage at the construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave., as well as planning documents filed with the Department of Buildings, show that Townhouse Builders, Inc, doing business as Promont, was the general contractor overseeing the construction project.

Building records show that the project involved excavation work directly adjacent to the three-story mixed-use building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. that fully collapsed on Wednesday, killing eight people, including two children, and leaving 18 others injured.

The construction project had a documented history of safety concerns flagged by DOB inspectors, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani says there will be a full investigation into whether any issues at the Bedford Ave. construction site contributed to the collapse.

"If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them accountable," the mayor said.

Now, court records reviewed by Realtor.com® show that Townhouse Builders was accused in a 2020 lawsuit of causing "a breached wall, substantial shifting, settlement and cracking" to an adjacent property during a separate construction job.

New York state records list Mordachai Waisbrod as the CEO of Townhouse Builders. The company and an attorney listed as representing the Townhouse in the 2020 lawsuit did not respond to requests for comment from Realtor.com.

Townhouse Builders has worked on numerous projects across New York, including a retail location on Atlantic Ave., a residential tower on Delancey St. in the Lower East Side, and the redevelopment of a residential tower on Park Row.

In 2016, Townhouse Builders was hired by developer Moris Yeroshalm to serve as general contractors on the construction of a six-story hotel at 1200 Broadway in Brooklyn's Bed-Stuy neighborhood.

In a lawsuit filed in Kings County Supreme Court in 2020, Yeroshalmi alleged that "the construction activity performed by Townhouse at the Project caused damage and compromised the structural integrity of Plaintiff's property and adjacent properties."

The suit alleges that "the construction caused, among other things, a breached wall, substantial shifting, settlement and cracking of Plaintiff's property and the adjacent properties, in addition to broken footing of the adjacent properties and structural destabilization of Plaintiff's property and the adjacent properties."

The suit lists the allegedly damaged properties as 1196 Broadway, and 15 and 17 Patchen Avenue, all located in Brooklyn.

The lawsuit further alleges that 1196 Broadway "was severely damaged by the excavation activity" and that 15 and 17 Patchen Ave. "were severely damaged by the pile driving activities."

In the suit, Yeroshalmi alleges Townhouse "breached their duty and were negligent … by allowing construction activities to compromise and destroy the structural integrity of Plaintiff's property and adjacent properties."

Further, the lawsuit accuses Townhouse of "failing to perform a physical inspection and prepare a proper pre-construction survey of Plaintiff's property prior to performing excavation and underpinning, failing to support the premises walls and by allowing the excavation and underpinning to compromise the structural integrity of Plaintiff's property and adjacent properties."

Yeroshalmi sued for damages totaling more than $1.1 million. The suit remains open with the next hearing in the case to be held in January 2027.

A review of Department of Buildings complaints and violations related to 1200 Broadway show that Townhouse Builders received a Class 2 or "major" violation in 2016 for "failure to monitor adjoining structures for movement in all directions during excavation-related activity that may adversely affect adjoining structures."

That same year, it received a Class 1 violation for "failure to safeguard all persons and property affected by construction operations," noting that the excavator's bucket damaged the brick foundation wall of an adjoining building during excavation. Class 1 violations are "Immediately Hazardous violations" that "must be corrected immediately."

In 2017, it received another Class 2 violation for failure to monitor cracks on adjacent buildings during excavation.

In total, the DOB fined Townhouse Builders $10,400 for those three violations.

Court records show Townhouse Builders, under their own name and Promont, have been sued 67 times since 2012. Thirteen of those cases, including the one mentioned above, remain open. It appears the bulk of those cases have to do with injuries on job sites.

On Wednesday, the Brooklyn district attorney's office announced it was opening a criminal investigation into the cause of the collapse.

“We are working closely with the Department of Buildings and our law enforcement partners to determine whether any criminal conduct contributed to this tragedy,” District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said in the statement.

On Thursday afternoon, Mamdani announced the city would be sweeping 100 other sites associated with five "entities" involved in a construction project adjacent to the collapsed building. The city has since expanded that search to 160 properties. Mamdani and Department of Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani declined to name the five companies they would be focusing their investigation on.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty.
