#5571. More Roofing Choices Without More Complexity

For roofing professionals, the expectations surrounding a roofing project continue to expand. A roof is no longer evaluated solely on its ability to protect homes from the elements. In addition to standing up to increasingly unpredictable weather, roofing products are expected to deliver lasting value while complementing and even elevating the architectural style and character of a home.

With greater regularity, roofing professionals are learning to navigate a market where performance expectations, design preferences, and project requirements have become more challenging.

It’s a combination of factors that has made flexibility increasingly important. A roofing solution that works well for one architectural style or climate may not be the right fit for another. There’s a growing need to access materials that can meet a range of aesthetic preferences and performance demands, while homeowners want the confidence that their choices will provide both the protection they expect and the look they envision.

Against that backdrop, a roofing brand called US Tile is bringing two established roofing materials—concrete and clay—together under a single, made-in-the-U.S. portfolio. The aim is to offer a more comprehensive selection of tile roofing options while simplifying the process of navigating those choices.

Benefits of Concrete and Clay From a Single Source

Rather than looking across multiple sources to find the right combination of styles, profiles, colors, and performance characteristics, roofing contractors and builders can explore a broader portfolio within a unified offering.

Some projects may call for the versatility and design range of concrete, while others may benefit from the distinctive character of clay. With both materials represented within the same portfolio, there’s greater flexibility to match a roof to the look of the home, the preferences of the homeowner, and the durability demands of the local environment.

Beyond aesthetics, having access to concrete and clay roofing from the same manufacturer makes it easier to spec and offer homeowners two energy-efficient, Class A fire-rated materials that hold up to prolonged exposure to the elements and extreme weather.

More Productive Conversations Between Roofing Professionals and Homeowners

A broader range of materials and possibilities can make homeowner discussions more fruitful. Instead of starting with a limited set of materials and working backward from what is available, offering concrete and clay from the same source means each project can be approached with a wider range of potential solutions. There’s more opportunity to balance appearance, performance, budget, and other project considerations without unnecessarily complicating the specification process.

A unified portfolio can result in simplified access to product information and support while reducing some of the hurdles that can arise when coordinating different materials and suppliers. Across multiple busy projects, those efficiencies can matter just as much as the products themselves.

A Broader Portfolio and Greater Design Flexibility

Ultimately, combining concrete and clay roofing under one made-in-the-U.S. brand is about giving professionals more ways to meet the demands of their projects. A broader portfolio allows for greater design flexibility, while the performance characteristics of concrete and clay tile roofing help address homeowners’ growing expectations for resilience and long-term value.

With more options and a more streamlined path to finding them, roofing professionals can approach each project with greater confidence—and homeowners can have more faith in their next roof as a smart long-term choice that adds value and peace of mind.

#5570. More Than a Closing: The Growing Role of Financial Services in Home Building

Historically, financial services have occupied a relatively straightforward role in the home builder business model. Mortgage, title insurance, and related services could generate ancillary revenue while helping buyers move from contract to closing.

Today, that traditional role has shifted amid a challenging affordability environment, mounting pressure on margins, and heightened buyer expectations. Financial services have elevated from an adjacent business opportunity to a more strategic part of the home building platform.

The question is increasingly not simply how much revenue these services can generate, but how they can help builders sell homes, create a more consistent home buyer experience, and operate more efficiently at scale.

Mortgage services may provide the most obvious example. With mortgage rates recently returning to the 7% range, affordability remains a defining challenge for the industry. In September, 66% of builders surveyed by the National Association of Home Builders reported using sales incentives. Zonda similarly reported that more than 80% of new-home communities offered incentives on quick move-in homes in August.

In that environment, financing is no longer simply what happens after a buyer decides to purchase a home; rather, it becomes a core part of what makes the purchase possible in the first place.

It may be with this in mind that large builders have placed such emphasis on their mortgage capabilities. For example, two of the nation’s largest public builders recently reported mortgage capture rates above 80%, underscoring how closely financing has become integrated with the home sale.

The strategic value goes beyond capturing mortgage revenue. An effective financing platform gives builders another lever to address affordability, tailor incentives, and help qualified buyers get across the finish line.

The same strategic thinking increasingly applies to title, settlement, and other services surrounding the transaction.

Consider title and closing. These services sit at a critical point in the home buyer journey: the moment when months of searching, financing, construction, and anticipation culminate in ownership.

For the buyer, those distinctions between companies and functions may matter very little. The mortgage process, communications leading up to closing, signing experience, and delivery of the keys can all become part of a single perception of the builder’s brand. Delivering a consistently superior closing experience becomes an increasingly important element of how buyers remember the home builder.

For builders operating across multiple markets, however, delivering consistency can be difficult. Growth through geographic expansion or acquisition can leave behind fragmented networks of local providers, processes, and systems.

“What works well across a handful of communities can become much harder to manage across dozens of markets and thousands of closings,” says Anne Law, president of First American Title’s Homebuilder Services Division. “That’s why builders are increasingly looking at financial services as a scalable platform with consistent processes, strong underwriting, and an excellent closing experience, rather than a collection of individual transactions.”

Importantly, a more integrated strategy does not necessarily mean bringing every capability in-house. Builders are placing greater emphasis on capital efficiency and asset-light operating models, and those same principles now drive decisions on how they approach financial services.

The objective is not necessarily ownership. It is control over the things that matter most: the customer experience, service standards, data visibility, operating consistency, and economics. Scale adds another consideration. Licensing, regulatory requirements, and operating standards can vary across jurisdictions, adding complexity as builders expand into new markets. Experienced financial services partners like First American Title can provide infrastructure and expertise to help navigate those requirements.

That creates room for a range of models, including wholly owned operations and strategic partnerships. The right structure will vary by builder, service, and market. What matters is whether the model balances control, investment, and operating responsibility while supporting scalable growth, regulatory compliance, and a consistent customer experience.

From Ancillary Revenue to Strategic Infrastructure

The evolution of financial services ultimately reflects a broader change in how builders compete.

When affordability is strained, financing can help sell the home. When buyers expect a seamless process, well-executed and consistent title and closing services can reinforce and enhance the home-buying experience. And when builders operate across expanding footprints, standardized financial-services relationships can create greater consistency, visibility, and efficiency.

Revenue matters. But there are other parts of the equation that are important. For example, builders today are closely examining how mortgage, title, and settlement fit into the broader operating model and whether those capabilities are structured to support the next stage of growth.

In that sense, financial services are becoming less ancillary to the home building business and more integral to how modern builders sell, serve, and scale.

#5569. Exclusive: Onyx Security brings AI agent governance to Glean’s enterprise AI platform

AI agent security startup Onyx Security Inc. today announced an integration with enterprise artificial intelligence platform company Glean Technologies Inc. to help enterprises govern the AI agents they build and run on Glean.

Onyx and Glean are pitching the integration at companies that are moving quickly to roll out autonomous, connected agents across their departments. Onyx claims, however, that most of them are not yet prepared to manage the risks that agents bring.

According to Onyx, security teams now need to keep continuous track of agent access, actions and policy compliance. Under the partnership, Glean provides the platform to build, deploy and operate the agents, while the Onyx secure AI control plane is used to extend governance and security across the AI environment.

At the core of the integration is discovery, with Onyx able to inventory every Glean agent and the access and capabilities it holds. Ownership, business purpose and a risk classification can then be assigned to each agent, according to the companies.

Enterprise AI governance and compliance policies can also be applied through the integration, after which Onyx continuously assesses changes to the permissions, tools and data access granted to each agent. Intent-aware runtime controls, which Onyx applies to prompts, responses and agent actions, provide protection while the agents are running.

Unsafe requests can be blocked outright under the controls. In other cases, the controls are said to steer unintended agent actions back in line with company policy. Centralized audit evidence is also maintained across AI environments. From deployment through ongoing operation and expansion, the companies say, agents fall under a single governance model.

“As agents gain greater access and autonomy, security teams need visibility and control over what they can do,” said Gil Elbaz, co-founder and chief AI officer at Onyx, who previously worked under Nvidia Corp.’s chief technology officer. “By combining Glean’s enterprise context with Onyx’s security control plane, customers can govern agent activity consistently and confidently across their AI environment.”

Glean regards context and governance as “foundational to making enterprise AI both useful and trustworthy,” according to Zubin Irani, the company’s vice president of partnerships. The Onyx integration is said to build on that foundation as organizations deploy agents across their business.

Coming into the partnership, Onyx has raised $153 million to date, including a $113 million Series B round led by Bessemer Venture Partners in July. The company launched in March with $40 million in seed and Series A funding.

Glean, for its part, last raised $150 million in a Series F round at a valuation of $7.2 billion in June 2025.

#5568. Former Century Communities CFO David Messenger Named CEO of Villa

Offsite home builder Villa has named David Messenger, former chief financial officer of Century Communities, as CEO. In the role, Messenger will lead the company as it seeks to expand into larger residential communities and grow partnerships with home builders, land developers, and multifamily owners.

Messenger spent more than a decade as CFO of Century Communities, helping scale the company from 150 to 1,800 employees across 18 states. The company is also developing the 25-home Acacia Village in Santa Rosa, California, and Alpine Village in Westminster, Colorado.

#5567. Fed Boss: Superintelligence Will Rule, Good or Bad, Going Forward

In remarks on Nov. 16 that will likely impact the housing market going forward, Federal Reserve Open Market Committee Chairman Kevin Warsh emphasized that new ideas borne from “superintelligence” can move things forward idea-wise, which may impact economic policy and interest rates.

“The implications for economic policy can hardly be overstated,” he said. “While an idea can be costly to discover, it’s free to use. And because an idea is non-rival, one person’s use does nothing to diminish that of anyone else; its value grows with the number of people who use it. In the U.S., over the last several decades, breakthrough ideas have been harder to find.”

Warsh did not specifically address housing or future rate hikes, choosing to target how theoretically “superintelligence”—an alternative term for AI preferred by President Donald Trump—could affect every aspect of the economy. Following his remarks, he convened panels to solicit opinions from various business leaders.

“As a result, productivity growth has fluctuated, and while in recent quarters it has been reasonably strong, it hasn’t yet broken out definitively, structurally, reliably to the upside, at least not yet. Long-run growth is also a function of the rate of increase in the number of people producing these ideas, setting them in motion. The conventional view holds that as population growth slows, there may be fewer new ideas to drive prosperity.”

Earlier on the same day Warsh spoke, Fed Governor Michael Barr, in a speech at the Seventh Annual Association for Computing Machinery International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Finance, addressed some of the same issues, offering a more critical view of AI (and using the more common terminology).

Barr also addressed specific usages of AI around lending and housing, saying that while “institutions may increasingly use AI to expand household credit access through alternative data analysis,” care must be taken to avoid errors.

“AI poses significant compliance challenges,” he said. “The technology can function as a black box, making it difficult to explain adverse decisions or ensure compliance with fair lending laws. Alternative data sources such as rental payments, utility bills or employment patterns may expand access to credit if they are used appropriately, but they may also inadvertently serve as proxies for protected characteristics like race or national origin. Thus, care must be taken. Unlike traditional credit reports, consumers often cannot review or dispute this information.”

With one more Fed meeting scheduled this year, economists are predicting that there will be a rate hike which, in turn, would likely raise mortgage rates.

The Fed, in a late October meeting, left interest rates unchanged, despite inflationary pressures continuing to mount. The move was also not unanimous, as Federal Reserve officials voted 10-2 to keep interest rates unchanged, which varied greatly from the previous meeting in mid-September, which came with a unanimous vote to hike interest rates, after many economists predicted that outcome.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5565. Presley Gerber’s Hollywood Hills Home Hits the Market for $3.6 Million—Nearly 2 Months After His Death

Presley Gerber’s Hollywood Hills home has hit the market for $3.59 million, less than two months after the model’s death at age 27.

The son of Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber, who passed away on Sept. 20, snapped up the property for $3.4 million in March 2023.

Now, nearly two months after his tragic death, the property has hit the market for $3.6 million with real estate agent Cindy Ambuehl of Christie's AKG, as first reported by TMZ.

The dwelling is described as "beautifully reimagined mid-century architecture meets modern luxury in the heart of the Hollywood Hills."

The home features four bedrooms, three bathrooms, and sprawls across 3,000 square feet.

Built in 1955, the home sits behind gates in the Hollywood Hills. Canyon views frame the property, while the living spaces connect to outdoor areas through large sliding glass doors.

Inside, the main gathering space combines wood floors and a fireplace with access to the kitchen and dining areas.

The primary suite and guest bedrooms also open onto the pool and patio, allowing residents to step outside directly from their rooms.

The guest accommodation is attached to the house, according to the listing. It contains one bedroom and one bathroom, along with its own kitchen, laundry facilities, and private entrance.

That arrangement offers visitors a place to stay with access to everyday essentials beyond a bedroom and bathroom. The listing also presents the space as an option for extended stays or additional living quarters.

Outside, the pool shares the property’s roster of amenities with a Jacuzzi, cold plunge, and sauna. A dedicated gym area adds another fitness feature.

The sales description identifies updates to the roof, heating and air-conditioning system, floors, lighting, and sliding doors. Landscaping and outdoor lighting have also been improved.

Other advertised features include reverse osmosis water filtration and smart entry technology. Parking consists of a gated motor court and an oversized garage with epoxy flooring.

The property is marketed near Runyon Canyon, with access to Hollywood and West Hollywood.

"Offering true tranquility amid the surrounding hills, this architectural retreat is just moments from Runyon Canyon, the best of West Hollywood, Hollywood, and beyond," the listing adds.

Gerber died Sept. 20 while staying at a rehabilitation facility in Santa Monica. Police investigated his death as a suspected overdose, and the medical examiner initially deferred the cause of death while further investigation was underway.

The reported suspicion should not be confused with a confirmed medical finding. Us Weekly’s account cited a police statement indicating that there was no evidence of foul play at that time.

Following his death, Crawford and Rande shared a touching tribute remembering their son’s kindness and vulnerability and thanking those who had offered support.

“Presley Walker Gerber. July 2, 1999-September 20, 2026. We are beyond heartbroken to lose our beloved son and brother. We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years. He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever. We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability. We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain. Til we meet again our sweet boy," they shared in the joint statement.

His sister, model and actress Kaia Gerber, also shared an October tribute reflecting on her grief and their close relationship.

“Prez, I don’t have the words, and maybe the tiny mercy is that we didn’t need them all along. Words fail and words subtract and words summarize and words always lack truth. And how naive of me to believe that language could transcend grief. I’ve read all of the books and I have none of the answers. My articulation is no match against this, the magnitude of losing you. I am, quite literally, down on my f—ing knees," she penned.

Now publicly offered for sale, the Hollywood Hills property brings together a midcentury home, guest accommodation, and extensive outdoor amenities at an asking price just below $3.6 million.

#5564. Massive Microsoft outage disrupts businesses, government agencies worldwide

A glitch in Microsoft Corp.’s network has disrupted the work of businesses and government agencies in more than 70 countries.

The bug, which reared its head on Thursday about 12:35 p.m. EST, knocked the company’s popular Exchange Online platform offline. Organizations use the cloud service to store employees’ inboxes and calendars. Microsoft has still not fully restored its infrastructure.

Deployments of Exchange Server, a version of the platform that users run on-premises, are not affected. However, the outage did disrupt a number of Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Copilot 365 features that rely on data from users’ Exchange inboxes. Intune, a tool that administrators use to manage employee devices, is also experiencing technical issues.

The outage has hit numerous companies worldwide. Workhorse Group Inc., an electric vehicle maker, pushed back its earnings call from today to Monday. Shipping giant Maersk and stock exchange operator Euronext notified customers that they’re experiencing communications issues.

The public sector is also impacted. Several U.S. municipalities reported technical problems, while a number of court cases had to be delayed. In the U.K., the National Pharmacy Association warned that the Exchange Online outage may slow prescription processing. Hospitals, public transportation agencies and schools are affected as well.

The operator of Downdetector, an outage tracking service, received downtime reports from hundreds of thousands of users.

Parts of Microsoft’s infrastructure started recovering early this morning. In an update published at 2:30 a.m., the company stated that it was seeing “positive results” after patching an “upstream authentication/routing configuration” module. About three hours later, Microsoft’s systems in the Asia Pacific region began regaining service access. North America and Europe followed suit shortly there.

Microsoft shared its first explanation of what went wrong around noon today. “The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company explained. “We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”

Microsoft added that the outage wasn’t caused by a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

The company’s status page indicates that infrastructure restoration work is still ongoing. As a result, some users may have trouble accessing Exchange Online and certain Microsoft products that interact with it. The company is monitoring the backlog of emails that piled up while the service was offline to ensure no data loss occurs.

Microsoft plans to release a detailed technical report about the outage once all its services are fully restored.

#5563. Robert Pattinson Named the Next James Bond—Months After Joking His Beverly Hills Move Made Him ‘Bougie’

Robert Pattinson is taking over as James Bond—months after the British actor revealed that he and Suki Waterhouse had traded Los Angeles’ east side for a rental in Beverly Hills.

The 40-year-old will succeed Daniel Craig in the 26th Bond film, becoming the seventh actor to play 007 in the official series.

Denis Villeneuve will direct the still-untitled movie, with Steven Knight writing the screenplay and Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing. Craig last appeared as the British spy in 2021’s "No Time to Die."

Five months before the casting announcement, Pattinson told GQ that he, Waterhouse, and their young daughter were renting a house in Beverly Hills.

The move took him to a part of town where he said he’d never lived. In his earlier years in Los Angeles, he owned a large home in Los Feliz, which he eventually sold.

“I always thought I was an Eastside hipster guy. I would only ever come to Beverly Hills for my agency and stuff. Now I'm like, everything's kind of nice. Maybe I've turned bougie," he told the outlet.

One feature of the rental had a practical purpose: its home gym. Pattinson told GQ he was using it to train for "The Batman: Part II," the sequel to his 2022 debut as the superhero.

He recalled working out twice a day during preparations for his first turn as Batman and said that comments he’d made in interviews had given some people the wrong impression about how much he trained.

“[People said,] ‘You didn't work out at all.' I worked out every f—ing day. Even after that, I still look like I didn't work out. I worked out twice a day at, like, three o'clock in the morning," he told the outlet.

Pattinson has lived in Los Angeles on and off since his "'Twilight' years" in a "giant home that he wandered like a ghost," but his work still takes the family far from Beverly Hills.

He said his 2-year-old daughter had already joined Waterhouse on tour and accompanied him to film sets.

He also joked that fatherhood had changed his routine at home, where he now found himself going to bed far earlier than he used to.

The Batman sequel was set to shoot in London, and Pattinson said he had already looked into a possible school for his daughter while there.

The one that caught his attention was the school set up for the young actors on Warner Bros.’ new Harry Potter television series.

Pattinson has his own history with the franchise, having played Cedric Diggory before his breakout as Edward Cullen in "Twilight."

Bond will also reunite Pattinson with Villeneuve, who directed him in "Dune: Part Three." Before taking on 007, Pattinson had moved between major franchises and smaller films such as "Good Time" and "The Lighthouse."

His casting follows years of speculation about who would take over from Craig and marks the first Bond film since Amazon MGM Studios gained creative control of the franchise.

#5562. Lindsay Clancy’s Murder Retrial Set for March 2027—Inside the Massachusetts Home Where Her 3 Children Died

Lindsay Clancy is set to face a second murder trial on March 29, 2027—less than one year after her first case ended in a hung jury and more than three years after she was accused of murdering her three children inside the family's Massachusetts home.

Clancy, 36, has admitted to taking the lives of her daughter, Cora, 5, and sons Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan, but has pleaded not guilty to the three first-degree murder charges against her, with her attorneys arguing that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time of their deaths.

Over the course of the five-week trial, her defense team sought to convince jurors that Clancy should not be held legally accountable for the killings because of a "lack of criminal responsibility," according to the Boston Globe.

Following 19 hours of deliberation, the 12-person jury was declared deadlocked after telling state Judge William Sullivan it was unable to reach a unanimous verdict. Sullivan instructed the jurors to return to the deliberation room and continue their efforts to reach a verdict, before eventually declaring a mistrial.

Then, mere weeks ago, Clancy returned to court, where her legal team attempted to argue that she can't be retried due to double jeopardy in hopes to have the charges dropped. Meanwhile, the prosecution asked the judge to decline the motion to dismiss the charges, claiming they could have a retrial.

Now, it has been revealed that the prosecution will be retrying Clancy on the same charges, with pretrial hearings scheduled for Dec. 30 and Feb. 18.

Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, previously claimed that he was ready to begin the retrial as soon as possible. He also requested President Donald Trump pardon Clancy; however, presidents can only pardon federal offenses.

Though Clancy was present in the courtroom in Plymouth, MA, she did not testify during the trial, which featured sworn testimony from dozens of witnesses, including her former husband, Patrick Clancy, medical professionals who treated her for mental health issues, and a former nanny who looked after her children.

The former nurse accused several medical providers of malpractice and negligence, claiming that she was repeatedly misdiagnosed, even as her symptoms continued to worsen. On the night of Jan. 24, 2023, she reportedly experienced suicidal hallucinations and heard a voice telling her that it was her "last chance" to kill herself and her children.

The prosecution, however, argued that she wasn't diagnosed with postpartum depression and that the murders seem premeditated, calling attention to the fact that Clancy had reportedly looked up ways to murder on her cellphone prior to the deaths of her children.

While her husband, Patrick, was picking up a takeout meal, Clancy strangled her children and tried to take her own life by cutting her neck and wrists, then throwing herself out of her bedroom window at the family's Duxbury, MA, home.

Cora and Dawson were pronounced dead that same night, while Callan died in the hospital a few days later. Lindsay survived her injuries, but was left paralyzed from the waist down.

Clancy's husband took to the stand to testify on behalf of his wife—as did the couple's former nanny, Elaine Rossi, who described the former nurse as a "wonderful mother."

"I observed a wonderful mom who loved her kids," the nanny said, according to NBC10 Boston. "She cared for their safety, she was very concerned with Callan's eating and sleeping. She was a wonderful mother."

Rossi also told the court that Clancy had revealed to her she was "suffering from postpartum."

Patrick previously spoke out about his wife's horrifying crimes, sitting down with The New Yorker in October 2024 to defend her against critics, insisting that she was not "a monster."

At the time of the interview, the father of three explained that he had since relocated from Massachusetts to an apartment in New York City, quietly selling off the family's Duxbury home in an off-market deal.

In the interview, Patrick insisted that he "wasn't married to a monster," explaining how his wife had been suffering from anxiety and insomnia, which were brought on by her pregnancy with Callan.

Weeks before the terrible tragedy, he said, she had been hospitalized before being sent home with antidepressants. Despite all this, he said that he believed that her only diagnosis was a generalized anxiety disorder.

“I wasn’t married to a monster—I was married to someone who got sick,” he told the publication, adding that he had chosen to speak out to prevent further "lies and misinformation" from being spread.

Shortly after the deaths of his children, Patrick had issued a personal statement in which he asked the public to forgive his wife.

"A lot of people have said they can’t imagine and they’re right, there’s absolutely nothing that can prepare you," he wrote in the statement, which was shared on a GoFundMe page set up by his loved ones.

"The shock and pain is excruciating and relentless. I’m constantly reminded of them and with the little sleep I get, I dream about them on repeat. Any parent knows, it’s impossible to understand how much you will love your kids until you have them.

"The same goes for understanding the devastation of losing them. Cora, Dawson, and Callan were the essence of my life and I’m completely lost without them.

"My family was the best thing that ever happened to me. I took so much pride in being Lindsay’s husband and a dad to Cora, Dawson, and Callan. I always reminded myself that each day with them was a new gift."

He then shared touching tributes to each of his children, calling attention to his favorite things about them, including son Dawson's "bold, brown eyes" and daughter Cora's "infection laugh."

However, despite his grief, Patrick insisted that he had forgiven his wife, while urging the public to do the same.

"I want to ask all of you that you find it deep within yourselves to forgive Lindsay, as I have," he continued.

"The real Lindsay was generously loving and caring towards everyone—me, our kids, family, friends, and her patients. The very fibers of her soul are loving. All I wish for her now is that she can somehow find peace."

While the Clancy family home does not appear to have been listed for public sale since the tragic events unfolded inside it, Patrick revealed to The New Yorker that he had, in fact, sold it to an anonymous buyer, adding during the interview that he'd just been informed the sale has officially closed.

“There’s no house anymore,” he said. “There are no kids. All that’s left is me and Lindsay.”

He explained that he cleared out the house shortly after taking a solo trip to Central America and Europe in February 2024. He drove around his neighborhood gifting his children's stuffed animals and unused arcade cards to their friends.

Built in 1972, the home has been updated with refinished hardwood floors, a newer roof, and a redone kitchen with granite counters and new appliances and flooring. The three-bedroom, 1.5-bath interior spans 1,732 square feet with a remodeled extra room between the garage and kitchen.

The home sits on a tree-lined lot on almost an acre, with a deck, stone patio, and grassy lawn. The coastal town offers an "acclaimed" school system and a beautiful beach.

According to Realtor.com® records, the home last changed hands in 2018 for $500,000.

#5560. NiCE’s next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The contact center has been the low-hanging fruit for the artificial intelligence industry. Ask any information technology or business leader what they want to use agentic AI for, and they will say it’s to improve the customer experience, which starts with the contact center.

However, to date, the industry has spent the past two years arguing over which AI agent is the smartest. That’s the wrong debate. Model capabilities are improving so quickly and are getting so much cheaper that raw intelligence and reasoning are becoming the least differentiated part of the stack.

The real challenge for enterprises is operating a fleet of AI agents reliably across complete customer journeys, with the visibility and control a large business requires. Without that, the human, or worse, the customer, is left connecting the dots among the outputs of the growing number of agents they are communicating with.

That’s the thesis behind the next generation of NiCE Cognigy, which NiCE Ltd. launched this week. The release includes a redesigned Agentic Experience Studio, an AI Assist companion spanning the building, testing and improvement of agents, reusable “skills” that package instructions and tools, turn-by-turn tracing and native voice-to-voice model support.

Default speech-to-text, text-to-speech and large language models are now included in the per-conversation price, with premium models from Deepgram, ElevenLabs and Anthropic available with a few clicks and billed by usage.

Ahead of the launch, I attended an analyst briefing with Nhu Ho, senior product marketing manager at NiCE Cognigy, and with Clement Boutier, director of product management, who leads the team that built the release and owns the platform roadmap.

Here are the important points from this release:

Ho opened with a chart showing how long AI can work on its own before a human has to step in. In 2020, it was seconds; in 2024, it was minutes; and this year it’s roughly 16 hours. The footnote was interesting, as it calculated that figure at a 50% success rate. “Capable and dependable do not always mean the same thing,” Ho said. “That is exactly where the platform matters.”

For CX leaders, that’s a solid benchmark to consider. A 50% success rate is a research milestone. In a contact center, it’s a churn event or a compliance violation. As models commoditize, value shifts to the system around them: testing, tracing, guardrails and deterministic fallbacks. NiCE doesn’t build frontier models, and frontier model builders don’t run contact centers. Positioning Cognigy as the layer that makes AI dependable is a smart place to plant a flag.

Cognigy earned its pre-acquisition leadership position by handling complex production deployments for large brands such as Lufthansa, Mercedes and DHL. But that flexibility and customizability added complexity. Boutier put it this way: “The large number of options when configuring an agent creates friction to get started, which slows things down.” The new studio lets a builder stand up an agent in a few clicks, with models already provisioned, while power-user tools, including full access to the agent’s system prompt, are available in advanced sections.

This is important because NiCE aims to create a “1+1=3” value proposition for its current customers. NiCE needs Cognigy to expand broadly across the CXone installed base, not just among expert teams at the largest enterprises. Boutier described three builder personas: smaller businesses building simple agents, contact center administrators and team leads, and engineers at technically sophisticated companies. AI Assist is aimed squarely at the first two.

In the demo, it built an agent, tested it, fixed the problems it found, and deployed it to WhatsApp. The flip side is that lowering the barrier means more agents built by less experienced people, which makes the governance features the real story of this release.

Despite all the agentic hype, most enterprises aren’t ready to hand over entire journeys to an autonomous agent. Boutier outlined three modes: traditional natural language understanding, hybrid and fully agentic. Hybrid “is actually where most of our customers are,” he said, while fully agentic deployments are at the “beginning of the adoption curve.” This approach lets customers ease into agentic, build confidence and move to fully autonomous at their own pace.

NiCE designed the product for that approach. An agent can serve as the orchestration layer, calling existing flows as tools. Flows can also be placed in front of agents, for example, to scrub credit card numbers or other personal data before any data reaches a model. Ho described the release as “an evolution, not a replacement,” with production deployments, application programming interfaces and integrations continuing to run unchanged.

That’s a meaningful advantage over AI-native challengers whose pitch effectively requires a rebuild. Contact centers are the fastest-moving environments, and deterministic workflows aren’t legacy baggage. They’re how a business enforces what a large language model shouldn’t be deciding.

“You can have the best builder experience, but if you don’t have any feedback loop on what you’re building, you’re never going to build a great agent,” Boutier said. The new tracing shows each turn: which skill loaded, which tool was called and with what arguments, and when the agent handed off to a flow.

The Simulator now supports multivariate testing of up to 10 variants, using an LLM-as-judge to run synthetic customers against an agent. Boutier ran the same agent on two models and found that one was faster and consumed fewer tokens. This shifts model selection from a preference to a data-backed economic decision.

Voice-to-voice support may be the first feature customers deploy. Boutier noted that buyers are open to using a speech-to-text and text-to-speech cascade, “but what they realize is that voice-to-voice models sound just better.” In the demo, the agent delegated tool calls to a separate model while continuing to talk, making the conversation sound far more natural.

Cognigy now serves as both a Model Context Protocol client and server and supports agent-to-agent connections, including one customer linking Cognigy to agents built with Microsoft’s tooling. NiCE is also co-developing the Personal Agent Protocol with Meta and Sierra, which isn’t live yet. Boutier described Cognigy as “the front door” of the contact center, where a consumer’s personal agent must authenticate before it can proceed. It’s great to see NiCE collaborating with Sierra, a direct competitor, on this, as it makes things easier for a customer.

The industry views agent identity as a shared responsibility. But as Sierra outlines, companies can also let personal agents work through their websites and APIs, so the front-door position depends on enterprises routing that traffic through Cognigy. This lets brands interact with personal agents safely.

There has been a wave of companies banning personal agents, which I think is a mistake. If something is good for a consumer, it will happen, so it’s better to be on the leading edge of enabling it rather than fighting it.

This release is less about new capabilities and more about NiCE betting on where value will accrue as AI agents mature. Intelligence is getting cheaper. Dependability, governance and the ability to blend autonomous reasoning with deterministic control are not.

NiCE is the market leader in contact center as a service, as Cognigy was in conversational AI. Now the challenge is to get an easier-to-work-with Cognigy into the hands of thousands of CXone customers without creating a sprawl of individually governed agents. This will allow NiCE to maintain its industry leadership as personal agents arrive. As it does that, the Cognigy acquisition will move from an add-on to a core component of the NiCE platform.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5559. What Happened to Lindsay Clancy’s Home? How Duxbury House Was Quietly Sold to Former DA in Off-Market Deal Just a Year After Kids’ Deaths

Lindsay Clancy is set to face a second murder trial in March 2027—months after the jurors serving in the highly-publicized trial revealed they were deadlocked, forcing the judge to declare a mistrial, after an intense five-week courtroom showdown, during which they heard testimony from dozens of witnesses—and even visited the Massachusetts house where the former nurse is accused of murdering her children.

Clancy, 36, who did not testify in the case but was present in the Plymouth, MA, courtroom for the entirety of the trial, has admitted to taking the lives of daughter Cora, 5, and sons Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan.

However, she pled not guilty to the three first-degree murder charges she is facing, alleging that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time of their deaths. On Sept. 4, the judge declared a mistrial.

Now, it has been revealed that she will be back in court in March 2027 to face a retrial on the same charges.

The trial began on July 31, when the jurors traveled to Clancy's former home in Duxbury, MA, where her three children were found in the basement by their father, Patrick Clancy, on Jan. 24, 2023, having been strangled with exercise bands.

According to the Associated Press, the jury was escorted into the home in groups of six and spent a total of 40 minutes at the property, walking through the entire abode, as well as the yard where Clancy was found after throwing herself out of her bedroom window in an apparent suicide attempt.

The visit took place just a few weeks after the property's new owner, former Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Michael C. Phippen, filed an objection to the juror viewing at a pretrial hearing in June, stating through his lawyer that it would be "massively disruptive" to his day-to-day life.

According to The Patriot Ledger, Phippen's attorney, Peter Maguire, told Judge William Sullivan, that his client's domestic partner would be home at the time of the visit, while also claiming that the jurors arriving at the property with their police escort would upset his pets, as well as his neighbors.

Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague, who is leading the prosecution team in Clancy's trial, noted that Phippen was made aware when he purchased the home that he may have to open it for a jury visit.

While Judge Sullivan overruled Phippen's objection, he put certain restrictions in place for the visit, limiting it to jurors, attorneys, and any court staff that were deemed necessary. He also barred any jurors from opening any closets or touching any of Phippen's personal items.

Phippen—who served as an assistant DA from April 2016 until December 2018, according to his LinkedIn page—purchased the home from Clancy's husband in an off-market deal in January 2024, almost a year to the day after the killings took place.

Property records show that he paid $675,000 for the three-bedroom dwelling, despite the fact that it was estimated to be worth closer to $800,000 at the time.

After Clancy's trial began, social media users began speculating that Phippen was involved in her case in some way, because it was being handled by the same District Attorney's office that he once worked for.

However, Phippen had not worked as an assistant DA for six years by the time he bought the property and his LinkedIn page shows that he established his own legal office in December 2018—and also now works as an attorney for Stark | Lattuca.

Other than the objection that he filed during the pretrial hearing, Phippen is not thought to have had any involvement in Clancy's trial. He has also never publicly discussed how he came to purchase the home.

The former nurse's husband, Patrick, first revealed that he had sold the property in October 2024, when he took part in an interview with The New Yorker, telling the outlet that he had offloaded the residence and relocated to an apartment in New York in the wake of his children's deaths.

He and Clancy had purchased the property for $500,000 in 2018, according to records.

In the interview, Patrick insisted that he "wasn't married to a monster," explaining how his wife had been suffering from anxiety and insomnia, which were brought on by her pregnancy with Callan.

Weeks before the terrible tragedy, he said, she had been hospitalized before being sent home with anti-depressants. Despite all this, he said that he believed that her only diagnosis was a generalized anxiety disorder.

“I wasn’t married to a monster—I was married to someone who got sick,” he told the publication, adding that he had chosen to speak out to prevent further "lies and misinformation" from being spread.

Closing arguments in Clancy's trial took place on Aug. 27, with the former nurse's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, reemphasized his argument that his client was in a "state of psychosis" when her children were killed, insisting that she cannot be found guilty of murder because of a "lack of criminal responsibility."

"This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect, as his honor instructed you, and they’re not going to be able to prove otherwise," he told the jury.

Prosecutor Sprague, however, said that—while there is no denying that Clancy was "suffering from mental illness and that she tried to kill herself"—the jury must decide what her state of mind was on the night that her children died.

"What's on trial here, what the issue is here is what Lindsey Clancy did the night of Jan. 24, 2023, and what her mental state was at the time," she said.

Sprague also claimed that witness testimony heard during the trial indicated that she was a "functioning mom" in the months leading up to the killings.

"You know that she knew the difference between right and wrong during that time," she added. "That’s a rational thought ... She knew it was wrong.

At the end of closing arguments, Judge Sullivan dismissed the jury to begin its deliberations, urging them to "have confidence" in the decision that they were being asked to make—whether Clancy was guilty of first-degree murder or the lesser charge of manslaughter.

"Please have confidence in what you're about to do, all right? I have that confidence in you," he said, according to NBC News. "I don't think I've ever seen a more dedicated group of jurors in any trial that I've ever been involved in."

It is not known exactly how long jury deliberations will take, however some legal experts have suggested that they could last for up to a week.

#5558. HOA Trade Group Presses for More Protections After DC Shooter Targeted Building Manager

The trade group representing homeowners associations is calling for stronger protections after a shooting in Washington, DC, left a community manager dead.

The Community Association Institute said that it would renew efforts support laws that address harassment, threats, and intimidation against community managers before they escalate into violence.

The group had pressed for such legislation in Nevada in 2025 and plans to do so at the federal level in 2027. New Jersey and Minnesota are also reportedly considering some legislation to address harassment.

Thursday's shooting in DC's Logan Circle neighborhood claimed the life of James “Jimmy” Stuart, manager of the Metropole and injured five others. The suspected shooter, Dr. Matt Wade Lambert, a resident of the complex, reportedly was in a dispute with the community over renovations he said damaged his penthouse unit.

“We mourn Jimmy's loss and extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, colleagues, and the entire Metropole community,” the CAI statement reads. “Our thoughts are also with the other victims, residents, and building staff whose lives have been forever changed by this tragedy.”

Lambert was in the middle of a protracted legal dispute with his building's HOA at the time that the shooting happened.

Social median posts reputedly made by him criticized the community for months after he alleged repairs caused water damage and mold. Police say that, after Lambert killed Stuart and injured four others, he subsequently took his own life during a police standoff.

According to legal filings, Lambert had incurred damages topping $100,000 as a result of the HOA's "failure to take corrective action to remedy the moisture accumulation."

“No one should have to fear for their safety while doing their job or serving their community. Community association managers, building staff, and volunteer board members dedicate themselves to maintaining the places millions of Americans call home. They deserve to carry out those responsibilities without threats, harassment, intimidation, or violence,” the statement concludes.

#5556. Inside Warren Buffett’s Surprisingly Modest Property Portfolio as He Steps Down as Berkshire Hathaway Chairman

Billionaire investor Warren Buffett has officially stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway—marking the end of an extraordinary era for the 96-year-old businessman, whose approach to real estate has long been almost as unconventional as his investing career.

Berkshire Hathaway announced on Sept. 18 that Buffett has been named chairman emeritus, effective immediately, while his son, Howard G. Buffett, has been elected chairman of the board. Buffett will remain a director and continue to offer his insight to the company.

“As Chairman Emeritus, Mr. Buffett will remain a member of the Board of Directors and will continue to offer his valued judgment and perspective,” Berkshire said.

The transition comes months after Buffett relinquished his CEO duties to longtime Berkshire executive Greg Abel, completing a carefully planned changing of the guard at the company Buffett has been associated with since 1965. Berkshire Hathaway sold $426 million more in stocks than it bought in the third quarter of 2026 under Abel. It was the 15th quarter out of the past 16 in which the company’s stock sales exceeded its purchases.

"I have served Berkshire since 1965," Buffett said in a letter to shareholders, released alongside the announcement. "Sixty-plus years in, I still have the best job in the world."

Buffett isn't disappearing from Berkshire entirely. As chairman emeritus, he will remain on the company's board, while Howard takes over as chairman and Abel continues running Berkshire as CEO.

"Serving as your Chairman has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I have never taken your trust for granted," Buffett wrote to shareholders while announcing the transition.

While Buffett's decades at Berkshire turned him into one of the wealthiest people on the planet, he has never amassed the sprawling collection of mansions and lavish vacation retreats often associated with billionaire status.

Instead, his property history is surprisingly limited—and anchored by the same Nebraska house he purchased nearly seven decades ago.

At the center of Buffett's real estate story is his longtime residence in Omaha, NE, which he purchased in 1958, when he was 28 years old.

Buffett paid just $31,500 for the five-bedroom property, which was built in 1921 and spans roughly 6,570 square feet. The home, where Buffett and his late wife, Susan Buffett, raised their three children, has remained his primary residence ever since.

Despite the enormous fortune he went on to accumulate, Buffett never traded the residence for a more extravagant billionaire compound.

The house has become closely associated with Buffett's famously restrained approach to spending, particularly when compared with the vast portfolios owned by many of his fellow billionaires.

The property is estimated to be worth about $1.44 million—a substantial increase from its 1958 purchase price, but still a relatively modest sum for a man whose fortune has climbed well into the billions.

Buffett has also made clear over the years that his attachment to the home goes beyond its financial value, repeatedly speaking about his satisfaction with the property rather than seeking out something larger or more luxurious.

Buffett's interest in properties began well before he purchased his Omaha residence.

As a teenager, the future billionaire used $1,200 of his savings to acquire a 40-acre Nebraska farm in 1944, making his first property investment at just 14 or 15 years old, depending on the timing of the purchase relative to his birthday.

Rather than working the land himself, Buffett arranged for a tenant farmer to operate it and split the proceeds—giving the budding investor an early lesson in owning an income-producing asset.

Decades later, he returned to farmland as an investment.

In 1986, Buffett paid $280,000 for a 400-acre Nebraska farm located north of Omaha, as per Architectural Digest.

The purchase further demonstrated his interest in land that could generate tangible, long-term returns rather than property acquired purely for status.

Buffett's land holdings extend beyond Nebraska and include farmland in Arizona and South Africa.

One of the biggest departures from Buffett's otherwise understated real estate history came in 1971, when he and Susan purchased a vacation home in the exclusive Emerald Bay community of Laguna Beach, CA.

They paid $150,000 for the property at a time when the surrounding area was far less developed than it is today.

Buffett later said the decision wasn't driven by an investment strategy—he bought the home because his wife liked it.

The three-level residence offered around 3,600 square feet of living space and six bedrooms, as well as a large deck with ocean views. Despite its coveted location, its interiors were relatively understated, with gray carpeting and white laminate kitchen countertops.

The property became a longtime family getaway, with Buffett and his family spending summers and Christmases there.

As the family expanded, so did their California footprint. Buffett acquired a neighboring residence to accommodate additional guests and connected the two properties with a staircase. He referred to the second house as the family's "annex."

But Buffett's connection to the California retreat began to fade after Susan died in 2004.

He sold the neighboring property in 2005 and ultimately decided to part ways with the original vacation house as well.

Buffett initially put his Laguna Beach residence on the market for $11 million in 2017—46 years after paying $150,000 for it.

By August 2018, the asking price had been reduced to $7.9 million. The property ultimately sold for that amount later that year, according to previous reporting on Buffett's real estate holdings.

Even at the reduced figure, the deal represented a dramatic increase over Buffett's original purchase price.

It also left his property portfolio without one of its few traditional luxury homes.

The Laguna Beach residence stood in stark contrast to the Omaha house that Buffett has steadfastly held on to throughout his ascent from ambitious young investor to one of the most influential figures in American business.

Now, as he relinquishes the Berkshire chairmanship he held for more than five decades, that Omaha residence remains one of the most enduring constants of his life.

She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5555. FAA grounds all domestic flights after reported network outage

The Federal Aviation Administration today grounded all domestic flights in the U.S.

The rare order was issued by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC. It’s an FAA facility in Northern Virginia that is responsible for monitoring air traffic and mitigating potential risks. When ATCSCC identifies issues such as airport congestion, it provides local officials with guidance on how to address them.

The ATCSCC sent today’s ground stop order to all 22 regional air traffic control centers in the U.S. The memo explained that the move was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy elaborated in a post on X that the FAA “issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”

The post didn’t provide any details about the communication issue. According to CBS News, the problem affects a “private communications network” that connects components of the U.S. air traffic control system. The outlet cited sources as saying that an update caused the network to reboot, which in turn led it to crash.

On Tuesday, the FAA announced that it was expanding its use of an artificial intelligence system called SMART. The software analyzes weather patterns, flight paths and related data points to generate air traffic scheduling recommendations. The FAA says that the software is designed to reduce delays and fuel consumption.

The agency last issued a national ground stop in January 2023. It was a response to an issue in the FAA’s NOTAM system, which it uses to notify pilots about hazards such as closed runways. The shutdown lasted about two hours and grounded 9,500 flights.

The current shutdown is already much longer, having started at 3:54 p.m. EST. More than 13,000 flights have reportedly been delayed or canceled. Eurocontrol, an organization that helps European Union member states coordinate air traffic, suspended flights to the U.S. at the request of the FAA.

FAA officials said that inbound international flights will be “handled on a case by case basis.” American Airlines, meanwhile, stated that flights already airborne will proceed to their destinations. The airline reportedly expects the disruption to last all day.

#5554. Sunlight, Weather and Childcare: A Year of New Data on Redfin Home Listings

In 2026, Redfin added information about sunlight, weather, childcare access and more to home listings. Here is everything you need to know about what’s new.

A home listing has always been good at telling you about a house: the square footage, the year it was built, the number of bedrooms. Historically, it has been less good at telling you what living there is actually like. Does the kitchen get morning sunlight? How hot are the summers? Is there a daycare within walking distance?

Those are the questions we set out to answer this year. Multiple new data sets arrived on Redfin in 2026, and they now sit alongside other information that was already there, including scores about a property’s walkability, transit access and climate.

Sunscore shows exactly how much sunlight a home gets

Natural light is one of the hardest things to judge from listing photos or a single showing, and it matters more than you might expect. In a recent Redfin survey, nearly 70% of people said the amount of sunlight in their home affects their satisfaction with where they live, and 11% said it is non-negotiable when searching for a home.

Sunscore is a property-level rating from 0 to 100 that shows how much sunlight a home gets. We co-created it with Shadowmap, a sunlight analysis platform, using 3D modeling that tracks how shadows fall across a home throughout the day and across the seasons. Here are the score breakdowns:

Each score accounts for the home’s 3D shape and structure, surrounding buildings, trees and terrain, the sun’s position throughout the day, and seasonal changes across the year. In other words, it catches the things you would only discover after moving in—like a neighboring building that blocks the afternoon light in winter.

And it is not only about comfort and aesthetics. A home’s sun exposure also says something about its solar potential, which can translate into real savings on energy costs over time.

Weather data helps predict precipitation and heat

Weather turns out to be one of the biggest reasons people move. In a recent Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos, 22% of Americans planning to move to another state said better weather was motivating the move—the most cited reason out of nearly 30 options, ahead of affordability, job opportunities and moving closer to family. Another 21% said concerns about climate change or natural disasters were shaping where they wanted to live.

In July, we partnered with The Weather Company, owner of The Weather Channel app and weather.com, to bring historical weather data to every for-sale listing on Redfin. As our exclusive historical weather provider, it supplies the same data hundreds of millions of people check every month.

Each listing shows ZIP code-level averages for:

Consider this information the difference between the weather on the day you tour a home and the climate you might actually live in.

Childcare data displays daycare and preschool options

For families with young children, childcare access can determine a neighborhood’s fit as much as school boundaries do. However, it’s historically been missing from the home browsing experience. Redfin is the first major real estate portal to partner with Winnie, the largest marketplace for childcare and early education in the U.S., to bring local childcare information to for-sale listings.

Nearby daycare and preschool options now appear on for-sale home listings with details that determine whether a spot is realistic for your family, such as:

Location scores capture everything from wellness access to noise

While Walk Score, Bike Score and Transit Score already existed on home listings, Redfin has expanded these location scores to capture more information about a neighborhood’s vibe using Local Logic data.

Start exploring homes on Redfin.com or the Redfin app to learn everything you’d want to know about a property. Need a place to start? Use Redfin’s conversational search to begin your homebuying journey.
