#5553. Inside Dolly Parton’s Eclectic Property Portfolio and Legacy as the Music Legend Receives Posthumous Grammy Nods

Dolly Parton has left behind a legacy that will continue to grow for years to come.

The music legend—who passed away following a brief battle with cancer at the age of 80 on Aug. 25—was recently honored by the Recording Academy, receiving three posthumous nominations ahead of the 69th Annual Grammy Awards.

The "9 to 5" hitmaker has received two nominations in the Best Country/Duo Group Performance category for "Light of a Clear Blue Morning" with Lainey Wilson, Reba McEntire, Miley Cyrus, and Queen Latifah, and her "Butterfly" collaboration with the Zac Brown Band.

Parton's memoir, "Star of the Show: My Life on Stage," has also received a nod in the Best Audio Book, Narration, and Storytelling Recording category.

As Parton's contributions to the entertainment industry continue to receive their deserved recognition, it's worth noting another talent the country icon showcased throughout her lifetime: property investment.

To honor the country icon, Sept. 25 was hailed as "Dolly Parton day," and is set to be celebrated all across the country with parades, library fairs, community singing, and more.

Many hailed her on-stage talents, her generosity of spirit, and her philanthropic work—something that she demonstrated even through her love of property investment when she donated a longtime home to charity in 2023.

Parton's homes also provided her with a much-needed sanctuary, a place where she was able to retreat from the glare of the public spotlight and savor a private life at home with her husband, Carl Dean, who passed away in March 2025.

Indeed, despite her enormous celebrity profile, the "Jolene" singer still managed to keep her personal life at home largely hidden from the public, particularly when it came to the Brentwood, TN, estate she and Dean shared for years.

Parton also attempted to shield the public from her private health struggles—admitting earlier this year that she had neglected her own wellbeing while caring for Dean at the end of his life, but insisting that she was receiving the help she needed.

It was only revealed after news of her passing was announced that she had been quietly battling cancer, although it is not known what type she had been diagnosed with.

Parton's death was shared in an Instagram post on her personal account, which featured a video filmed by her nephew Bryan Seaver.

"My name is Bryan Seaver, son of Cassie Parton, and I’m representing the Parton and Owens family today announcing the passing of my aunt, Dolly Rebecca Parton Dean, Sister, Sis, and Granny to one generation and Gigi to the next," he said.

"This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality. As her head of security for more than two decades, a role my father Larry held before me, I have imagined the heaviness of this moment but haven’t truly felt it til now."

He added: "Dolly was a farmer, just like her daddy; he farmed the soil, she farmed songs and happiness. Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton because after a life of wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest."

Seaver went on to praise his aunt as someone who "lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents, and countless others." He did not share a cause of death.

"A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family," an obituary shared with Realtor.com® reads.

"Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience. With a seven-decade career, she inspired multiple generations of artists and fans with her music and an unwavering commitment to making the world a better place.

"Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages, and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact."

Hours after the news of her death was revealed, the late singer's family shared that she had spent her final days being treated for cancer.

“Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched. Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand," the statement read.

It continued, "“Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact.

"After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones."

Parton's death marks the end of an extraordinary life and career, one that also saw her build an impressive real estate empire that reflected her Tennessee roots and her superstar status.

Before she became a country music legend with a sprawling real estate portfolio, Parton was one of 12 children growing up in a tiny, rustic cabin tucked away in the Smoky Mountains of East Tennessee.

Parton spent her childhood in a one-bedroom cabin in Locust Ridge, which is situated just outside of Sevierville, TN, and had no electricity or running water, according to records.

Parton was born on Jan. 19, 1946 to Avie Lee Caroline and Robert Lee Parton Sr. in Pittman Center, TN. The songstress and her siblings, Willadeene, David, Coy, Robert Jr., Stella, Cassie, Randy, Larry, Floyd, and twins Freida and Rachel, all grew up in the humble home.

Although the property where she was raised is not available for fans to visit, they can gawk at a replica, which the country star recreated at her Dollywood theme park, which is located in Pigeon Forge, TN, and boasts “original treasures” from her early days.

The replica was constructed by Parton's brother, Bobby, and received a thumbs up from the country star's mom.

Outside, there is a sign that reads, “These mountains and my childhood home have a special place in my heart. They inspire my music and my life. I hope being here does the same for you! Dolly.”

Although fans are not able to tour the grounds of the home where she was raised, they can still enjoy the city sights and view the statue of the country legend at the Sevier County Courthouse’s lawn.

In 2007, Parton and her husband purchased the two-bedroom, two-bathroom property for $1.2 million, but it never served as her main residence.

She then listed the home for sale for $1.4 million in 2014—although records show that it only changed hands in 2023, when it sold for $1.2 million. It's unclear whether Parton quietly offloaded the home before its most recent sale.

Then, in July 2026, the property hit the rental market for $12,000 a month.

Built in 1923, the property sprawls across 1,091 square feet and offers guests a "rare opportunity to lease the legendary former home of Dolly Parton," per the listing, which is held by Richard Schulman of KW Westside Estates.

Situated in the heart of the city's Design District, the fully furnished home perfectly marries vintage charm with modern finishes while placing residents just steps away from Melrose Avenue, Santa Monica Boulevard, trendy restaurants, boutique shopping, and nightlife.

Upon entering the property, guests are greeted with an open floor plan that shows off the expansive living area and kitchen.

The living room boasts plenty of lounging space as well as a cozy fireplace for guests to enjoy on California's chilly evenings.

Moving into the chef's kitchen, there is wraparound marble counter that matches the patterned backsplash. The cuisine center also boasts state-of-the-art appliances.

"Inside, the open-concept living area is filled with natural light and stylish finishes, flowing into an updated kitchen with stainless steel appliances and designer tile," the listing notes.

The primary bedroom features enough room for a king bed and a seating area. It also boasts a glamorous walk-in closet, an en suite bath, and easy access to the lush backyard.

The second bedroom is just as charming thanks to its own private covered balcony. The property also boasts a humble laundry room, complete with seating areas.

Moving outside, there's a perfect entertaining area thanks to an open-air kitchen, a dining area, patio, and covered deck.

"Outdoor spaces include a tropical-inspired patio and covered deck ideal for dining and entertaining," reads the listing, which states that the property is available from Aug. 15, 2026.

The property's description also calls attention to the home's ideal proximity to many of Los Angeles' most interesting communities, stating: "This coveted neighborhood is known for its walkability, creative energy, and long-standing ties to entertainment and cultural history."

Parton and Dean owned a mountainside sanctuary for decades before she decided to gift it over to the Ronald McDonald House Charities of Southern California, which offloaded it in July 2024, according to records.

The same month Dean passed away, the home was put back on the market for $770,000—just one year after it was sold for $585,00 by a charity that the musician donated it to in November 2023.

Just 30 days after being listed, the property was sold for above asking for $800,000.

Before being snapped up, the listing called attention to the singer, describing the home as "Dolly Parton's former Idyllwild retreat—a home as iconic as the legend herself."

"If walls could sing, this charming three-story mountain retreat would be belting out a country classic," the description continues, noting that "nearly everything inside remains just as Dolly left it."

Indeed, the property is filled with many of the personal items and collectibles that sat in the dwelling when Dolly last occupied the home, having used it as an escape for many years—although several modern updates have been made in the eight months since it last changed hands.

The listing noted that the home has been outfitted with a new luxury shingle roof, while an electric vehicle charger was also installed in order to add another layer of convenience, particularly given the home's rather remote location.

Still, the new owners took pains to ensure that Parton's presence remains in every room, with the listing photos revealing that a tea set has been placed on the kitchen table, along with printed instructions addressed "to Dolly, from Steve," which detail how to make the perfect brew.

Elsewhere in the home, various knickknacks, including framed art, collectible plates, and various pieces of china can be seen adorning wooden shelves that run throughout many of the wood-paneled rooms.

A signed photo of Parton in her youth hangs on one of the walls, while one of the bathrooms has been outfitted with a guitar-shaped toilet seat for an added homage to her musical career.

Multiple fireplaces can be found in the living spaces and in the primary bedroom, adding a cozy feel to the 1,800-square-foot property.

Intriguingly, though the home now—quite literally—screams "Dolly Parton," her ownership of the property remained a closely guarded secret for many years and was only brought to light when it was sold in July 2024.

According to property records, the cabin was originally built in 1996, before being sold for just $126,000 in December 1994, which is when Parton is believed to have purchased it.

The "Jolene" hitmaker and Dean snapped up another quaint California house in 2004 and owned it for a decade, before quietly offloading it in 2014, when it sold for $940,000.

Located "in the heart of" the Danish-inspired town of Solvang, the adorable mini compound, which still retains many of the features added by the country music star during her ownership, features three petite properties: a main residence and two rental units.

"This one-of-a-kind property features the country legend's original, authentic 'Wig Room,'" state the listing for the home, which was being sold by its current owner, Chris Lapp.

A plaque stationed at the front of the dwelling proudly signals its impressive heritage as the "former home of Dolly Parton: singer, actress, and American icon," while a stained-glass window above the front door of the property's main residence features the legend's name, along with a butterfly.

However, one of the more eye-catching details at the front of the property has nothing to do with Parton at all, but rather pays tribute to Solvang's longstanding ties to Denmark and Europe: a miniature windmill that has been painted to match the home's distinctive gray, white, and red color palette.

Lapp, who bought the property in 2022 for $1.3 million, explained to SFGate that he'd heard Parton was inspired to purchase the dwelling because it "reminded her of her grandmother's home."

Meanwhile, local resident and business owner Wes Leslie noted that the songstress may well have "hung on to" the dwelling as an "investment property," although he said it has also been rumored that she had family who used the home.

After he bought the home, Lapp spent a great amount of time restoring it to its original glory—and said that he has ensured the tenants who currently live in the rental units have not made any significant changes to its interiors, many of which he believes were curated by Parton herself, including several heart stencils on the walls.

Beyond the special touches that Parton incorporated throughout the home, the property features a number of very unique features across all of its spaces: a three-bedroom, two-bathroom main house, a three-bedroom, two-bathroom rear unit, and a one-bedroom lower unit, all of which offer "private patios and off-street parking."

Upon entry to the main residence, which has a cheerful red front door, visitors will find a bright, airy living room, a small, yet well-equipped kitchen, and three comfortable bedrooms.

The aforementioned "wig room" has been outfitted with an enormous mirror and a built-in vanity perfect for trying on different styles—however, a future occupant could easily use this space as a flex room or office.

Featuring large windows throughout, the property gets ample natural light—while the sun-soaked patio space provides another charming area for guests to relax and kick back.

For those eager to turn their next property investment into a lucrative business opportunity, the home's impressive history as a successful rental will no doubt be one of its most appealing features. According to the listing, it generated a "gross annual income of $116,000" via the rental units—which are both tenant-occupied.

Dean and Parton met on the day that she moved to Nashville when she was just 18 years old—bumping into one another outside of the Wishy Washy Laundromat, according to the Associated Press.

Two years later, the couple tied the knot in a heartfelt ceremony in Ringgold, GA, and opted to stay out of the spotlight, tucking away at their ultraprivate Nashville home where they lived throughout the entirety of their marriage.

The couple spent their days in a five-bathroom property that sits on 63 acres and is informally known as Willow Lake Plantation.

Although it's unknown how much the couple splashed out for the property, Realtor.com estimates that the property is now worth $8.8 million.

In 2014, Parton garnered approval from the Brentwood board to build a barn on the property that "architecturally matches" the other three barns on the residence and doesn't exceed 17 feet in height.

Because of the couple's bid for a private life, little is known about their two-story property.

Although Dean decided to remain out of the public eye, he frequently inspired his wife's career, most notably influencing her hit song "Jolene."

In 2008, Parton told NPR that the song came to life after a bank teller developed a "terrible crush" on Dean.

"She got this terrible crush on my husband, and he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention.

"It was kind of like a running joke between us when I was saying, ‘Hell, you’re spending a lot of time at the bank. I don’t believe we’ve got that kind of money.’ So it’s really an innocent song all around, but sounds like a dreadful one," she explained.

Their marriage has long been a hot topic as Dolly previously revealed that they have an emotionally "open marriage," and that she had even developed feelings for another man.

In 2017, Parton revealed in her book "Dolly on Dolly: Interviews and Encounters with Dolly Parton" that she developed crushes on other men while married.

"I've had crushes on some very unusual men, but Carl knows I'll always come home, and I'm not having sex with these people, I'm just flirting and having fun.

"Yes, it's an open relationship, but not sexually, and I would kill him if I thought he was doing that.' He would shoot me too. At the end of the day, we love each other madly.

"I think so much of it is the fact that we are honest and open, and we have a warped sense of humor!" the singer explained while speaking to BBC.

Parton has also previously revealed that the couple opted to not have kids because she didn't believe "God" meant it for her.

"Since I had no kids, and my husband was pretty independent, I had freedom, so I think a big part of my whole success is the fact that I was free to work."

"I didn't have children because I believed that God didn't mean for me to have kids so everybody's kids could be mine, so I could do things like Imagination Library because if I hadn't had the freedom to work, I wouldn't have done all the things I've done. I wouldn't be in a position to do all of the things I'm doing now," Parton said in a 2020 episode of "The Oprah Conversation"

She added that she has made "sacrifices" but is doing what she is "supposed to do."

"I've made sacrifices, but I think, like I said, I believe what I know I'm supposed to do,” she said of her purpose.

#5551. EXCLUSIVE: Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg Sell Longtime Illinois Home for $2.6 Million

Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg have sold their Illinois residence for $2.6 million—two months after listing the sprawling St. Charles property for $2.8 million.

The singer, 57, and the actress, 53, owned the residence for more than a decade, having purchased it for $1.1 million in 2015.

Built in 1996, the four-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom home spans 7,236 square feet and sits on 1.26 acres.

Described as "an extraordinary St. Charles estate," the property underwent extensive renovations during Wahlberg and McCarthy's time there, with the couple transforming it into a personalized retreat designed for both entertaining and relaxing.

Inside, the home boasts an expansive living room and family room, a formal dining room, den, game room, recreation space, exercise room, and finished lower level.

The kitchen comes with an island, breakfast bar, walk-in pantry, and butler's pantry, while hardwood and stone flooring can be found throughout much of the main level.

Adding to the home's cozy appeal are six fireplaces, which are spread throughout spaces, including the living room, family room, primary bedroom, and basement.

The primary suite serves as its own private retreat and features an en suite bathroom with a soaking tub, double sinks, and a full-body spray shower.

However, some of the property's most impressive amenities can be found in its entertainment and wellness spaces.

The lower level features a bar and recreation areas, while the home also comes equipped with an exercise room and sauna.

"The reimagined English basement offers an entire recreation level with a home theater, sauna, cold plunge, bar, and generous gathering spaces," the listing read.

Outside, the couple created a resort-style setup with a swimming pool, waterslide, waterfall, spa, putting green, expansive patios, and lush landscaping.

Wahlberg and McCarthy also put their own stamp on the property through a number of highly personalized additions made during their renovations, including door handles shaped like their initials and a custom poker table bearing their names.

The property also holds plenty of sentimental value for the pair. In 2019, they revealed that it was the very first home they toured together while searching for a place where they could embrace the small-town lifestyle they envisioned.

Their decision to sell comes after Wahlberg revealed in late 2025 that he and McCarthy had discussed the possibility of relocating to California to be closer to his adult sons, Xavier and Elijah, whom he shares with ex-wife Kim Fey.

At the time, Wahlberg explained that his sons were among the few things that could tempt him back to the West Coast, noting that one of them had repeatedly encouraged him to move closer.

“I have a 24-year-old son and I can’t tell you how many times he’s asked me in the last year to move back to California to be close to him. Probably the only thing that could ever get me back to California is my two sons. And if they keep asking, Jenny and I are going to start going on Realtor.com® and figuring things out," he told People in 2025.

It is not yet clear where Wahlberg and McCarthy plan to settle after selling their Illinois residence.

The couple have called the St. Charles property home for more than a decade, having purchased it one year after tying the knot in 2014.

The $2.8 million listing was held by Cory Jones of eXp Realty.

#5550. AT&T uses agentic AI to reinvent business processes from the ground up

CASE STUDY by Paul Gillin

AT&T Corp. is moving beyond using artificial intelligence to improve employee productivity, increasingly applying autonomous agents to redesign how its business operates. Nearly 500 agentic workflows are already in production, and the telecom giant plans to triple that number next year.

AT&T now processes about 45 billion AI tokens daily across the company, according to Luke Corbin (pictured, below), assistant vice president of digital transformation and AI at AT&T Business. Its agentic AI platform handles more than 1 million transactions monthly. Many of those workflows now operate autonomously, handling tasks ranging from customer provisioning to sales prospecting.

Speaking at an Amazon Web Services Inc. event in Boston earlier this month, Corbin said the company’s approach emphasizes rethinking entire processes rather than simply automating individual tasks. AT&T has moved quickly from experimenting with generative AI to systematically identifying business processes that can be redesigned around agentic capabilities.

At the heart of the transformation is Business Agent Foundry, a group established in early 2025 to work with individual business units. Rather than soliciting isolated automation ideas from employees, the foundry maps business processes using industry frameworks and identifies opportunities to eliminate unnecessary steps, organizational handoffs and legacy application dependencies, Corbin said.

One early initiative involved automating interactions with AT&T’s mainframe computers. Changes to customer fiber installation orders previously required employees to retrieve tickets from queues, manually update records and return them to the workflow.

Agentic automation eliminated portions of that manual process, reducing delays and accelerating service delivery.

“It was kind of cool having some of the most advanced technology talking to some of the oldest that we have,” Corbin said.

In another example, AT&T halved the time required to provision dedicated internet connections in buildings where fiber infrastructure was already installed.

AT&T’s architecture breaks from conventional approaches that build large numbers of independent, specialized agents. Instead, the company maintains a relatively small set of agents that execute business workflows using centrally managed business logic.

“We store the business logic in context or in memory,” Corbin said.

Retrieval agents identify applicable knowledge, while planning agents determine the actions, tools and data needed to complete a task.

“We’ve democratized agents to the point where people can use them for personal productivity, but not to where you would drive business workflows that could touch your customers or materially have an impact on your business,” Corbin said.

Every production workflow initially includes human oversight. Only after accuracy reaches the mid- to high 90% range within a permissible risk profile can agents operate autonomously. Continuous monitoring evaluates performance and detects drift.

Success metrics include labor savings, revenue generation, operating costs and customer satisfaction. Corbin said production AI investments are achieving fivefold returns within a year.

A 151-year-old company that has been using computers since they were invented “is built on a lot of legacy processes and applications,” Corbin said. “The cost of maintaining those applications, training employees to use them and ongoing maintenance is very high. When you can offset some of that with simpler generative workflows, you’ve got a business case that’s built for itself.”

Sales prospecting is one beneficiary. Agents identify promising customers by validating their locations and checking fiber availability before representatives invest time pursuing sales opportunities.

Scaling up those capabilities requires more than AI models. AT&T has had to consolidate fragmented data and provide reliable connectivity across data centers, cloud infrastructure and mobile workers.

“We’ve been through a lot of mergers and acquisitions,” Corbin said. “You can imagine what our data infrastructure looks like.”

Encouraging employees to come forward with ideas for using agents has helped limit resistance from those who worry AI could replace them. So has the opportunity to replace inefficient processes.

“There are a tremendous number of people in the organization who have knowledge and passion about the business process that they used to use but that they didn’t like,” he said.

Corbin said AT&T is now shifting its focus from improving existing processes toward using agents to launch services, enter markets and support new sales channels.

Ultimately, Corbin said responsibility for AI-driven business transformation should be distributed throughout the organization, rather than concentrated in a specialized team like Business Agent Foundry.

“I feel privileged to have the team that I do, but in the long run, my team shouldn’t exist,” he said. “What we do should be completely distributed.”

#5549. October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices

For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended.

The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s  the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year, even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023.

With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices.

Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County.

In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market.

Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand.

National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020.

This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33%, a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before.

All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

“It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.”

Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier.

The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand.

Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters.

With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025.

More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage:

“Buyers are nervous about rates, the economy, and everything they’re seeing in the news– so they need the house and the price to line up perfectly before they’ll make an offer,” said Callie Kimmel, a Redfin Premier agent in Philadelphia. “I’m advising sellers to price just below current market value from day one–and not comps from six months ago, but homes that are listed right now. Otherwise, the home is likely to end up sitting on the market for a bit and selling for less than they hoped. There are a few exceptions: Move-in ready homes in the most desirable neighborhoods are still competitive; in those cases, sellers have the upper hand.”

While total housing supply is growing, fewer sellers are adding new inventory to the pool. New listings of homes for sale fell 1% month over month to the lowest level in more than two years. Would-be sellers are pulling back as homebuying demand slows and sale prices lose steam.

The figures below are based on a list of the 50 most populous U.S. metropolitan areas. Some metros may be removed from time to time to ensure data accuracy. Refer to our metrics definition page for explanations of metrics used in this report. All changes below represent year-over-year changes.

#5548. Noah Kahan Says ‘Life Goes On’ After Grammys Snub—Inside the Vermont Town the Artist Calls Home When He Wants to Escape Nashville

Noah Kahan had a very levelheaded response to his apparent snub from the 69th Annual Grammy Awards.

The singer-songwriter received only one nomination from the organization, securing a nod for best contemporary folk album for “The Great Divide: The Last of the Bugs”—the deluxe edition of his fourth studio album, which explores his complicated feelings toward leaving and eventually returning to his hometown of Strafford, VT.

Kahan’s exclusion from the most prominent categories of the awards show—album of the year, record of the year, and song of the year—has come as a surprise to the music industry.

“Life goes on,” Kahan, 29, said in a Nov. 16 social media post shared shortly after the nominees were announced.

While the statement is vague, it’s an apparent response to a comment he made the night before the highly anticipated nominations were rolled out.

“Whatever happens tomorrow I love you all and I have done everything I’ve ever needed to in my career because of YOUR support,” he wrote in a Nov. 15 X post.

Kahan’s response isn’t entirely surprising, as he’s often shared his candid feelings about the music industry and his newfound fame.

In the 2026 Netflix documentary “Noah Kahan: Out of Body,” the star speaks at length about the ways in which his life has changed as his career has grown. Perhaps one of the most tangible differences was a move to Nashville, TN.

Kahan and his now-wife, Brenna Nolan, whom he has been with for more than a decade, purchased a home in Music City for its proximity to the industry.

While the couple tend to keep their home life private, they did share quite a bit of the home in the documentary, particularly the backyard where their beloved dog, Penny, digs lots of holes, the generously sized porch Kahan enjoys playing guitar on, and the room dedicated to an at-home golf simulator that he joked shows just how “out of touch” he’s become.

At the time the documentary was filmed in 2024, Kahan and Nolan had recently moved to Tennessee.

“We moved from a one-bedroom apartment in Boston to here, and it was really jarring,” Nolan explained.

“It’s a huge change, and it’s a lot to deal with,” Kahan agreed. “We’ve tried to make it feel as much like Vermont as we can.”

The cameras certainly captured a few of the home’s New England-inspired decor, including a funky fawn print runner that decorates the stairs and a gallery wall with a Vermont license plate prominently displayed.

While the home’s beautiful interiors didn’t get quite as much screen time as most interior design-obsessed viewers may have wanted, there is one tiny Easter egg that gives a bit more color: a special thanks to Corey Morris Studios, a Nashville-based firm that specializes in “timeless, functional spaces rooted in traditional style and executed with a modern flair,” per their Instagram account.

Owner Corey Morris thanked Kahan for the shoutout in an April 2026 Instagram post.

“Never expected in a million years to see my name in a Netflix special!” he wrote. “One of the greatest honors of my career has been helping make the family’s Nashville house feel like home.”

Although Kahan did his best to bring the Vermont vibes down South, it seems as if no amount of home decor could replicate what he loves most about Strafford.

During a trip up North, Kahan explained that when he’s in Vermont—which is where he feels most at home—there’s less pressure around his career.

“Being here ... no one’s like, ‘What’s next, Noah?’ You know? It’s never about me as much as it is down in Nashville, which I like,” he said in the documentary. “I do love Nashville. I love the people I have down there. But like, it’s all my career, all the time. Everyone around me is a musician. Everyone around me is working on music. When I’m here, I feel like I’m in my home.”

The special also followed Kahan to New York City, where he previously lived at one point.

“I loved the memories I had here, but I just felt like I wasn’t meant to be in New York,” he explained. “I had expectations of myself. I thought living in a city would make me be social and, like, want to go outside and, like, go do things. It was a place where I was at my most burnt-out.”

In fact, Kahan spends much of the hour and 34 minutes of “Out of Body” grappling with his apparent discomfort just about everywhere he’s lived, given the stark contrast between each of the locations.

“I wonder if I can actually be fully satisfied in any setting at all,” he questioned. He added that he felt “suffocated” by his pre-fame life in Vermont and New Hampshire, but “yearned” for the “simplicity” when he left.

“You can't just escape who you are because you moved to a different place,” he said. “That’s not how it f-cking works.”

Towards the end of the documentary, Kahan and Nolan are seen driving through Strafford, taking a look at homes with “for sale” signs out front.

“We’re trying to make an imminent move back to where we’re from,” he said. “Looking for our next place, and coming back home, basically.”

On that note, it’s not a surprise that the newlyweds have yet to confirm if they’ve purchased a new abode in Strafford.

#5547. Bitcoin Holiday? Thailand Opens the Door to Nationwide Crypto Payments for Tourists

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Thailand is giving crypto holders another reason to book a holiday. Foreign tourists can now convert their digital assets into Thai baht and spend them at shops and restaurants across the country.

The new WORPT payment app connects crypto wallets with Thailand popular QR PromptPay network. Visitors can make purchases without opening a Thai bank account, bringing crypto closer to everyday spending.

The launch comes as Thailand looks for fresh ways to attract international visitors and revive tourism spending. This latest Thailand crypto initiative could turn digital asset holders into another valuable source of tourism revenue.

JUST IN: 🇹🇭 Thailand launches payment system allowing tourists to convert crypto into its national currency for purchases.

WORPT was developed by Wipay and Waan Exchange (Waanx), with support from Tether, the company behind USDT. The service operates under Thailand’s TouristDigiPay regulatory sandbox, overseen by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The system supports cryptocurrency-to-baht conversions, including stablecoins such as USDT and USDC. Tourists deposit supported assets into the platform, convert them into baht, and use their available balance to scan Thai QR PromptPay codes.

The process works with existing merchant payment infrastructure. Restaurants, hotels, and retailers receive Thai baht through their usual payment channels rather than handling cryptocurrency themselves.

Foreign visitors also avoid the usual requirement of having a local Thai bank account. They can complete identity verification through the app before connecting an external digital asset wallet.

WORPT initially charges a 1.5% conversion fee, according to Thai media reports. The company is also preparing Visa prepaid card services, with physical cards planned for November and virtual cards expected in early 2027.

The Mall Group has joined as an early retail partner, making it the first department store group to support the service. Its participation gives WORPT a major retail environment to demonstrate how crypto-funded spending works in practice.

The rollout has an ambitious financial target behind it. Wipay expects WORPT to attract approximately 200,000 users during its first year. The company projects around 15 billion baht, worth $440 million, in spending throughout the initiative’s 18-month trial.

Its target markets include South Korea, Japan, the Middle East and Southeast Asia. These regions offer potential access to travelers who already hold digital assets and could use them to finance international trips.

Thailand’s foreign arrivals are heading toward a second consecutive annual decline, while international tourism revenue has also weakened. But tourism remains an important economic driver, making higher-spending visitors particularly attractive. Crypto holders offer another potential customer base, especially as stablecoins become increasingly common for holding and transferring money internationally.

Having lived in Thailand for three to four years, I know that spending crypto there wasn’t always straightforward. Before services like WORPT, tourists holding crypto generally had to find a way to convert their digital assets into Thai baht before paying for everyday expenses. That could mean going through an exchange, arranging an OTC transaction, withdrawing cash, or transferring money through a local bank account.

These added several steps to something as simple as paying for dinner, booking accommodation, or shopping at a mall. For someone who wanted to live on crypto, the process could quickly become frustrating.

There was another problem: trust. Thailand has also seen scams involving fraudulent crypto OTC brokers, fake exchanges, and people offering attractive conversion rates before disappearing with customers’ funds. Finding someone willing to exchange crypto for baht wasn’t necessarily difficult, but finding someone legitimate was another matter.

#5546. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

#5545. Sellers Vastly Outnumber Buyers as Top Metros Shift Further: Report

Buying house, real estate deal and investment. Tiny woman carrying money in shopping cart to buy family home, agent or broker giving building model and apartment key cartoon vector illustration

Sellers have largely had the upper-hand in the housing market since the pandemic as home prices reached new peaks, giving sellers max equity to see large returns on their investments. Now, as the market is observing some shifts, a new report from Redfin found that seller’s markets are losing ground.

Homebuyers have gained more negotiating power across the country, as Redfin data estimated there were 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October. This was the biggest recorded gap seen since 2013, as well as the sixth month in a row this measure has reached a new record.

Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan said that sellers are “increasingly competing for buyers’ attention,” which has led to more “price reductions, concessions and other savings.”

“First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle—but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate,” he continued. “With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting—and can afford today’s costs—may have an opportunity to make a move.”

Looking at the 50 most populous metros in the U.S., only three were seller’s markets in October. Redfin used “proprietary” data on buyer behavior and MLS listings to estimate the balance of buyers and sellers.

Notably, all three of the seller’s markets were located in the Northeast, where home prices remain higher than other regions. These three markets saw home prices rise 3.3% year-over-year in October, compared to prices increasing only 0.3% in buyer’s markets.

The top of the three seller’s markets was Nassau County, New York, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers, a gap that actually shrank from 28.3% the month prior. The other two markets were Newark, New Jersey (14.3% fewer sellers, down from 17.6% the month prior) and Montgomery County, Pennsylvania (12.1% fewer sellers, down from 20.1% the month prior).

Another difference from September’s data was the loss of a fourth seller’s market—Milwaukee, Wisconsin, which is now balanced between buyers and sellers.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

“A price cut tells you the seller’s first number did not work. It does not tell you what the home is worth,” says one real estate professional. “Some reductions create a legitimate opportunity. Others simply bring an unrealistic price closer to where it should have started.” Read more.

#5544. Unlicensed Plumber Accused of Squatting and Subleasing Rooms in Senior Woman’s Home

A California woman who hired a plumber to make repairs to her home while she was living elsewhere says he took over the property, moved strangers into the house, and locked her out—sparking a two-year nightmare that left her fighting to reclaim her own home.

Jordy Smith, 76, said the man working on the plumbing at her home in San Diego's City Heights neighborhood allegedly transferred the utilities into his own name and began renting out rooms to strangers, pocketing the payments.

Smith and her partner, who owned the home, later discovered the man was not a licensed plumber; but by then, the situation had spiraled out of control. When the couple returned home, they were locked out of their own house and couldn’t get the new occupants to leave, she claimed.

"He just took over and, like, before we knew it, there was like 15 people," Smith told ABC 10News. "Once that happened, it really made it look like to the homeless people that were coming in, that made it look like it was his house.”

The couple tried to confront the people living in the home but Smith said they had locked the door and wouldn’t talk.

"I couldn't sleep at night," Smith said. "I mean, it just seemed like we'd never get back home."

Meanwhile, the property had attracted multiple visits by the police. San Diego police were called to the home more than 30 times between Jan. 1, 2024, and Aug. 17, 2026, for reports of suspected drug activity, trespassing, and smoke coming from the property, according to dispatch records.

In an attempt to get the squatters removed from the property, Smith turned to police and the courts for help but quickly ran into multiple roadblocks.

One of the issues being that Smith’s partner couldn’t find the trust agreement that had been given to him by his mother decades before, which established ownership of the home.

They ultimately listed the home for sale and reached out to the Squatter Squad, a company that helps homeowners remove unauthorized occupants.

“He knew that he was the one that was the successor trustee, but they couldn't find the trust anywhere,” Kimrey Kotchick, co-founder of the Squatter Squad said, referring to Smith’s partner, who owned the property.

He told 10News that squatter squatter disputes are often treated as civil matters, meaning that even when police respond to a home, if someone claims to be a renter, it is often left for the courts to resolve.

Fortunately for Smith and her partner, Kotchick was able to locate the missing ownership documents through the county recorder's office. But it took another five months before the squatters could be legally evicted.

After years of trying to regain access to the house, Smith and her partner were faced with another loss–the home was left in disrepair and many of Smith's cherished antiques were missing.

The couple has since sold the house but Smith says the emotional toll from the ordeal has taken its toll.

Now, Smith is urging other homeowners to keep their ownership documents readily accessible and think twice before leaving contractors unsupervised in their homes.

#5543. Detectify’s Agentic Tooling lets AI agents test suspected flaws in running applications

Swedish application security company Detectify AB today launched Agentic Tooling, a set of tools aimed at letting an organization’s own artificial intelligence agents test whether suspected vulnerabilities can be exploited in running applications.

A new Security Ledger, also part of the launch, is designed to record the evidence behind each test. Detectify is pitching the release at DevSecOps teams that are unsure whether they can trust what their AI agents report.

Detectify customers report that roughly 80% of the findings from their AI-driven static application security testing tools are noise. Under pressure to deliver an answer, an agent can also produce a convincing report about a test it never ran, the company warned.

Even before AI agents enter the picture, many security teams are falling behind. Nine in 10 open critical and high-severity vulnerabilities had stayed exposed for more than 90 days, according to Detectify’s H2 2026 Cyber Hygiene Index. In a study by researchers at Fudan University and Tencent Holdings Ltd., 76% of the static-analysis alerts examined were found to be false positives. Each one took developers 10 to 20 minutes to review.

Through Agentic Tooling, agents can tap the testing engines Detectify has built over more than a decade. Included are payload assessments sourced from its ethical hacker community, attack surface data from its Surface Monitoring product and Alfred, an AI system the company launched in March 2025 to automate tests for known vulnerabilities.

Running in a customer’s own environment, the tools connect to agents through either the Model Context Protocol or a command-line interface. They operate only on the data a customer provides and are said to work with whichever agent the customer already uses.

At the center of the design is loop engineering, an emerging practice of running AI agents in automated, repeating workflows rather than prompting them by hand. Kicking off each loop is a trigger such as a continuous integration run. Whether it comes from a code scan, a bug bounty report, a red team or Detectify’s own attack surface data, each finding is turned into a ticket.

Once an agent picks up a ticket, it reads the relevant code before testing the live application from the outside, as an attacker would. Run continuously, the loop becomes what Detectify calls a verification factory.

The requests sent, the payloads used and the results returned are all logged in the Security Ledger each time an agent uses Detectify’s tools. Written by Detectify rather than the agent, the append-only ledger lets teams separate findings backed by actual tests from unsupported AI conclusions. Any ticket that could cause harm, such as a denial-of-service test, is marked unsafe for a person to decide on.

“Ask an agent to write your code, then ask the same agent whether it’s secure. If it says yes, you don’t actually know,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Rickard Carlsson. There are plenty of examples of agents fabricating proof to please the person asking, according to Carlsson, who described Detectify’s aim as “building proof that an agent can’t fabricate.”

Available on request starting today, Agentic Tooling builds on the Detectify MCP Server that the company announced in May to give AI agents access to its security findings. Investors include Insight Partners, which took a majority stake in October 2024, along with Balderton Capital (UK) LLP, Inventure, First Fellow Partners Oy and SquareOne App Ltd.

#5541. Inside Harry Styles’ Multimillion-Dollar Property Portfolio as He’s Snubbed in the 2027 Grammy Nominations

Harry Styles was 18 when he reportedly bought his first house in North London. More than a decade later, the One Direction alum’s real estate deals have taken him from a gated midcentury retreat in Los Angeles to one of Tribeca’s most star-studded condo buildings.

But some of his biggest purchases have brought him back to the same London neighborhood where he started.

The singer was shut out of the 2027 Grammy nominations on Nov. 16, despite a year in which his fourth studio album—"Kiss All the Time. Disco, Occasionally.— reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and its lead single, “Aperture,” topped the Hot 100.

His previous album, "Harry’s House," won album of the year and best pop vocal album in 2023.

Styles’ first reported purchase was a white-stucco house near Hampstead Heath in 2012, when he was still in One Direction.

According to Architectural Digest, he paid about $4.8 million for the four-bedroom home. High walls shield the property from the street, while French doors and skylights bring light into the roughly 2,300-square-foot interior.

The house also has a home gym and a landscaped back garden.

Several years later, Styles reportedly paid $11.6 million for another house in the area and $5.5 million for the adjoining property. It’s those two homes that he has reportedly moved to combine.

According to The Standard, work had begun on the project in December 2025 after planning approval that spring. The plans call for a cinema and swimming pool on the lower level, as well as a sauna, gym and gallery.

The project also comes with a requirement for some considerably smaller homes. The Standard reported that the approved plans include boxes for bats and hedgehogs and two insect shelters.

Neighbors raised concerns about how the work could affect the light reaching their homes, and Styles’ team submitted revisions in response.

When reports linked Styles to an $8.71 million Tribeca condo in 2017, the purchase had been made through a trust.

The building was already drawing celebrity buyers, including Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds.

While details of Styles’ own interiors have largely stayed private, the building’s shared amenities include an indoor lap pool, private fitness studios, and a landscaped rooftop terrace.

Styles’ first reported California purchase was a $4 million property in the Beverly Hills Post Office area in 2014.

Architect Alejandro Ortiz designed the midcentury compound, where a wood bridge runs through the trees and a pool sits in a courtyard below the surrounding decks.

The grounds also have a detached guesthouse. Styles sold the property off-market for $3,175,000 in 2016, about $825,000 below his purchase price.

His next Los Angeles home traded the wooded setting for city and ocean views above the Sunset Strip.

The roughly 4,400-square-foot Hollywood Hills house had four bedrooms, a home theater, and terraces overlooking the city. Below the main living area, a covered lounge opened to a pool and spa bordered by bamboo.

Styles bought the Hollywood Hills property for about $7 million in 2016 and put it back on the market the following year for nearly $8.5 million.

It took roughly two years and several price cuts to find a buyer. The home was sold for $6 million in 2019, the same year Styles reportedly made the first of the two purchases behind his Hampstead renovation.

#5540. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”

Millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another big expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

But their housing burden fell quickly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

Millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”

That dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze shows up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

How to read the results by age.  Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. #5539. Exaforce’s ExaU lets security staff spin up a personal team of AI agents

Agentic security operations startup Exaforce Inc. today announced the launch of ExaU, a service that lets any security staff member spin up a personal team of artificial intelligence agents.

The new service seeks to move past the first wave of AI agents in security, which Exaforce says were built to offload a single task such as alert triage, risk assessment or penetration testing.

Exaforce argues that as AI absorbs more of the routine work, security staff are now responsible for outcomes that cannot be handed off one task at a time. Added to the mix is that staff are also facing a backlog of tasks, such as checks they mean to run, questions they plan to chase down and briefings owed to senior management.

Leading the list of ExaU features is the ability to create an agent by describing the job in plain language, down to the way a practitioner wants it done. Templates are also available. Each agent is designed to retain decisions, exceptions and past instructions.

To use, a security staff member begins by telling an agent what they are responsible for. The agent then works out what needs doing next and when. The response includes discoveries, questions and recommendations.

The new service also supports sharing agents across a security organization. A chief information security officer’s briefing agent can gather status from the agents used by every team. Exaforce’s own example has a finding setting off a threat hunt, an activity audit and outreach to an employee at the same time. A single assessment then pulls the results of all three together.

Everything runs inside Exaforce on the customer’s own data. With connections to identity providers, cloud services and security telemetry already part of the platform, there are no tokens to mint for ExaU agents. The company’s real-time security knowledge graph is claimed to give each agent an understanding of how systems relate from its first task.

Investigations are carried out by the agents on their own. Under the controls built into ExaU, any action affecting employees, systems or communications requires approval first. Recorded in the Exaforce audit log, every step an agent takes can be reviewed later.

Exabots, the agents Exaforce manages itself, already handle threat detection, alert triage and investigation for every customer on the platform. ExaU is pitched as a complement to that standing workforce. Available now as part of the Exaforce platform, the release follows the September launch of Exaforce AI Security, a kill switch for AI agents that go rogue.

HarbourVest Partners, Peak XV Partners, Mayfield Fund, Khosla Ventures and Seligman Ventures were among the investors in Exaforce’s $125 million Series B round in May. Including that round, total funding since the company’s 2023 founding comes to $200 million.
