#5504. Using AI for listings, where marketing ends and misrepresentation begins

As AI speeds up listing copy and outreach, fewer checkpoints can increase compliance, disclosure, and fair housing risk. The column argues for training, tool controls and meaningful human review.  AI Summary

Over the years, I have seen too many six-figure lawsuits over the words ‘fully-renovated.’

In real estate, a single, seemingly innocuous word or phrase can carry significant legal ramifications and consequences. Descriptions with words including “fully renovated,” “brand new,” “resolved” and “permitted” can and too often do cause years of unexpected, costly litigation for buyers, sellers and even their respective agents more often than people may think. Each word can change a buyer’s understanding of a property and potentially expose a seller, agent, and/or brokerage to liability if the property description no longer matches the reality of the property’s true condition.

By modifying agent and seller property descriptions, AI has inadvertently and undeniably introduced this new layer of exposure and risk to the way agents and their clients do business.

According to the National Association of Realtors 2026 Technology Report, nearly half of Realtors surveyed use AI daily or weekly. Among those agents surveyed who use AI, 75% use it to write listing descriptions and more than half use it for social media posts, emails, or follow-up communications. Other industry research shows that AI adoption may be moving even faster. A 2026 Delta Media survey found that 82% of real estate agents asked use AI to write listing descriptions, which is up from 58% in 2024.

Creating consumer-facing content is the most common use of AI in our industry, helping to craft the words consumers see when considering one of the most important decisions of their lives. At the same time, the biggest challenges brought by AI appear to be growing far more rapidly than the policies and oversight needed to control them.

Surely, most sellers or agents are not deliberately leveraging AI-generated property descriptions to misrepresent properties. The more likely outcome is that an agent will provide accurate information into an AI tool to create a more compelling description, and in turn, the AI tool changes the description to one that is less accurate, thereby exposing an agent and seller to unexpected pitfalls.

For instance, rulings in lawsuits can depend on specific legal issues concerning whether a property is represented, whether by an agent or AI, as partially or fully renovated  or whether a defect was described as repaired or permanently resolved. Lawsuits pertaining to undisclosed permitting issues often concern whether work awaiting approval is described as being in the “final stages of permitting.” The aforementioned are only a few of examples of obstacles an agent or seller may encounter and such compliance issues are challenging companies across industries more often than ever before

The pitfalls of AI are not limited to the sale of real estate. AI has rapidly morphed from an experimental marketing tool to common resource for many areas of business, but especially marketing. Teams use it for everything from drafting copy to generating or cleaning up images to analyzing customer behavior. Work that used to take hours can be done in minutes, if not faster.

Marketing across industries relies on speed that the AI gods are now supercharging. Through their use of artificial intelligence, marketing teams can create dozens of variations of print or digital ads, internal or external emails, social media posts and listing descriptions. The speed at which content is being created naturally removes some of the checkpoints that were in place when it took longer to create or more people were involved in the process.

However, increased efficiency and speed often translate to increased exposure to risk and liability.

A listing description does not have to be completely fabricated to cause a problem. It can come down to the embellishment of one or two words.

Outside of real estate, AI-generated marketing can introduce unsupported claims, make definitive statements from what was originally nuanced, or alter the meaning of disclosures. Without the necessary checkpoints, it can lead to tremendous legal issues.

Accordingly, companies and their employees must take seriously the need for more extensive oversight to stay compliant.

The reason real estate is a great example of how AI can impact compliance is the industry’s significant regulatory requirements, including fair housing laws.

For example, if an agent uses AI to make a listing description more appealing to a certain buyer profile, the language used could potentially implicate protected characteristics or discourage certain groups from being interested in the property without the agent even realizing it.

Even if the agent did not intend to be discriminatory, it is still a compliance issue.

Fortunately, most real estate professionals recognize and consider the risks associated with AI use. A 2026 Realtors Property Resource survey found that 92% of agents surveyed were using or planning to use AI, while 63% identified accuracy of AI-generated content as their top concern.

A common answer to how to lower AI risk is to keep a “human in the loop.” If your strategy includes having someone simply click “approve” before AI-generated content goes out, that’s not enough. Reviewers need to know what they are looking for and the potential risks this content creates, such as unsupported claims, industry-specific advertising rules, and whether it misleads consumers. In addition, has confidential or proprietary information been entered into an AI platform to create the content?

The same principle applies when employees or consumers turn to AI for legal, financial, or other professional advice. I find myself repeating one simple phrase constantly: “AI is not an attorney.”

AI can certainly be useful to organize information, generate ideas, and streamline work processes. But it can never replace professional judgment.

A glaring problematic approach taken by many businesses these days appears to be that they are thinking of AI oversight backwards: providing employees free rein to use it and then creating a policy only after something goes wrong.

Instead, real estate professionals must be armed with tools, policies, and guidelines, and practical guardrails now, before AI continues to be utilized further.

At minimum, businesses should identify which AI tools employees are approved to use, what information can and cannot be entered into them, when AI-generated content requires additional review, and an approval and compliance review for any public-facing content.

The level of oversight must reflect the level of risk. Generating ideas for an article headline is a lot different than using AI to determine which consumers should receive a certain ad. Summarizing notes from an internal brainstorming meeting is not the same as synthesizing confidential client information to create a strategy.

Training is just as important as policy, and it is not enough to send out a document once via email announcing how employees are expected to use AI in the workplace.

The companies that manage AI most effectively will be those where legal and marketing work collaboratively.

Legal and compliance teams need to understand marketing workflows and how AI is being used so they can create guardrails. Marketing needs to involve the legal teams early enough in the process so it’s not an afterthought right before launch.

With the way AI is accelerating work, things are happening too quickly for either to operate in a silo.

We are not trying to slow innovation. We are working to create an environment where teams can move quickly because there are established boundaries and protections to keep risk as low as possible.

AI is going to continue to transform marketing, and businesses should be able to leverage this tool while remaining compliant. At the end of the day, the technology may be new, but accountability is not.

Hila Pooli is general counsel at First Team and a 2026 HousingWire Insider.

#5503. At KubeCon 2026, the illusion of AI control meets the reality of implementation

GUEST COLUMN by Jason English

I revisited Salt Lake City for KubeCon/CloudNativeCon NA 2026 hoping to find practical approaches to delivering customer value amidst a rapidly shifting kaleidoscope of artificial intelligence-driven solutions that are making it increasingly difficult to trust our own eyes and ears.

This year, the host Cloud Native Computing Foundation set its theme as “Cloud Native Without Limits,” and judging by the record-shattering pace of new community developments with more than 230 active projects, and the increasing adoption rate of AI for building and consuming applications, the momentum will only grow.

“If you look back at last year’s KubeCon in Atlanta, OpenClaw was not released yet, MCP was less than a year old, and inference in cloud native was just getting started,” Chris Anzyzcyk, chief technical officer of CNCF, said in the opening remarks.

“We knew we were moving out of a phase where most of the AI compute was used for training and we were going to massively ramp up inference,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director of CNCF. “Just in the last eight months, we’ve seen a 4X increase in inference traffic across the industry. That’s really an incredible increase in the AI footprint. Inference is no longer just an opportunity, it’s now a cloud-native production workload.”

With more than 350K CNCF contributors and 21.2 million cloud-native developers worldwide, fully three-quarters of them are already using AI coding agents, according to the latest State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report, and a show of hands in the room hinted at a much higher presence of AI tooling on the engineer’s desktop.

Likewise, two-thirds of self-described AI-driven organizations are standardizing on Kubernetes and related open-source technologies.

There’s a clear connection here, but AI is not the whole story. Enterprises still need to modernize their application fleets, and deploy, scale, secure and observe their most critical systems, in order to get beyond the AI hype and realize business value.

With an open mind and a skeptical eye, here were some of the interesting new perspectives and vendor solutions I encountered at the show.

With the rapid enterprise rollout of agentic AI, every developer is being challenged to apply human decision insight while working at agent speed, one of the major themes of the show.

Getting there will take more than new technologies, it will also require a lot of collaboration and understanding. The Kubernetes AI Conformance Program launched at KubeCon NA 2025 now has 42 major participating vendors agreeing to consistent standards, and this year there are new Kubernetes AI Certifications for upskilling engineers, whether they are just starting out, or if they are “Golden Kubestronauts” who already passed every course CNCF offers.

“Kubernetes has become the standard API for deploying a workload to a computer, including AI,” said Dan Ciruli, vice president and general manager for cloud native at Nutanix Inc. “The reason, in my opinion, is because the CNCF gave a safe haven for anyone from the smallest startup of two people to the largest companies on Earth to feel safe in donating labor, and code, and IP, and agreeing on things. And that, in turn, gave everybody, from governments to financial services to hot startups, the confidence that they could consume it.”

The firm recently introduced their Nutanix Agent Gateway and an NKP Metal solution that allows Kubernetes clusters and workloads to run on bare metal as well as virtual machines in EKS, AKS or GKE for what they call a “dual-native” experience.

“How are you going to safely and sustainably connect thousands of agents to the systems of record that actually run the business such as customer loyalty or inventory?” asked Matt DeBergalis, CEO, Apollo Graph Inc., doing business as Apollo GraphQL, which supports the popular open source GraphQL query language, presenting a new semantic domain model for deterministically interpreting AI prompts and controls for each record.

Last year CNCF announced a Dynamic Resource Allocation or DRA capability, which unlocked new possibilities for the community to optimize AI workloads running in Kubernetes. This year, sandboxing, or running agents in secure instances to prevent escapes, hijacking and overprovisioning, was the watchword.

Development has moved fast in this area, with two new projects: a Agent Substrate layer contributed by Google that optimizes resource consumption of thousands of agent sandboxes, and OpenShell, an Nvidia Corp.-contributed project for secure sandboxed runtimes.

Startup Apelogic Inc. doing business as HyperShell built an operational agent envelope based on OpenShell that defines guardrails what systems an autonomous agent can access, and what actions it can take, based on the business or system intent the agent was intended to serve.

Cast AI started out as a cloud cost optimization layer for rightsizing clusters on major hyperscalers, but as cloud native infrastructure started taking over enterprise environments, it now finds itself automating and optimizing more AI workloads across CPUs and GPUs, memory and storage. New at KubeCon, their Kimchi code agent governs and deploys application infrastructures from a prompt, which allows developers shift left agentic reviews before production tuning.

Floxdev Inc., which I covered as a startup with their Nix-based lean containerized environment deployments in 2025, put its Flox platform directly in the AI delivery path, giving agents skills to stamp out identical complete environments that include all dependencies, without reproducing any element of the software supply chain inventory that wasn’t intended to change. This moves agentic loops faster with lower compute costs, but the real value is when human engineers can reduce future maintenance and security remediation costs.

This year’s CNCF graduation of the OpenTelemetry project couldn’t come at a better moment, making OTel the lingua franca of application performance, scalability and reliability.

While observability was traditionally considered the domain of engineers and operators, now everyone from data analysts to business executives may be using an LLM or an agent to interact with enterprise applications, potentially changing software, or delivering more agents, in the process.

Splunk, a division of Cisco Systems Inc. has added to its agent observability suite with a specialized language model called Eval-G1 that can run prompt-and-response evals in sub-second times at sub-cent costs, giving engineers the ability to interrupt a faulty response in real time, before it reaches customers. A new Evaluation Studio helps teams generate guardrails in a low-code graphical environment. Also cool, a tokenomics feature (from the recent acquisition of Galileo, which we just covered) that analyzes token spend versus system and business performance metrics.

“It’s been exciting to see how OpenTelemetry, which started out as tens of thousands of adaptors for every application and client, has transitioned with the AI revolution so that now, we have frameworks that just emit OTel natively,” said Morgan McLean, senior director of product management at Splunk and OpenTelemetry co-creator. “So Splunk, and our competitors, can just launch new observability features without putting 30 people on writing new integrations.”

Since a lot of AI projects start out as experiments, observability stalwart Dynatrace LLC has made several moves to meet smaller teams where they are in validating each feature for performance and reliability before enterprise-scale rollouts. It recently acquired Bindplane for OTel-native telemetry pipelines, BlueBox, which gives developers a custom agent for debugging and checks within a coding IDE, and Arize, which maintains the popular Phoenix open-source tool for AI evaluations.

New Relic Inc. released a new Autopilot Kubernetes Agent, a virtual SRE that users can interact with via natural language to look across telemetry and APM data to assess the health of the cluster and application, triage issues with a complete stack trace, and recommend resolutions.

“Especially when you bring agents into your environment, you can’t just take your telemetry and throw it over to a general-purpose LLM, because there are known deterministic patterns and historical insights about Kubernetes we’ve been working to resolve for years,” said Jemiah Sius, vice president of market strategy and developer relations at New Relic.

A lot of the governance difficulty with agents and sandboxes and policies isn’t a technical problem; it is about user experience. Human engineers don’t like being “in the loop” for AI, aka “Meat Proxies,” that continuously pass along approvals. Humans need to be in control, with less toil and more focus on what customers want out of AI applications.

“You can try to create a secure agent sandbox with a policy where everything is disabled by default until a human approves it, but eventually, someone gets tired of being in that approval loop,” said Simone Morellato, senior director of product marketing, Rafay Systems Inc., an AI infrastructure delivery platform used by leading neoclouds. “So you give an agent access to one thing, and eventually you end up giving them access to everything. And at that point, you are back at square one.”

Since I covered Edera Inc. last year, this hardened runtime container vendor is finding new traction in this agentic age by continuing to strengthen the stack from the bottom up, with an agent runtime and OCAP bounded authority that acts as a switchboard for discretely defined agent capabilities, rather than assigning agents credentials or access to MCP servers or APIs or other agents that can be expanded or exploited for another HuggingFace-type incident.

“You can consume capabilities in our system and publish capabilities,” said Edera founder and Chief Technology Officer Alex Zenla. So, for example, for an MCP server, we publish each tool call as a capability. And then when you spin up your agent, you ask for the tool calls that you want. And then it consumes just those capabilities. And we’re able to enforce policies because we have one central pathway for everything to go through, so we can know exactly which agents are using which capabilities.”

“I love the focus on reliability that I’ve seen in the talks and on the floor here at KubeCon,” said Kolton Andrus, CEO of Gremlin Inc., which was there demonstrating their new Foresight AI solution that proactively injects failure conditions in order to identify and remediate failure risks. “You can no longer wait for things to fall apart before taking action. “Everyone’s moving 100 miles an hour trying to keep up with AI, and waking up to the fact that reliability can’t be an afterthought anymore. You can no longer wait for things to fall apart before taking action.”

This being my eighth KubeCon, I keep coming back because the community atmosphere here is unparalleled. There’s a real sense of camaraderie among developers and engineers from wildly different backgrounds, as they build new fundamentals and enjoy the journey toward a cloud native future.

We’ve come a long way over the last eleven years since Kubernetes was introduced. Interoperability, portability, control planes, observability, networking, identity, security and many more mature capabilities are there for the taking. Now AI is being layered on top. But that’s not the story here.

What really impresses me is how much this open source community gives back for the benefit of everyone. All of these people have real jobs to do, and yet they invest their own time, as much as the software industry invests in them.

Indeed, as CNCF’s own Jonathan Bryce said: “Some problems can only be solved in the open.”

Jason English is a principal analyst and chief marketing officer at Intellyx. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE. At the time of writing, Gremlin and Rafay are current Intellyx customers, Dynatrace, New Relic, Nutanix and Splunk are former customers, and none of the other companies mentioned here is an Intellyx customer. #5502. Armada Named a Priority Team Leader in the American SI Exports Program

American Sovereign SI Stack, built on the Armada Sovereign SI Grid, gives allied nations super intelligence infrastructure they own, operate, and control, in months, not years

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Armada, the Sovereign SI Infrastructure company, today was named a priority team leader in the American SI Exports Program, the U.S. Department of Commerce's national accelerator for bringing complete American Super Intelligence (SI) technology solutions to global markets. Armada leads the American Sovereign SI Stack, a consortium with Microsoft and Dell.

Nations and enterprises that want to own their intelligence face the same infrastructure gap. Traditional data centers take years to build, concentrate capacity in single points of failure, and leave critical operations dependent on providers, networks, and jurisdictions they don't control. The result is customers who are delayed, exposed, and dependent.

The American Sovereign SI Stack closes that gap. It is built on the Armada Sovereign SI Grid, a distributed network of factory-built modular data centers that customers own, operate, and run as one system. The stack combines Armada's Galleon and Leviathan modular data centers and the Armada Platform with Dell compute and storage and Microsoft Azure Local and Foundry Local.

Armada and WinDC, the Australian SI factory and colocation provider, have signed a letter of intent to expand their partnership, turning curtailed wind and solar power at Australia's renewable energy sites into tokens. The companies plan approximately 11 MW on Armada Leviathans across five Australian states, a further 230 MW targeted for 2027, and 3 GW across approximately 40 sites in Australia and New Zealand by the end of 2030. They estimate more than $30 billion in project investment, including more than $20 billion in Armada's U.S.-manufactured infrastructure.

Speed, scale, and sovereignty for U.S. allies and partners

Speed to compute. Galleons and Leviathans are fabricated, not constructed. Every unit ships with compute, power, cooling, networking, and connectivity tested as one and goes where power is available now, including stranded, renewable, and behind-the-meter sources. Customers go from available power to new compute capacity in months.

Scale with demand. A customer can start with a single site and grow the grid as demand does, from a suitcase-sized Galleon for inference where the work happens to 10 MW Leviathans for fine-tuning and inference at factory scale. The Armada Platform places workloads, balances load, and fails over across every site from a single control plane.

Sovereignty at every layer. Customers own the hardware, the data, the models, and the keys, inside boundaries they define: in-region, private, or fully air-gapped. The stack is built on an open architecture, so customers keep the partners they already trust.

Through the Program, designated consortia receive U.S. Government advocacy for strategic projects, prioritized processing of export license applications at the Bureau of Industry and Security, and priority access to federal financing referrals. U.S. Government representatives are also available to facilitate deals between trusted foreign buyers and designated consortia. Designated packages, including Armada's, are listed on a "menu" that U.S. and Foreign Commercial Service representatives will offer to foreign buyers globally.

Armada manufactures its American-designed modular data centers in the United States at Galleon Forge One in Gilbert, Arizona, creating the jobs and supply chain the SI race depends on. In Europe, they are manufactured at Galleon Forge Two in Dublin, Ireland.

"Every nation now has to decide who controls its intelligence. Until today, the options were to rent it from someone else or wait years to build it," said Dan Wright, Co-founder and CEO of Armada. "Our Galleons and Leviathans are fabricated, not constructed, so a country can go from signature to sovereign SI in months, not years, on infrastructure it owns, operates, and controls. This designation puts U.S. Government advocacy, export licensing, and financing support behind the allies and partners who make that choice."

Armada is the Sovereign SI Infrastructure company. The Armada Sovereign SI Grid is a distributed network of factory-built modular data centers that organizations own, operate, and run as one system, from suitcase-sized Galleons for inference where the work happens to 10 MW Leviathans for fine-tuning and inference at factory scale, delivering speed to compute, scale with demand, and sovereignty at every layer. Founded in 2022 and headquartered in San Francisco, Armada manufactures its modular data centers at Galleon Forge One in Gilbert, Arizona, and Galleon Forge Two in Dublin, Ireland, in partnership with Johnson Controls.

Armada is backed by investors including Founders Fund, Lux Capital, Shield Capital, 8090 Industries, and M12. Learn more at www.armada.ai.

#5501. Lenders increasingly pull with new credit score model, but few use it for pricing

Bank of America Global Research, using Recursion data, found that more than 170 lenders now pull VantageScore 4.0, but only a small share of conventional loans are actually priced with VS4. In October, 20% of issuance reported a VS4 score, yet roughly 8% of total issuance used VS4 for pricing.  AI Summary

Mortgage lenders are frequently pulling credit scores with VantageScore 4.0, but most of them still price with Classic FICO, according to a new Bank of America Global Research report based on Recursion data. The report, released on Friday, shows that Rocket Mortgage and United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) are driving nearly all of the production actually priced with the new scoring model in the agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS) market.

Since October, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have required that agency MBS pools disclose both Classic FICO and VantageScore 4.0 whenever both are pulled, and to identify which score was used for pricing.

According to Bank of America, 148 sellers in October delivered agency MBS loans for which a VS4 score had been pulled. That figure rose to 173 sellers during the first 10 days of November. But the number of lenders actually pricing loans with VS4 remains much smaller. Only eight lenders sold loans priced with VS4 in September, which rose to 22 in October and 37 to date in November.

In October, 20% of conventional issuance reported a VS4 score, BofA said. Of that subset, 39% used VS4 as the pricing score, which works out to roughly 8% of total conventional issuance. Most of these loans had both scores: 18% of issuance reported both FICO and VS4, while only 2% reported VS4 alone.

Thus far in November, 21% of issuance had VS4 reported and 32% of these loans used VS4 for pricing, or about 7% of total issuance.

Rocket and UWM are the main early adopters on the pricing side. In October, BofA found that Rocket and UWM together accounted for 65% of all loans with a VS4 score pulled. They also were the sources for 95% of loans that used VS4 as their pricing score in the agency MBS market.

Among other lenders that have shown they can pull VS4, just 13% of their production had a VS4 score reported and only 1% of loans actually used VS4 to set prices.

“We think this disconnect largely reflects a gradual ramp-up in operational and infrastructure readiness,” BofA analysts said. “Pulling and reporting an additional score is relatively straightforward, while actually incorporating VS4 into loan pricing likely requires more extensive changes to lenders’ pricing systems and operational infrastructure.”

BofA’s report also notes that loans priced with VS4 have distinctive collateral characteristics. VS4-priced loans tend to have higher average loan balances, a lower share of first-time homebuyers, and higher shares of cash-out and rate-and-term refinance loans.

Among VS4-priced loans where both scores were reported, the VS4 score was on average about 43 points higher than FICO. For FICO-priced loans with both scores present, the two models are broadly comparable, the analysts said.

Because lenders can choose between scores when both are present, the emerging “best-of-two” selection framework is affecting the distribution of published scores. BofA found that among October loans with both scores reported, 24% had FICO scores below 700 and 21% had VS4 scores below 700, but only 17% had a pricing score below 700.

BofA also addressed investor concerns that borrowers in legacy low-FICO pools who have materially higher VS4 scores could see a one-time chance to refinance as markets and pricing grids adjust to VS4.

“We acknowledge that legacy low-FICO pools are exposed to this risk,” the analysts said. “However, newly issued low credit score pools may offer a way to mitigate this risk and potentially access even better convexity collateral.”

According to the report, low credit score pool collateral today generally consists of loans that either have both FICO and VS4 reported with both scores below 700, or are VS4-only loans. Loans with both FICO and VS4 below 700 have already been screened against the risk that a significantly higher VS4 score would give borrowers a one-time refinancing opportunity.

Additionally, a historical analysis indicates that loans with both scores below 700 exhibit better convexity than loans defined only by FICOs below 700.

#5500. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5499. XRP Price at the $1 Line: Should You Sell or Add More to Your Bag?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP is dangerously close to losing the $1 price mark, putting holders in an uncomfortable position. Some holders may see another buying opportunity, while others are wondering if it is time to cut their losses.

The token briefly slipped below $1 this morning, hitting an intraday low close to $0.99 before recovering. XRP subsequently moved to $1.02, leaving its most important psychological support level under pressure.

The selloff has become harder to ignore. XRP has fallen by 37% from its October highs of $1.60, while Bitcoin’s decline has dragged the wider crypto market lower.

For those who bought XRP above $1.30, the current price is making for a difficult decision. Selling now locks in losses, but holding through another breakdown could mean enduring an even deeper correction.

Is XRP approaching an attractive accumulation zone or simply preparing for another leg down?

The $1 level has always been a psychological support that can influence how investors behave. A clean breakdown could trigger stop-loss orders, liquidations, and additional selling from nervous holders. There is also a technical reason to watch this area closely.

XRP previously found support around $0.985 in August. That level is now an important line for buyers attempting to prevent a new 2026 low. Meanwhile, the technical indicators are showing considerable weakness. XRP’s daily RSI recently dropped to 21.5, placing it deep inside oversold territory. Its MACD also remains bearish, suggesting sellers still control short-term momentum.

Retail investors may be increasingly uncomfortable holding XRP through another breakdown, particularly those who entered during the summer rally. Larger holders, meanwhile, could view the correction as an opportunity to accumulate at substantially lower prices.

Exchange balances, whale wallet activity, and large transaction volumes are important indicators to monitor. If large holders begin accumulating while retail investors distribute their tokens, XRP could be approaching a meaningful change in market positioning.

But if selling pressure spreads across both groups, the $1 level could become difficult to defend. But price action is not the only factor XRP investors should consider.

Ripple continues positioning its ecosystem around institutional payments, financial infrastructure, and stablecoin adoption. Its ambitions could eventually strengthen the long-term investment case surrounding XRP.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

While Ripple continues pursuing institutional adoption, another project is betting on a different combination: Bitcoin’s liquidity and Solana-style execution.

Bitcoin Hyper is developing a Bitcoin Layer 2 network that integrates the Solana Virtual Machine (SVM) for faster transactions and smart contract execution. Its architecture aims to combine Bitcoin settlement with high-speed execution, potentially opening the door to DeFi applications and institutional partnerships.

The proposition is interesting: Bitcoin provides the underlying liquidity narrative, while SVM technology aims to deliver the speed needed for more sophisticated financial applications.

The project has raised more than $33 million, showing considerable early fundraising momentum. It also offers 35% APY staking rewards, another incentive for early participants. Holders can stake their tokens and accumulate additional HYPER rather than simply leaving their allocation idle.

The project’s November 26, 2026 presale conclusion and token launch deadline is approaching quickly, potentially creating additional FOMO among early participants. Bitcoin Hyper is another project entering the conversation as the market searches for faster and more scalable blockchain networks.

The next few trading sessions could determine whether XRP stages a recovery or extends its correction. A bullish scenario requires buyers to reclaim $1.10, followed by a stronger move above $1.17. That would suggest selling pressure is finally weakening.

The neutral scenario would involve XRP holding between $1 and $1.10 while investors wait for a clearer market direction. The bearish scenario is more concerning. A sustained daily close below $0.985 could expose XRP to another decline toward $0.90, potentially creating fresh selling pressure.

For now, the XRP price outlook remains fragile. Oversold conditions offer some hope for a relief rally, but buyers need to demonstrate conviction.

Those betting on Ripple’s long-term institutional ambitions may see the current correction as an opportunity. Short-term traders, however, have good reason to wait for confirmation that $1 support can survive.

#5498. CSMI Selected by the State of Connecticut to Support Defense CyberSecure Program CMMC Initiatives

SALEM, N.H., Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CSMI has been selected by the State of Connecticut Office of Manufacturing as an advisory council member for the Defense CyberSecure Program (CT-DCP) to support the development and execution of cybersecurity strategies for Connecticut's defense and aerospace manufacturing sector.

"CSMI brings an exceptional depth of experience, and a demonstrated understanding of what manufacturers need to navigate the CMMC process, with a particular sensitivity to the needs of small to medium-sized manufacturers," said Michelle Hall, Director, Office of Manufacturing, Connecticut Economic and Community Development. "Their technical expertise, industry relationships, and commitment to hands-on support makes them an exceptional choice as an advisory council member and trusted service provider. They will be invaluable in helping Connecticut manufacturers strengthen their cybersecurity capabilities, protect sensitive information, and remain competitive in the defense supply chain."

Through the CT-DCP initiative, CSMI will help manufacturers access funding, training, technical assistance, and qualified cybersecurity providers as they work toward Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) Level 2. Achieving certification is essential for organizations seeking to maintain eligibility for current and future Department of War contracts.

"Our goal is to ensure that Connecticut suppliers have access to a full complement of tools, guidance, and support, necessary to continue their crucial roles in support of the U.S. Warfighter," said Christopher Knox, CSMI Senior Program Manager and CT-DCP Board Member.

CSMI currently conducts cybersecurity uplift programs for suppliers throughout the U.S. Defense Industrial Base (DIB), as well as international partners by performing initial gap analysis and all aspects of supplier preparation for final CMMC accreditation. This skillset will help Connecticut manufacturers strengthen cybersecurity practices, develop policies and procedures, safeguard sensitive data, and meet applicable defense contracting requirements. CSMI, as a Managed Services Provider (MSP), provides CMMC compliant network support services which covers a significant number of CMMC Level 2 controls, enhances network security and greatly impacts achievement of CMMC certification.

About CSMI - Founded in 2002, CSMI provides cybersecurity consultancy, training, mission support, and integrated logistics services to the U.S. Government, defense industry, and allied nations. #5496. CCM leader Brady Mullen’s playbook to win reverse mortgage referrals without a hard sales pitch

At NRMLA Annual in San Antonio, Brady Mullen of CrossCountry Mortgage outlined a plant, nourish, harvest approach to referral development for reverse mortgages. He said LOs should avoid money-focused pitches, validate concerns, and emphasize HECM protections and product basics.  AI Summary

Brady Mullen, divisional business development manager for CrossCountry Mortgage (CCM), spent 20 years as a financial adviser before selling his practice in 2021. In his experience, advisers are rarely trained on how to properly handle real estate, the biggest asset owned by most of their clients.

In seeking to close that gap, Mullen changed his career trajectory by moving into reverse mortgages, first at American Liberty Mortgage before his arrival at CCM in late 2024. He believes that reverse mortgages are the most misunderstood and underappreciated financial tools on the market.

In his work to grow reverse mortgage originations at one of the nation’s largest independent mortgage banks, Mullen has focused on helping loan officers build a steady stream of referral partners, including financial planners, real estate agents and attorneys. That task often meets resistance as referral sources can have the same stigmas about the products as consumers.

At last week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Conference & Expo and San Antonio, Mullen discussed ways to create stronger referral networks. His advice in a nutshell? Take what works and let go of the rest.

Mullen chooses to organize his business development efforts in similar fashion to a farmer growing crops. Planting season involves prospecting and presentations. Fertilizing and nourishing involves follow-up conversations. Harvesting is what occurs when the leads arrive.

Each of the three stages includes its own subprocesses, he explained, a structure that allows a loan officer or branch manager to see where leads stall and fix the bottleneck.

When interacting with a potential referral source, Mullen suggests that reverse mortgage professionals remove words like “educate” and “teach” from their vocabulary. Telling another adult that “I want to educate you” sounds condescending, he said. Instead, offer a benefit that has nothing to do with money, such as continuing education credits.

“If it’s structured as CE, you’ve set the tone to have a discussion that, by design, was created by you to go through the topics in the order that you want and to deliver them with the visuals,” Mullen said.

Mullen told the NRMLA audience that advice on money-making activities should not be part of referral partner conversations. Other professionals know how to make money, he said, and people who have misconceptions about the product are likely to be turned off by the phrase, “Here’s how I can help you make money.” Instead, frame the discussion around providing answers. A financial adviser’s clients, for example, may want to know how they can help their parents or grandparents.

“You’re not trying to sell reverse mortgages. You’re not trying to get a referral. What are you trying to get? A presentation. … That’s all you want. Don’t ask for more because you’ll spoil the opportunity,” he explained.

Once the seeds have been planted and a referral partner has agreed to learn more, reverse mortgages professionals should create an arc with their presentations. The first step is validation, as referrals partners won’t recommend something they won’t use themselves.

With Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs), emphasize the built-in protections of mortgage insurance premiums. Someone clinging to the idea that reverse mortgages are scams needs to know about their robust regulations through the Federal Housing Administration and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

He also calls for simplified language. Describe the HECM product as an expanding line of credit and avoid creating confusion by explaining principal limit factors. Outline the key features that define every reverse mortgage — optional monthly payments, no balloon payments and nonrecourse provisions.

From there, give a clear explanation of the financial benefits for borrowers. He used the example of a $300,000 loan at a 7% rate. A forward mortgage that amortizes over 15 years costs roughly $2,700 a month, while a 30-year loan costs about $2,000 a month. Interest-only options may only trim a few hundred dollars per month.

But reverse mortgages do not require a payment and can be more efficient in terms of opportunity costs. For instance, a 75-year-old couple can take $50,000 out of a retirement account or they can borrow it, but their net worth is still the same. Borrowing offers the potential added benefits of tax savings and asset control.

“Your balance sheet doesn’t care whether it’s paying an opportunity cost or interest. It treats them indifferently. It’s going to reflect both of those equally,” Mullen said. “If we’re not looking at the other side of the balance sheet, we’re missing half the picture, and that’s a lot of picture for an expert to miss.”

For the right type of referral relationship, Mullen believes that longer educational videos, rather than shorter sound bites, are more helpful. He said his most popular YouTube video on reverse mortgages is 43 minutes long. When assigned as homework before a meeting, this type of content allows the referral partner to fully absorb the concepts and share them with clients, who can potentially screen themselves out without further time and energy spent by the LO.

“Would you rather have a distribution list of 1,000 and very little engagement, or a distribution list of 80 and have a lot of engagement? The second is by far more effective,” Mullen said.

#5495. S&P Global Announces Pricing of Public Offering of $750,000,000 Senior Notes due 2031, $600,000,000 Senior Notes due 2034 and $650,000,000 Senior Notes due 2036

NEW YORK, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- S&P Global (NYSE: SPGI) (the "Company") today announced that it has priced a public offering of $750,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 5.600% senior notes due 2031, $600,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 5.800% senior notes due 2034 and $650,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 6.000% senior notes due 2036. BofA Securities, Inc., Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Citigroup Global Markets Inc., Deutsche Bank Securities Inc., J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, Mizuho Securities USA LLC, Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, UBS Securities LLC and Wells Fargo Securities, LLC are acting as joint book-running managers in connection with the offering.

The senior notes due 2031 were priced at 99.841% of their principal amount with a yield to maturity of 5.635%, the senior notes due 2034 were priced at 99.927% of their principal amount with a yield to maturity of 5.814% and the senior notes due 2036 were priced at 99.985% of their principal amount with a yield to maturity of 6.001%. Each series of notes will be an unsecured obligation of the Company and will be guaranteed by its subsidiary, Standard & Poor's Financial Services LLC. The closing of the sale of the notes is expected to occur on or about November 18, 2026, subject to customary closing conditions.

The Company intends to use the net proceeds from the offering for general corporate purposes, which may include, without limitation, funding of possible acquisitions, repayment, redemption or refinancing of indebtedness, capital expenditures, working capital, satisfaction of other obligations or repurchase of the Company's outstanding common stock. The Company may temporarily invest the net proceeds of this offering in short-term, liquid investments until they are used for their stated purpose.

The offering is being made pursuant to an effective automatic shelf registration statement on Form S-3 (File No. 333-299594 and 333-299594-01), filed by the Company with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (the "SEC") on October 23, 2026, and only by means of a prospectus supplement and accompanying prospectus. A preliminary prospectus supplement and an issuer free writing prospectus relating to the offering have been filed, and a final prospectus supplement relating to the offering will be filed with the SEC. Prospective investors should read the preliminary prospectus supplement, the final prospectus supplement (when available), the accompanying prospectus, the issuer free writing prospectus,  and the other documents that the Company has filed with the SEC for more complete information about the Company and the offering. These documents are available at no charge by visiting EDGAR on the SEC website at www.sec.gov. Alternatively, the underwriters or any dealer participating in the offering will arrange to send you the prospectus and the prospectus supplement if you request them by calling BofA Securities, Inc. at 1-800-294-1322 or by emailing [email protected] or Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC at 1-866-471-2526 or by emailing [email protected], Citigroup Global Markets Inc. at 1-800-831-9146, Deutsche Bank Securities Inc. at 800-503-4611 or by emailing [email protected], J.P. Morgan Securities LLC at 212-834-4533, Mizuho Securities USA LLC at 866-271-7403, Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC by emailing [email protected], UBS Securities LLC at (833) 481-0269 or Wells Fargo Securities, LLC at 1-800-645-3751 or by emailing [email protected].

This press release does not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy any of the Company's notes, nor shall there be any sale of the notes in any jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such jurisdiction.
